abstract: Bumptrees are geometric data structures introduced by Omohundro (1991) to provide efficient access to a collection of functions on a Euclidean space of interest. We describe a modified bumptree structure that has been employed as a neural network classifier, and compare its performance on several classification tasks against that of radial basis function networks and the standard mutIi-Iayer perceptron.
originalAbstract: Bumptrees are geometric data structures introduced by Omohundro (1991) to provide efficient access to a collection of functions on a Euclidean space of interest. paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a geometric data structure can serve as a useful neural network classifier. Its starting point is the bumptree, a structure designed to make a collection of functions over Euclidean space efficiently accessible. Here, Euclidean space is the coordinate space in which the inputs are represented.

The authors modify that structure and use it to assign inputs to classes. This connects two concerns that are often considered separately: how functions are organized for efficient access, and how a learning system uses them to make classification decisions. The modification turns the bumptree into a candidate network architecture.

The study compares the resulting classifier with radial basis function networks and a standard multilayer perceptron across several classification tasks. Its contribution is therefore both architectural and comparative: it introduces a modified structure and evaluates it alongside established network types. The supplied abstract identifies the comparison but does not state which method performs best, so it supports no overall ranking.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts a bumptree geometric structure into a classifier and compares it with radial basis function networks and multilayer perceptrons.

title: A Comparative Study of a Modified Bumptree Neural Network with Radial Basis Function Networks and the Standard Multi Layer Perceptron

abstract: This paper presents results from the first use of neural networks for the real-time feedback control of high temperature plasmas in a tokamak fusion experiment. The tokamak is currently the prin(cid:173) cipal experimental device for research into the magnetic confine(cid:173) ment approach to controlled fusion. In the tokamak, hydrogen plasmas, at temperatures of up to 100 Million K, are confined by strong magnetic fields. Accurate control of the position and shape of the plasma boundary requires real-time feedback control of the magnetic field structure on a time-scale of a few tens of mi(cid:173) croseconds. Software simulations have demonstrated that a neural network approach can give significantly better performance than the linear technique currently used on most tokamak experiments. The practical application of the neural network approach requires high-speed hardware, for which a fully parallel implementation of the multilayer perceptron, using a hybrid of digital and analogue technology, has been developed.

paragraphs: The paper presents neural network feedback control of a high-temperature plasma in a tokamak fusion experiment. Strong magnetic fields confine the plasma, and controlling its boundary requires adjustments to the magnetic field structure. The control task concerns both the plasma's position and its shape, with feedback needed within a few tens of microseconds.

Software simulations show significantly better performance from the neural network approach than from the linear technique described as common in tokamak experiments. This motivates using a learned nonlinear approach for the control task. The simulation comparison establishes the reported performance advantage, while the paper also presents results from using neural networks in real-time plasma control.

Meeting the timing requirement requires specialized hardware. The authors develop a fully parallel multilayer perceptron implementation combining digital and analog technology. The work therefore links a control method to the hardware needed to execute it quickly enough. Its practical importance lies in bringing neural computation into a feedback loop whose usefulness depends on both control quality and response time.
summary.tldr: A parallel neural network implementation enables real-time tokamak plasma control, with simulations showing advantages over a conventional linear technique.

title: Real-Time Control of a Tokamak Plasma Using Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce a novel algorithm for factorial learning, motivated by segmentation problems in computational vision, in which the underlying factors correspond to clusters of highly correlated input features. The algorithm derives from a new kind of competitive clustering model, in which the cluster generators compete to ex(cid:173) plain each feature of the data set and cooperate to explain each input example, rather than competing for examples and cooper(cid:173) ating on features, as in traditional clustering algorithms. A natu(cid:173) ral extension of the algorithm recovers hierarchical models of data generated from multiple unknown categories, each with a differ(cid:173) ent, multiple causal structure. Several simulations demonstrate the power of this approach.

A natu(cid:173) ral extension of the algorithm recovers hierarchical models of data generated from multiple unknown categories, each with a differ(cid:173) ent, multiple causal structure. Several simulations demonstrate the power of this approach.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a factorial learning algorithm motivated by segmentation problems in vision. Its underlying factors correspond to groups of strongly correlated input features. This sets up learning as a search for components that can jointly explain an example, allowing multiple factors to contribute to the same observed input.

The key change concerns what cluster generators compete over. In the proposed model, they compete to explain individual features and cooperate to explain whole examples. Traditional clustering, as described in the abstract, organizes this relationship the other way around. By moving competition to the feature level, the method supports an explanation assembled from several feature groups.

An extension recovers hierarchical models when data come from multiple unknown categories, each with its own structure of multiple causes. This adds category organization to the factor-based explanation of individual examples. Several simulations demonstrate the approach. The central contribution is a clustering formulation designed to uncover cooperating factors, together with a hierarchical extension for data whose causal organization differs across categories.
summary.tldr: A clustering algorithm discovers factors by making generators compete over features and cooperate to explain complete examples.

title: Factorial Learning by Clustering Features

abstract: Neural-network ensembles have been shown to be very accurate classification techniques. Previous work has shown that an effec(cid:173) tive ensemble should consist of networks that are not only highly correct, but ones that make their errors on different parts of the input space as well. Most existing techniques, however, only in(cid:173) directly address the problem of creating such a set of networks. In this paper we present a technique called ADDEMUP that uses genetic algorithms to directly search for an accurate and diverse set of trained networks. ADDEMUP works by first creating an ini(cid:173) tial population, then uses genetic operators to continually create new networks, keeping the set of networks that are as accurate as possible while disagreeing with each other as much as possible. Ex(cid:173) periments on three DNA problems show that ADDEMUP is able to generate a set of trained networks that is more accurate than sev(cid:173) eral existing approaches. Experiments also show that ADDEMUP is able to effectively incorporate prior knowledge, if available, to improve the quality of its ensemble.

paragraphs: An ensemble benefits from networks that are accurate individually and make different mistakes. If their errors occur in different parts of the input space, combining them can be more useful than collecting networks with similar behavior. This paper introduces ADDEMUP to search directly for a set with both accuracy and diversity.

ADDEMUP uses a genetic algorithm. It begins with an initial population and applies genetic operators to create additional networks. Selection retains a set whose members are as accurate as possible while disagreeing with one another as much as possible. The quality of the collection therefore explicitly influences which networks survive.

Experiments on three DNA problems show that ADDEMUP generates ensembles more accurate than several existing approaches. Additional experiments show that available prior knowledge can improve ensemble quality. The findings support treating ensemble construction as a joint search problem: a network's usefulness depends both on its own predictions and on how those predictions complement the other members of the set.
summary.tldr: ADDEMUP uses genetic search to build neural ensembles whose members combine individual accuracy with complementary predictions.

title: Generating Accurate and Diverse Members of a Neural-Network Ensemble

abstract: Humans use visual as well as auditory speech signals to recognize spoken words. A variety of systems have been investigated for per(cid:173) forming this task. The main purpose of this research was to sys(cid:173) tematically compare the performance of a range of dynamic visual features on a speechreading task. We have found that normal(cid:173) ization of images to eliminate variation due to translation, scale, and planar rotation yielded substantial improvements in general(cid:173) ization performance regardless of the visual representation used. In addition, the dynamic information in the difference between suc(cid:173) cessive frames yielded better performance than optical-flow based approaches, and compression by local low-pass filtering worked sur(cid:173) prisingly better than global principal components analysis (PCA). These results are examined and possible explanations are explored.

paragraphs: Visual speechreading uses visible speech movements to help identify spoken words. This paper systematically compares ways to represent changes across video frames, asking which visual features support better recognition. It examines both how images are prepared and how their changing content is represented and compressed.

Normalizing images to remove differences in position, size, and rotation within the image plane substantially improves generalization across the representations tested. This result makes image alignment a central finding of the comparison. Changes caused by framing can interfere with the useful speech signal, so controlling those variations helps the recognition system work on new examples.

Two further comparisons favor relatively direct processing choices. Differences between consecutive frames outperform optical-flow representations, and local low-pass filtering outperforms global principal components analysis for compression. Together, the results show that a more elaborate motion description or global compression method need not yield better speechreading. The paper examines these outcomes and possible explanations, with the strongest conclusions tied to the representations actually compared.
summary.tldr: Image normalization, consecutive-frame differences, and local filtering perform strongly in a systematic visual speechreading comparison.

title: Dynamic Features for Visual Speechreading: A Systematic Comparison

abstract: Determining the relationship between the activity of a single nerve cell to that of an entire population is a fundamental question that bears on the basic neural computation paradigms. In this paper we apply an information theoretic approach to quantify the level of cooperative activity among cells in a behavioral context. It is possible to discriminate between synergetic activity of the cells vs . redundant activity, depending on the difference between the infor(cid:173) mation they provide when measured jointly and the information they provide independently. We define a synergy value that is pos(cid:173) itive in the first case and negative in the second and show that the synergy value can be measured by detecting the behavioral mode of the animal from simultaneously recorded activity of the cells. We observe that among cortical cells positive synergy can be found, while cells from the basal ganglia, active during the same task, do not exhibit similar synergetic activity. titay,tishby}@cs.huji.ac.il Permanent address: Institute of Computer Science and Center for Neural Computa(cid:173) tion, The Hebrew University, Jerusalem 91904, Israel.

paragraphs: A population of neurons may convey information that cannot be recovered by simply adding what each neuron communicates individually. This paper measures that distinction during monkey behavior. It uses information theory to distinguish synergy, where joint activity adds information, from redundancy, where cells repeat information.

The authors define a signed synergy measure from the difference between joint and independent information. They estimate it by predicting the animal’s behavioral mode from simultaneously recorded neural activity. This ties the comparison to a concrete behavioral variable rather than measuring correlation alone.

Positive synergy appears among the observed cortical cells, while basal-ganglia cells active during the same task do not show a similar pattern. The contribution is both a measurement framework and a regional comparison in the studied recordings. It demonstrates why the informational role of a neural population can depend on interactions among cells, not only on the response of each cell in isolation.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic behavioral decoding reveals synergistic activity in the studied cortical cells but not comparable basal-ganglia recordings.

title: Synergy and Redundancy among Brain Cells of Behaving Monkeys

abstract: In hyperspectral imagery one pixel typically consists of a mixture of the reflectance spectra of several materials, where the mixture coefficients correspond to the abundances of the constituting ma(cid:173) terials. We assume linear combinations of reflectance spectra with some additive normal sensor noise and derive a probabilistic MAP framework for analyzing hyperspectral data. As the material re(cid:173) flectance characteristics are not know a priori, we face the problem of unsupervised linear unmixing. The incorporation of different prior information (e.g. positivity and normalization of the abun(cid:173) dances) naturally leads to a family of interesting algorithms, for example in the noise-free case yielding an algorithm that can be understood as constrained independent component analysis (ICA). Simulations underline the usefulness of our theory.

We assume linear combinations of reflectance spectra with some additive normal sensor noise and derive a probabilistic MAP framework for analyzing hyperspectral data. As the material re(cid:173) flectance characteristics are not know a priori, we face the problem of unsupervised linear unmixing. The incorporation of different prior information (e.g. positivity and normalization of the abun(cid:173) dances) naturally leads to a family of interesting algorithms, for example in the noise-free case yielding an algorithm that can be understood as constrained independent component analysis (ICA). paragraphs: A hyperspectral image pixel can combine the reflectance spectra of several materials. The mixture coefficients represent how abundant those materials are within the pixel. This paper develops a probabilistic approach to recovering that mixture structure when the materials' reflectance characteristics are not known in advance, making the task unsupervised.

The model assumes that spectra combine linearly and that sensor noise is additive and normally distributed. Under these assumptions, the authors derive a maximum a posteriori framework. Prior information can encode requirements such as positive abundances and normalization, bringing constraints on material proportions directly into the estimation problem.

Different choices of prior information produce a family of algorithms rather than a single fixed procedure. In the noise-free case, one resulting algorithm can be interpreted as constrained independent component analysis. Simulations support the usefulness of the theory. The contribution is a common probabilistic formulation that connects unmixing assumptions, abundance constraints, and algorithm design, with the connection to constrained ICA stated specifically for the noise-free setting.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic framework uses linear-mixture assumptions and abundance priors to derive algorithms for unsupervised hyperspectral unmixing.

title: Unmixing Hyperspectral Data

abstract: We investigate the short term .dynamics of the recurrent competition and neural activity in the primary visual cortex in terms of information pro(cid:173) cessing and in the context of orientation selectivity. We propose that af(cid:173) ter stimulus onset, the strength of the recurrent excitation decreases due to fast synaptic depression. As a consequence, the network shifts from an initially highly nonlinear to a more linear operating regime. Sharp orientation tuning is established in the first highly competitive phase. In the second and less competitive phase, precise signaling of multiple ori(cid:173) entations and long range modulation, e.g., by intra- and inter-areal con(cid:173) nections becomes possible (surround effects). Thus the network first ex(cid:173) tracts the salient features from the stimulus, and then starts to process the details. We show that this signal processing strategy is optimal if the neurons have limited bandwidth and their objective is to transmit the maximum amount of information in any time interval beginning with the stimulus onset.

paragraphs: This paper proposes that recurrent competition in primary visual cortex changes during the response to a stimulus. Fast synaptic depression weakens recurrent excitation after stimulus onset. In the proposed account, this moves the network from an initially strongly nonlinear operating regime toward a more linear one.

The two phases serve different processing roles. Strong early competition establishes sharp orientation tuning and extracts salient stimulus features. Later, weaker competition permits precise signaling of multiple orientations and modulation through longer-range connections, including surround effects. The network therefore begins with prominent features and subsequently processes more detail, rather than maintaining the same competitive strength throughout its response.

The authors show that this processing strategy is optimal under a specified information-transmission objective and constraint. Neurons must have limited bandwidth, and the objective is to maximize information transmitted over any time interval beginning at stimulus onset. This conditional result gives the proposed temporal sequence a computational rationale. It does not make weakening competition universally optimal; the conclusion depends on the stated bandwidth restriction and objective.
summary.tldr: A proposed decline in cortical competition supports early feature selection followed by detail processing, with conditional information-theoretic optimality.

title: Recurrent Cortical Competition: Strengthen or Weaken?

abstract: Discrete Fourier transforms and other related Fourier methods have been practically implementable due to the fast Fourier transform (FFT). However there are many situations where doing fast Fourier transforms without complete data would be desirable. In this pa- per it is recognised that formulating the FFT algorithm as a belief network allows suitable priors to be set for the Fourier coe(cid:14)cients. Furthermore e(cid:14)cient generalised belief propagation methods be- tween clusters of four nodes enable the Fourier coe(cid:14)cients to be inferred and the missing data to be estimated in near to O(n log n) time, where n is the total of the given and missing data points. This method is compared with a number of common approaches such as setting missing data to zero or to interpolation. It is tested on generated data and for a Fourier analysis of a damaged audio signal.

paragraphs: The fast Fourier transform makes Fourier analysis computationally practical, but many signals contain missing observations. This paper asks how to retain efficient Fourier computation when the data are incomplete. Its approach treats the transform as a probabilistic inference problem in which both the Fourier coefficients and missing signal values can be estimated.

The authors express the FFT algorithm as a belief network, allowing priors to be placed on its Fourier coefficients. They then use generalized belief propagation between clusters containing four nodes. This arrangement enables inference with a running time near n log n, where n counts both observed and missing data points.

The method is compared with common ways of handling gaps, including replacing missing values with zero or interpolation. It is tested on generated data and on Fourier analysis of a damaged audio signal. The contribution combines prior information, estimation of missing values, and efficient transform structure in one procedure, making incomplete-data Fourier analysis the direct target of inference.
summary.tldr: A belief-network formulation of the FFT jointly estimates Fourier coefficients and missing data in near n log n time.

title: Generalised Propagation for Fast Fourier Transforms with Partial or Missing Data

abstract: Log-concavity is an important property in the context of optimization, Laplace approximation, and sampling; Bayesian methods based on Gaus- sian process priors have become quite popular recently for classification, regression, density estimation, and point process intensity estimation. Here we prove that the predictive densities corresponding to each of these applications are log-concave, given any observed data. We also prove that the likelihood is log-concave in the hyperparameters controlling the mean function of the Gaussian prior in the density and point process in- tensity estimation cases, and the mean, covariance, and observation noise parameters in the classification and regression cases; this result leads to a useful parameterization of these hyperparameters, indicating a suitably large class of priors for which the corresponding maximum a posteriori problem is log-concave.
originalAbstract: Log-concavity is an important property in the context of optimization, Laplace approximation, and sampling; Bayesian methods based on Gaus- sian process priors have become quite popular recently for classification, regression, density estimation, and point process intensity estimation. Here we prove that the predictive densities corresponding to each of these applications are log-concave, given any observed data. We also prove that the likelihood is log-concave in the hyperparameters controlling the mean function of the Gaussian prior in the density and point process in- tensity estimation cases, and the mean, covariance, and observation noise parameters in the classification and regression cases; this result leads to a useful parameterization of these hyperparameters, indicating a suitably large class of priors for which the corresponding maximum a posteriori problem is log-concave.

paragraphs: The paper establishes log-concavity results for Gaussian-process-based methods in classification, regression, density estimation, and point-process intensity estimation. Log-concavity means that taking the logarithm of the relevant function produces a concave function. This mathematical shape property matters for optimization, Laplace approximation, and sampling, connecting the results to several computational aspects of Bayesian inference.

The authors prove that the predictive densities in the applications they consider are log-concave for any observed data. They also establish likelihood results for particular hyperparameters. In density and point-process intensity estimation, these concern parameters controlling the prior mean. In classification and regression, they concern mean, covariance, and observation-noise parameters.

The hyperparameter results lead to a useful parameterization and identify a substantial class of priors for which maximum a posteriori estimation is log-concave. The contribution thus reaches beyond the shape of predictions to the structure of parameter estimation. Its practical significance lies in supplying mathematical properties that can inform how these Gaussian process inference problems are formulated and computed.
summary.tldr: The paper proves log-concavity properties for predictions and specified hyperparameter estimation problems in several Gaussian process methods.

title: Log-concavity Results on Gaussian Process Methods for Supervised and Unsupervised Learning

abstract: We present a method for performing transductive inference on very large datasets. Our algorithm is based on multiclass Gaussian processes and is effective whenever the multiplication of the kernel matrix or its inverse with a vector can be computed sufﬁciently fast. This holds, for instance, for certain graph and string kernels. Transduction is achieved by varia- tional inference over the unlabeled data subject to a balancing constraint.
originalAbstract: We present a method for performing transductive inference on very large datasets. Our algorithm is based on multiclass Gaussian processes and is effective whenever the multiplication of the kernel matrix or its inverse with a vector can be computed sufﬁciently fast. This holds, for instance, for certain graph and string kernels. Transduction is achieved by varia- tional inference over the unlabeled data subject to a balancing constraint.

paragraphs: Transductive learning uses the particular unlabeled examples that need predictions as part of inference. Scaling that approach to large multiclass datasets is difficult if every operation requires handling a dense kernel matrix. This paper develops a Gaussian-process-based method that exploits faster matrix-vector computations.

Variational inference is performed over the unlabeled data under a balancing constraint. The algorithm is effective when multiplying a vector by the kernel matrix or its inverse is sufficiently cheap. Certain graph and string kernels satisfy that requirement, providing concrete settings where the method can operate at scale.

The contribution is a computational formulation of multiclass transduction whose feasibility depends on kernel operations rather than only on the number of examples. It highlights an important design route: structured similarity computations can make a rich probabilistic model practical on large datasets when generic dense linear algebra would be too costly.
summary.tldr: A variational multiclass Gaussian-process method scales transduction by exploiting fast kernel or inverse-kernel matrix-vector products.

title: Large-Scale Multiclass Transduction

abstract: We characterize the sample complexity of active learning problems in terms of a parameter which takes into account the distribution over the input space, the specific target hypothesis, and the desired accuracy.
originalAbstract: We characterize the sample complexity of active learning problems in terms of a parameter which takes into account the distribution over the input space, the specific target hypothesis, and the desired accuracy.
title: Coarse sample complexity bounds for active learning

abstract: A classic debate in cognitive science revolves around understanding how children learn complex linguistic rules, such as those governing restrictions on verb alternations, without negative evidence. Traditionally, formal learnability arguments have been used to claim that such learning is impossible without the aid of innate language-specific knowledge. However, recently, researchers have shown that statistical models are capable of learning complex rules from only positive evidence. These two kinds of learnability analyses differ in their assumptions about the role of the distribution from which linguistic input is generated. The former analyses assume that learners seek to identify grammatical sentences in a way that is robust to the distribution from which the sentences are generated, analogous to discriminative approaches in machine learning. The latter assume that learners are trying to estimate a generative model, with sentences being sampled from that model. We show that these two learning approaches differ in their use of implicit negative evidence -- the absence of a sentence -- when learning verb alternations, and demonstrate that human learners can produce results consistent with the predictions of both approaches, depending on the context in which the learning problem is presented.

paragraphs: This paper examines how people could learn linguistic restrictions without being explicitly told which sentences are wrong. It focuses on implicit negative evidence: a sentence never appearing in the input. Whether that absence is informative depends on assumptions about how the sentences a learner encounters were generated.

The authors contrast two approaches to learning verb alternations. One seeks to identify grammatical sentences in a way that remains reliable across input distributions, resembling discriminative learning. The other estimates a generative model and assumes observed sentences are sampled from it. Under the latter view, what fails to appear can carry information through the assumed sampling process.

The paper shows that these approaches use absent sentences differently. It also demonstrates that human learners can produce behavior consistent with either approach, depending on how the learning problem is presented. This helps explain why formal arguments about learnability and successful statistical models can appear to disagree: they make different assumptions about the input distribution. The human findings connect those assumptions to the context in which learning occurs.
summary.tldr: Human use of absent linguistic examples can match generative or discriminative learning predictions depending on context.

title: Differential Use of Implicit Negative Evidence in Generative and Discriminative Language Learning

abstract: Online learning algorithms have impressive convergence properties when it comes to risk minimization and convex games on very large problems. However, they are inherently sequential in their design which prevents them from taking advantage of modern multi-core architectures. In this paper we prove that online learning with delayed updates converges well, thereby facilitating parallel online learning.
originalAbstract: Online learning algorithms have impressive convergence properties when it comes to risk minimization and convex games on very large problems. However, they are inherently sequential in their design which prevents them from taking advantage of modern multi-core architectures. In this paper we prove that online learning with delayed updates converges well, thereby facilitating parallel online learning.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms process information through a sequence of updates. They have strong convergence properties for risk minimization and convex games, including very large problems. This paper focuses on a computational obstacle: a design that depends on successive updates is inherently sequential, which makes it difficult to take advantage of multicore hardware.

The authors analyze online learning when updates are delayed. Such a delay separates the availability of an update from the moment when the algorithm can use it. The central question is whether this weaker timing arrangement preserves useful convergence behavior. Their result proves that online learning with delayed updates can still converge well.

This matters because accepting delayed updates facilitates parallel online learning. Computation can be organized around a less restrictive update schedule while retaining a theoretical basis for progress toward the learning objective. The title captures this tradeoff: slower arrival of individual updates can enable a more parallel learning process. The stated contribution is the convergence analysis that supports this computational possibility.
summary.tldr: Online learning can retain good convergence with delayed updates, providing a theoretical basis for parallel execution.

title: Slow Learners are Fast

abstract: Contrast statistics of the majority of natural images conform to a Weibull distribution. This property of natural images may facilitate efficient and very rapid extraction of a scenes visual gist. Here we investigate whether a neural response model based on the Weibull contrast distribution captures visual information that humans use to rapidly identify natural scenes. In a learning phase, we measure EEG activity of 32 subjects viewing brief flashes of 800 natural scenes. From these neural measurements and the contrast statistics of the natural image stimuli, we derive an across subject Weibull response model. We use this model to predict the responses to a large set of new scenes and estimate which scene the subject viewed by finding the best match between the model predictions and the observed EEG responses. In almost 90 percent of the cases our model accurately predicts the observed scene. Moreover, in most failed cases, the scene mistaken for the observed scene is visually similar to the observed scene itself. These results suggest that Weibull contrast statistics of natural images contain a considerable amount of scene gist information to warrant rapid identification of natural images.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether simple statistics of image contrast capture information people use to recognize a scene at a glance. Contrast patterns in most natural images follow a Weibull distribution. The researchers use this regularity to build a model linking image statistics to measured brain responses, testing whether those statistics convey a scene’s overall visual character.

During a learning phase, 32 participants viewed brief presentations of 800 natural scenes while their EEG activity was recorded. The researchers combined these measurements with the images’ contrast statistics to construct a response model across participants. For new scenes, the model predicted EEG responses; identification then involved matching those predictions against the response actually observed.

The model identified the viewed scene in almost 90 percent of cases. When it failed, the selected scene was usually visually similar to the actual one. Together, these findings suggest that Weibull contrast statistics retain substantial information about scene gist. They support the usefulness of this statistical representation for rapid identification without establishing that it fully explains human scene recognition.
summary.tldr: A model linking natural-image contrast statistics to EEG responses identified viewed scenes in almost 90 percent of cases.

title: A Biologically Plausible Model for Rapid Natural Scene Identification

abstract: We study the problem of segmenting specific white matter structures of interest from Diffusion Tensor (DT-MR) images of the human brain. This is an important requirement in many Neuroimaging studies: for instance, to evaluate whether a brain structure exhibits group level differences as a function of disease in a set of images. Typically, interactive expert guided segmentation has been the method of choice for such applications, but this is tedious for large datasets common today. To address this problem, we endow an image segmentation algorithm with 'advice' encoding some global characteristics of the region(s) we want to extract. This is accomplished by constructing (using expert-segmented images) an epitome of a specific region - as a histogram over a bag of 'words' (e.g.,suitable feature descriptors). Now, given such a representation, the problem reduces to segmenting new brain image with additional constraints that enforce consistency between the segmented foreground and the pre-specified histogram over features. We present combinatorial approximation algorithms to incorporate such domain specific constraints for Markov Random Field (MRF) segmentation. Making use of recent results on image co-segmentation, we derive effective solution strategies for our problem. We provide an analysis of solution quality, and present promising experimental evidence showing that many structures of interest in Neuroscience can be extracted reliably from 3-D brain image volumes using our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper addresses extracting particular white matter structures from three-dimensional diffusion tensor brain images. Such segmentation supports studies that compare structures across groups, including groups defined by disease. Expert-guided segmentation can provide the desired regions, but repeating that interaction across large datasets is tedious.

The proposed method summarizes expert-segmented examples into an epitome of a target region. This epitome is a histogram of feature descriptors: a compact account of the kinds of image features that characterize the structure. When segmenting a new image, the algorithm adds constraints encouraging the extracted foreground to agree with that histogram. Expert knowledge therefore influences the overall composition of the selected region.

The authors develop combinatorial approximation algorithms for incorporating these constraints into Markov Random Field segmentation, drawing on image co-segmentation results. They analyze solution quality and present promising experimental evidence that many neuroscience structures can be extracted reliably from three-dimensional volumes. The approach connects reusable region-level guidance with a formal segmentation procedure.
summary.tldr: Feature histograms learned from expert segmentations guide automated extraction of specific white matter structures from three-dimensional brain images.

title: Epitome driven 3-D Diffusion Tensor image segmentation: on extracting specific structures

abstract: We consider least-squares regression using a randomly generated subspace G P\subset F of finite dimension P, where F is a function space of infinite dimension, e.g.~L 2([0,1]^d). G P is defined as the span of P random features that are linear combinations of the basis functions of F weighted by random Gaussian i.i.d.~coefficients. In particular, we consider multi-resolution random combinations at all scales of a given mother function, such as a hat function or a wavelet. In this latter case, the resulting Gaussian objects are called {\em scrambled wavelets} and we show that they enable to approximate functions in Sobolev spaces H^s([0,1]^d). As a result, given N data, the least-squares estimate \hat g built from P scrambled wavelets has excess risk ||f^* - \hat g|| \P^2 = O(||f^ ||^2_{H^s([0,1]^d)}(\log N)/P + P(\log N )/N) for target functions f^ \in H^s([0,1]^d) of smoothness order s>d/2. An interesting aspect of the resulting bounds is that they do not depend on the distribution \P from which the data are generated, which is important in a statistical regression setting considered here. Randomization enables to adapt to any possible distribution. We conclude by describing an efficient numerical implementation using lazy expansions with numerical complexity \tilde O(2^d N^{3/2}\log N + N^2), where d is the dimension of the input space.

paragraphs: The paper studies least-squares regression in a finite-dimensional space built from random features. Each feature combines basis functions from an infinite-dimensional function space using independent Gaussian coefficients. For multiresolution wavelet combinations, the resulting features are called scrambled wavelets: randomness mixes information across scales before the regression model is fitted.

The authors show that these features can approximate targets in Sobolev spaces, which describe function smoothness. For targets with smoothness greater than half the input dimension, the excess-risk bound has two competing terms. One decreases with the number of features and depends on target smoothness; the other increases with the number of features relative to the sample size. Both include a logarithmic sample-size factor.

A notable property is that these bounds do not depend on the data-generating distribution. Within the stated smoothness setting, randomization therefore supports guarantees across possible input distributions. The paper also describes an efficient implementation using lazy expansions, connecting the approximation analysis to a concrete computational approach.
summary.tldr: Random Gaussian mixtures of wavelets support least-squares regression guarantees independent of the input distribution under a stated smoothness condition.

title: Scrambled Objects for Least-Squares Regression

abstract: Given a set V of n vectors in d-dimensional space, we provide an efficient method for computing quality upper and lower bounds of the Euclidean distances between a pair of the vectors in V . For this purpose, we define a distance measure, called the MS-distance, by using the mean and the standard deviation values of vectors in V . Once we compute the mean and the standard deviation values of vectors in V in O(dn) time, the MS-distance between them provides upper and lower bounds of Euclidean distance between a pair of vectors in V in constant time. Furthermore, these bounds can be refined further such that they converge monotonically to the exact Euclidean distance within d refinement steps. We also provide an analysis on a random sequence of refinement steps which can justify why MS-distance should be refined to provide very tight bounds in a few steps of a typical sequence. The MS-distance can be used to various problems where the Euclidean distance is used to measure the proximity or similarity between objects. We provide experimental results on the nearest and the farthest neighbor searches.

paragraphs: Computing distances between high-dimensional vectors can be costly when many pairs must be considered. This paper develops a way to begin with inexpensive upper and lower bounds on Euclidean distance, then progressively improve them. The initial bounds use a proposed quantity called MS-distance, built from each vector's mean and standard deviation.

For n vectors with d coordinates, calculating those summary statistics takes O(dn) time. Once that preprocessing is complete, the initial bounds for a pair take constant time to obtain. The method also supports refinement: the bounds tighten monotonically and reach the exact Euclidean distance within d refinement steps.

The authors additionally analyze a random ordering of refinement steps. That analysis provides a justification for expecting tight bounds after only a few steps in a typical sequence, rather than promising that behavior for every pair. Experiments examine nearest- and farthest-neighbor search, illustrating applications where progressively narrowing a distance interval can help assess which objects are closest or most distant.
summary.tldr: Mean and standard deviation yield cheap Euclidean-distance bounds that tighten monotonically to the exact distance.

title: Convergent Bounds on the Euclidean Distance

abstract: Most existing Multiple-Instance Learning (MIL) algorithms assume data instances and/or data bags are independently and identically distributed. But there often exists rich additional dependency/structure information between instances/bags within many applications of MIL. Ignoring this structure information limits the performance of existing MIL algorithms. This paper explores the research problem as multiple instance learning on structured data (MILSD) and formulates a novel framework that considers additional structure information. In particular, an effective and efficient optimization algorithm has been proposed to solve the original non-convex optimization problem by using a combination of Concave-Convex Constraint Programming (CCCP) method and an adapted Cutting Plane method, which deals with two sets of constraints caused by learning on instances within individual bags and learning on structured data. Our method has the nice convergence property, with specified precision on each set of constraints. Experimental results on three different applications, i.e., webpage classification, market targeting, and protein fold identification, clearly demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning works with collections of instances called bags. Many existing methods assume independence and identical distributions at the instance or bag level, yet applications can contain additional relationships among those entities. This paper develops a framework that incorporates such structure instead of discarding information carried by dependencies.

The resulting optimization problem is non-convex. To solve it, the authors combine a concave-convex constraint programming method with an adapted cutting-plane method. The algorithm handles two sets of constraints: those arising from instances within individual bags and those arising from the additional structured data. Its convergence property includes specified precision for each constraint set.

Experiments cover webpage classification, market targeting, and protein fold identification. The authors report advantages over the state-of-the-art methods evaluated in these applications. The contribution joins a richer learning formulation with an optimization procedure designed for its two sources of constraints. The findings support using relationships among instances and bags when those relationships carry information relevant to the learning task.
summary.tldr: A structured multiple-instance learning framework incorporates dependencies and solves its non-convex objective with a combined constraint-handling algorithm.

title: Multiple Instance Learning on Structured Data

abstract: We describe a set of fast, tractable methods for characterizing neural responses to high-dimensional sensory stimuli using a model we refer to as the generalized quadratic model (GQM). The GQM consists of a low-rank quadratic form followed by a point nonlinearity and exponential-family noise. The quadratic form characterizes the neuron's stimulus selectivity in terms of a set linear receptive fields followed by a quadratic combination rule, and the invertible nonlinearity maps this output to the desired response range. Special cases of the GQM include the 2nd-order Volterra model (Marmarelis and Marmarelis 1978, Koh and Powers 1985) and the elliptical Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson model (Park and Pillow 2011). Here we show that for canonical form" GQMs, spectral decomposition of the first two response-weighted moments yields approximate maximum-likelihood estimators via a quantity called the expected log-likelihood. The resulting theory generalizes moment-based estimators such as the spike-triggered covariance, and, in the Gaussian noise case, provides closed-form estimators under a large class of non-Gaussian stimulus distributions. We show that these estimators are fast and provide highly accurate estimates with far lower computational cost than full maximum likelihood. Moreover, the GQM provides a natural framework for combining multi-dimensional stimulus sensitivity and spike-history dependencies within a single model. We show applications to both analog and spiking data using intracellular recordings of V1 membrane potential and extracellular recordings of retinal spike trains."

paragraphs: Understanding how a neuron responds to a high-dimensional stimulus requires capturing which stimulus patterns matter and how they combine. The generalized quadratic model represents this through linear receptive fields, a low-rank quadratic combination, an invertible response transformation, and exponential-family noise. It can also incorporate dependencies on earlier spikes.

For canonical-form models, the authors derive approximate maximum-likelihood estimators by spectrally decomposing the first two response-weighted moments. The derivation uses an expected log-likelihood quantity and extends moment-based approaches such as spike-triggered covariance. For Gaussian noise, they obtain closed-form estimators across a large class of non-Gaussian stimulus distributions.

The reported estimators are highly accurate while requiring much less computation than full maximum likelihood. This makes the approach useful for fitting multidimensional stimulus sensitivity without paying the full optimization cost. Applications include analog membrane-potential recordings from V1 and retinal spike-train recordings. These examples show the framework being used with both continuous neural measurements and discrete spiking responses, connecting its statistical construction to different forms of neural data.
summary.tldr: Spectral estimators fit generalized quadratic neural-response models accurately at much lower computational cost than full maximum likelihood.

title: Spectral methods for neural characterization using generalized quadratic models

abstract: In this paper we explore how machine learning techniques can be applied to the discovery of efficient mathematical identities. We introduce an attribute grammar framework for representing symbolic expressions. Given a grammar of math operators, we build trees that combine them in different ways, looking for compositions that are analytically equivalent to a target expression but of lower computational complexity. However, as the space of trees grows exponentially with the complexity of the target expression, brute force search is impractical for all but the simplest of expressions. Consequently, we introduce two novel learning approaches that are able to learn from simpler expressions to guide the tree search. The first of these is a simple n-gram model, the other being a recursive neural-network. We show how these approaches enable us to derive complex identities, beyond reach of brute-force search, or human derivation.

paragraphs: The paper explores whether learning can help discover mathematical expressions that compute the same quantity more efficiently. Its objective is analytical equivalence to a target expression together with lower computational complexity. This makes the search about finding useful mathematical identities, rather than merely producing expressions that resemble the target on selected inputs.

An attribute grammar represents expressions as trees assembled from mathematical operators. Searching these trees directly becomes impractical because the number of possible combinations grows exponentially with expression complexity. The authors therefore introduce two ways to learn from simpler expressions and use that knowledge to guide searches for more complex ones.

One approach uses an n-gram model, while the other uses a recursive neural network. Both supply learned guidance to the symbolic tree search. The authors report that these approaches derive complex identities they describe as beyond the reach of brute-force search or human derivation. The contribution is a combination of structured symbolic representation and learned search guidance for finding computationally cheaper equivalent expressions.
summary.tldr: Learned models guide symbolic tree search toward analytically equivalent mathematical expressions with lower computational complexity.

title: Learning to Discover Efficient Mathematical Identities

abstract: The paper studies transition phenomena in information cascades observed along a diffusion process over some graph. We introduce the Laplace Hazard matrix and show that its spectral radius fully characterizes the dynamics of the contagion both in terms of influence and of explosion time. Using this concept, we prove tight non-asymptotic bounds for the influence of a set of nodes, and we also provide an in-depth analysis of the critical time after which the contagion becomes super-critical. Our contributions include formal definitions and tight lower bounds of critical explosion time. We illustrate the relevance of our theoretical results through several examples of information cascades used in epidemiology and viral marketing models. Finally, we provide a series of numerical experiments for various types of networks which confirm the tightness of the theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: Information spreading through a network can undergo a transition from limited propagation to a super-critical cascade. This paper studies both the influence of an initial set of nodes and the timing of that transition in continuous-time diffusion. These questions connect how widely a contagion spreads with when its behavior changes.

The authors introduce the Laplace Hazard matrix and show that its spectral radius characterizes influence and explosion-time dynamics in the diffusion processes they study. This supplies a mathematical link between a matrix associated with the process and its spreading behavior. Using that link, they derive tight influence bounds that do not rely on an asymptotic limit.

The paper also formally defines critical explosion time, develops tight lower bounds for it, and examines the point after which contagion becomes super-critical. Examples drawn from epidemiology and viral marketing illustrate the theory. Numerical experiments across different network types support the tightness of the bounds, connecting the mathematical analysis to observed cascade behavior.
summary.tldr: The Laplace Hazard matrix links continuous-time cascade influence and explosion timing to a spectral quantity, enabling tight theoretical bounds.

title: Anytime Influence Bounds and the Explosive Behavior of Continuous-Time Diffusion Networks

abstract: We propose a general purpose variational inference algorithm that forms a natural counterpart of gradient descent for optimization. Our method iteratively transports a set of particles to match the target distribution, by applying a form of functional gradient descent that minimizes the KL divergence. Empirical studies are performed on various real world models and datasets, on which our method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods. The derivation of our method is based on a new theoretical result that connects the derivative of KL divergence under smooth transforms with Stein’s identity and a recently proposed kernelized Stein discrepancy, which is of independent interest.

paragraphs: Stein Variational Gradient Descent is a general-purpose method for approximating a target probability distribution. It represents the approximation with a collection of particles and repeatedly moves those particles to better match the target. This makes it a distributional counterpart to gradient descent: the object being improved is a probability approximation rather than a single parameter estimate.

The updates take the form of functional gradient descent aimed at minimizing KL divergence, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. The derivation rests on a theoretical connection between how KL divergence changes under smooth transformations, Stein's identity, and a kernelized Stein discrepancy. That connection supplies the mathematical basis for choosing particle movements.

Empirical studies on several real-world models and datasets found the method competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches. The reported evidence supports its usefulness across the evaluated inference tasks, without claiming that it consistently surpasses every alternative. The contribution combines a practical particle-based inference algorithm with a theoretical relationship that the authors identify as independently useful.
summary.tldr: Stein Variational Gradient Descent moves particles using functional gradient descent on KL divergence to approximate a target distribution.

title: Stein Variational Gradient Descent: A General Purpose Bayesian Inference Algorithm

abstract: This work provides a framework for addressing the problem of supervised domain adaptation with deep models. The main idea is to exploit adversarial learning to learn an embedded subspace that simultaneously maximizes the confusion between two domains while semantically aligning their embedding. The supervised setting becomes attractive especially when there are only a few target data samples that need to be labeled. In this few-shot learning scenario, alignment and separation of semantic probability distributions is difficult because of the lack of data. We found that by carefully designing a training scheme whereby the typical binary adversarial discriminator is augmented to distinguish between four different classes, it is possible to effectively address the supervised adaptation problem. In addition, the approach has a high “speed” of adaptation, i.e. it requires an extremely low number of labeled target training samples, even one per category can be effective. We then extensively compare this approach to the state of the art in domain adaptation in two experiments: one using datasets for handwritten digit recognition, and one using datasets for visual object recognition.

paragraphs: This paper studies supervised domain adaptation when only a few labeled examples are available from the target domain. The goal is to learn a shared representation that makes the two domains difficult to distinguish while aligning their semantic content. With very little target data, achieving appropriate alignment and separation of semantic distributions becomes especially difficult.

The proposed framework uses adversarial learning with a redesigned discriminator. Instead of the typical binary discrimination task, the discriminator distinguishes four classes within a carefully constructed training scheme. This change supports the simultaneous objectives of confusing domain identity and preserving semantic alignment in the learned embedding.

The authors report that adaptation can be effective with extremely few labeled target examples, including one per category. Here, adaptation speed refers to the number of labeled target samples required. They compare the method extensively with state-of-the-art domain adaptation approaches in handwritten digit recognition and visual object recognition experiments. The findings support the possibility of effective supervised adaptation with sparse target labels, without making a universal one-example guarantee.
summary.tldr: A four-class adversarial training scheme supports domain adaptation with very few labeled target examples, sometimes just one per category.

title: Few-Shot Adversarial Domain Adaptation

abstract: Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is an important task in many machine learning applications such as the prediction phase of low-rank matrix factorization models and deep learning models. Recently, there has been substantial research on how to perform MIPS in sub-linear time, but most of the existing work does not have the flexibility to control the trade-off between search efficiency and search quality. In this paper, we study the important problem of MIPS with a computational budget. By carefully studying the problem structure of MIPS, we develop a novel Greedy-MIPS algorithm, which can handle budgeted MIPS by design. While simple and intuitive, Greedy-MIPS yields surprisingly superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches. As a specific example, on a candidate set containing half a million vectors of dimension 200, Greedy-MIPS runs 200x faster than the naive approach while yielding search results with the top-5 precision greater than 75%.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search finds vectors that score highly against a query under an inner product. This operation appears in prediction for low-rank matrix factorization and deep learning models. The paper focuses on a practical requirement: performing the search within a computational budget while retaining useful results.

The authors develop Greedy-MIPS by examining the structure of the search problem. Its design explicitly accommodates a budget, making the trade-off between computation and search quality part of the method. This matters because a fast search procedure is more useful when its computational effort can be adjusted to the resources available.

The reported experiments show strong performance relative to existing approaches. In one example with half a million candidate vectors, each with 200 dimensions, Greedy-MIPS is 200 times faster than naive search while achieving top-five precision above 75%. This illustrates a substantial speed–quality trade-off in that example; it does not establish the same speedup or precision for every collection of vectors.
summary.tldr: Greedy-MIPS makes maximum inner product search adjustable to a computational budget, with strong reported speed–quality trade-offs.

title: A Greedy Approach for Budgeted Maximum Inner Product Search

abstract: Matrix factorization (MF) is one of the most popular techniques for product recommendation, but is known to suffer from serious cold-start problems. Item cold-start problems are particularly acute in settings such as Tweet recommendation where new items arrive continuously. In this paper, we present a meta-learning strategy to address item cold-start when new items arrive continuously. We propose two deep neural network architectures that implement our meta-learning strategy. The first architecture learns a linear classifier whose weights are determined by the item history while the second architecture learns a neural network whose biases are instead adjusted. We evaluate our techniques on the real-world problem of Tweet recommendation. On production data at Twitter, we demonstrate that our proposed techniques significantly beat the MF baseline and also outperform production models for Tweet recommendation.
originalAbstract: Matrix factorization (MF) is one of the most popular techniques for product recommendation, but is known to suffer from serious cold-start problems. Item cold-start problems are particularly acute in settings such as Tweet recommendation where new items arrive continuously. In this paper, we present a meta-learning strategy to address item cold-start when new items arrive continuously. We propose two deep neural network architectures that implement our meta-learning strategy. The first architecture learns a linear classifier whose weights are determined by the item history while the second architecture learns a neural network whose biases are instead adjusted. We evaluate our techniques on the real-world problem of Tweet recommendation. On production data at Twitter, we demonstrate that our proposed techniques significantly beat the MF baseline and also outperform production models for Tweet recommendation.

This is the item cold-start problem, and it becomes especially pressing when new items arrive continuously, as Tweets do. The paper addresses this setting with a meta-learning strategy designed to adapt recommendation models using an item's history.

The authors introduce two deep neural network architectures that implement this strategy in different ways. One learns a linear classifier whose weights depend on the item history. The other learns a neural network and adjusts its biases instead. Both make the item's history part of how the predictor itself is configured, giving the system a way to adapt its recommendations as information about an item becomes available.

The evaluation uses production data from Twitter. Both the matrix-factorization baseline and production Tweet recommendation models are outperformed by the proposed techniques, with significant gains reported over matrix factorization. These findings support the usefulness of the meta-learning approach in the continuously arriving-item setting examined by the paper.
summary.tldr: Two meta-learning architectures adapt predictors using item history and outperform matrix factorization and production models on Tweet recommendation data.

title: A Meta-Learning Perspective on Cold-Start Recommendations for Items

abstract: We propose a new randomized coordinate descent method for a convex optimization template with broad applications. Our analysis relies on a novel combination of four ideas applied to the primal-dual gap function: smoothing, acceleration, homotopy, and coordinate descent with non-uniform sampling. As a result, our method features the first convergence rate guarantees among the coordinate descent methods, that are the best-known under a variety of common structure assumptions on the template. We provide numerical evidence to support the theoretical results with a comparison to state-of-the-art algorithms.

We provide numerical evidence to support the theoretical results with a comparison to state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper develops a randomized coordinate descent method for a broadly applicable class of convex optimization problems. Coordinate descent updates selected parts of the variables, making the choice and treatment of those parts central to the algorithm. The paper targets convergence guarantees for problems that can include nonsmooth structure.

Its analysis combines four techniques through the primal-dual gap, a quantity connecting a candidate solution with its dual counterpart. Smoothing makes the problem easier to handle, acceleration improves progress, homotopy changes the smoothing treatment as optimization proceeds, and non-uniform sampling chooses coordinates with unequal probabilities. The contribution lies in bringing these ingredients together within one analysis.

Under a variety of common structural assumptions, the authors obtain convergence rates matching the best known for those settings and describe these as the first such guarantees among coordinate descent methods. Numerical comparisons with state-of-the-art algorithms support the theoretical results. The guarantees depend on the applicable problem structure, so the contribution is a collection of strong rates across supported settings.
summary.tldr: A randomized coordinate method combines smoothing, acceleration, homotopy, and non-uniform sampling to obtain strong structure-dependent convergence guarantees.

title: Smooth Primal-Dual Coordinate Descent Algorithms for Nonsmooth Convex Optimization

abstract: We analyze the information-theoretic limits for the recovery of node labels in several network models. This includes the Stochastic Block Model, the Exponential Random Graph Model, the Latent Space Model, the Directed Preferential Attachment Model, and the Directed Small-world Model. For the Stochastic Block Model, the non-recoverability condition depends on the probabilities of having edges inside a community, and between different communities. For the Latent Space Model, the non-recoverability condition depends on the dimension of the latent space, and how far and spread are the communities in the latent space. For the Directed Preferential Attachment Model and the Directed Small-world Model, the non-recoverability condition depends on the ratio between homophily and neighborhood size. We also consider dynamic versions of the Stochastic Block Model and the Latent Space Model.

For the Latent Space Model, the non-recoverability condition depends on the dimension of the latent space, and how far and spread are the communities in the latent space. For the Directed Preferential Attachment Model and the Directed Small-world Model, the non-recoverability condition depends on the ratio between homophily and neighborhood size. We also consider dynamic versions of the Stochastic Block Model and the Latent Space Model.

paragraphs: This paper studies when a network contains insufficient information to recover the labels of its nodes. It considers several ways networks can be generated, including stochastic block, exponential random graph, latent space, directed preferential attachment, and directed small-world models. The focus is on fundamental non-recoverability conditions, rather than the performance of a particular detection algorithm.

The relevant obstacles depend on the network model. For the stochastic block model, the condition involves the probabilities of edges within and between communities. For the latent space model, it depends on the space's dimension and on how far apart and how spread out the communities are. These results link recovery limits to the mechanisms that make communities distinguishable in each model.

For directed preferential attachment and directed small-world models, the non-recoverability condition depends on the ratio of homophily to neighborhood size. The analysis also covers dynamic versions of the stochastic block and latent space models. Together, these results identify model-dependent barriers that an algorithm cannot overcome merely by using a different computational strategy when the stated non-recoverability conditions hold.
summary.tldr: The paper derives model-dependent conditions under which network node labels cannot be recovered from the available information.

title: Information-theoretic Limits for Community Detection in Network Models

abstract: We study a safe reinforcement learning problem in which the constraints are defined as the expected cost over finite-length trajectories. We propose a constrained cross-entropy-based method to solve this problem. The method explicitly tracks its performance with respect to constraint satisfaction and thus is well-suited for safety-critical applications. We show that the asymptotic behavior of the proposed algorithm can be almost-surely described by that of an ordinary differential equation. Then we give sufficient conditions on the properties of this differential equation to guarantee the convergence of the proposed algorithm. At last, we show with simulation experiments that the proposed algorithm can effectively learn feasible policies without assumptions on the feasibility of initial policies, even with non-Markovian objective functions and constraint functions.

At last, we show with simulation experiments that the proposed algorithm can effectively learn feasible policies without assumptions on the feasibility of initial policies, even with non-Markovian objective functions and constraint functions.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with constraints expressed as expected costs over trajectories of finite length. The objective is to learn policies that satisfy those constraints. This formulation defines safety through an expectation over trajectories, so the stated constraint concerns aggregate cost rather than a separate guarantee for every individual trajectory.

The proposed algorithm adapts the cross-entropy method and explicitly monitors how well its policies satisfy the constraints. The authors analyze its long-run behavior through an ordinary differential equation, showing that this equation describes the algorithm asymptotically with probability one. They then give sufficient properties of the equation that guarantee algorithmic convergence.

Simulation results show that the method can learn feasible policies without requiring the initial policies to be feasible. The experiments also include objectives and constraints that are non-Markovian, meaning their evaluation can depend on trajectory history. These findings support the method’s ability to handle constrained learning beyond settings where a safe starting policy or purely current-state cost description is available.
summary.tldr: A constrained cross-entropy algorithm learns policies under expected trajectory-cost constraints, with sufficient convergence conditions and supporting simulations.

title: Constrained Cross-Entropy Method for Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The classic Mallows model is a widely-used tool to realize distributions on per- mutations. Motivated by common practical situations, in this paper, we generalize Mallows to model distributions on top-k lists by using a suitable distance measure between top-k lists. Unlike many earlier works, our model is both analytically tractable and computationally efficient. We demonstrate this by studying two basic problems in this model, namely, sampling and reconstruction, from both algorithmic and experimental points of view.

We demonstrate this by studying two basic problems in this model, namely, sampling and reconstruction, from both algorithmic and experimental points of view.

paragraphs: The classic Mallows model describes probability distributions over complete rankings, represented as permutations. In practical settings, however, the available ranking may include only a leading subset of items. This paper extends the model to top-k lists, allowing the probabilistic object being modeled to match that partial-ranking form directly.

The extension uses a distance measure suited to comparing top-k lists. Choosing such a distance is central because the model needs a coherent way to express differences between these incomplete rankings. The authors develop a formulation that is both analytically tractable and computationally efficient, addressing two requirements that can be difficult to satisfy together.

They investigate sampling and reconstruction through both algorithms and experiments. These problems examine the model from complementary directions: generating lists according to it and recovering modeled structure from data. The contribution is therefore more than a definition of a distribution. It supplies an extension of Mallows with mathematical and computational tools for working with top-k observations, demonstrating that partial rankings can support a practical probabilistic modeling framework.
summary.tldr: A tractable extension of the Mallows model handles top-k rankings and supports efficient sampling and reconstruction.

title: Mallows Models for Top-k Lists

abstract: Data parallelism can boost the training speed of convolutional neural networks (CNN), but could suffer from significant communication costs caused by gradient aggregation. To alleviate this problem, several scalar quantization techniques have been developed to compress the gradients. But these techniques could perform poorly when used together with decentralized aggregation protocols like ring all-reduce (RAR), mainly due to their inability to directly aggregate compressed gradients. In this paper, we empirically demonstrate the strong linear correlations between CNN gradients, and propose a gradient vector quantization technique, named GradiVeQ, to exploit these correlations through principal component analysis (PCA) for substantial gradient dimension reduction. GradiveQ enables direct aggregation of compressed gradients, hence allows us to build a distributed learning system that parallelizes GradiveQ gradient compression and RAR communications. Extensive experiments on popular CNNs demonstrate that applying GradiveQ slashes the wall-clock gradient aggregation time of the original RAR by more than 5x without noticeable accuracy loss, and reduce the end-to-end training time by almost 50%. The results also show that \GradiveQ is compatible with scalar quantization techniques such as QSGD (Quantized SGD), and achieves a much higher speed-up gain under the same compression ratio.

paragraphs: Training convolutional networks across multiple workers requires combining their gradients, and communication can consume much of the potential speedup. Existing scalar compression techniques can work poorly with ring all-reduce because their compressed gradients cannot be aggregated directly. This paper treats compatibility with aggregation as a central requirement for useful compression.

The authors empirically identify strong linear correlations among CNN gradients and introduce GradiVeQ to exploit them. It uses principal component analysis to reduce gradient dimensionality through vector quantization. Because the resulting compressed gradients can be aggregated directly, the system can run gradient compression and ring all-reduce communication in parallel.

Overall training time falls by almost 50%. GradiVeQ is also compatible with scalar quantization such as QSGD and achieves greater speedup at the same compression ratio. The results highlight that compression’s practical value depends on how well it fits the communication procedure.
summary.tldr: GradiVeQ compresses correlated CNN gradients into a directly aggregatable representation, substantially reducing distributed training time in experiments.

title: GradiVeQ: Vector Quantization for Bandwidth-Efficient Gradient Aggregation in Distributed CNN Training

abstract: Distributed sparse learning with a cluster of multiple machines has attracted much attention in machine learning, especially for large-scale applications with high-dimensional data. One popular way to implement sparse learning is to use L1 regularization. In this paper, we propose a novel method, called proximal SCOPE (pSCOPE), for distributed sparse learning with L1 regularization. pSCOPE is based on a cooperative autonomous local learning (CALL) framework. In the CALL framework of pSCOPE, we find that the data partition affects the convergence of the learning procedure, and subsequently we define a metric to measure the goodness of a data partition. Based on the defined metric, we theoretically prove that pSCOPE is convergent with a linear convergence rate if the data partition is good enough. We also prove that better data partition implies faster convergence rate. Furthermore, pSCOPE is also communication efficient. Experimental results on real data sets show that pSCOPE can outperform other state-of-the-art distributed methods for sparse learning.
