paragraphs: Sparse learning is useful for large, high-dimensional datasets, and L1 regularization is a common way to encourage sparsity. This paper introduces proximal SCOPE, or pSCOPE, for carrying out that learning across multiple machines. The method uses a cooperative autonomous local learning framework, allowing local learning to contribute to a distributed procedure.

A central finding is that the way data are partitioned across machines affects convergence. The authors define a metric for partition quality and use it to prove a linear convergence rate when the partition is sufficiently good. They also prove that better partitions lead to faster convergence, connecting data placement directly to the behavior of the optimization algorithm.

The guarantee is conditional on partition quality, making that quality an explicit part of the method's analysis. The authors additionally describe pSCOPE as communication efficient. Experiments on real datasets show that it can outperform other state-of-the-art distributed sparse-learning methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical results highlight both algorithm design and data partitioning as contributors to efficient distributed learning.
summary.tldr: pSCOPE enables communication-efficient distributed sparse learning with linear convergence when data partitions are sufficiently good.

title: Proximal SCOPE for Distributed Sparse Learning

abstract: Major internet companies routinely perform tens of thousands of A/B tests each year. Such large-scale sequential experimentation has resulted in a recent spurt of new algorithms that can provably control the false discovery rate (FDR) in a fully online fashion. However, current state-of-the-art adaptive algorithms can suffer from a significant loss in power if null p-values are conservative (stochastically larger than the uniform distribution), a situation that occurs frequently in practice. In this work, we introduce a new adaptive discarding method called ADDIS that provably controls the FDR and achieves the best of both worlds: it enjoys appreciable power increase over all existing methods if nulls are conservative (the practical case), and rarely loses power if nulls are exactly uniformly distributed (the ideal case). We provide several practical insights on robust choices of tuning parameters, and extend the idea to asynchronous and offline settings as well.

paragraphs: When organizations run many experiments in sequence, they need to limit false discoveries while still detecting real effects. Online false discovery rate control addresses this as tests arrive. The paper focuses on a practical obstacle: existing adaptive methods can lose considerable detection power when p-values under true null hypotheses tend to be larger than uniformly distributed values.

The proposed algorithm, ADDIS, uses adaptive discarding and comes with a proof of false discovery rate control. Its central aim is to exploit the conservative behavior of null p-values so that valid error control does not come with such a large loss of useful discoveries. This targets a distributional feature that the abstract describes as common in practice.

The authors report appreciable power improvements over existing methods when null p-values are conservative. When they are exactly uniform, ADDIS rarely loses power; this is a qualified claim, not a promise of improvement in every setting. The work also offers guidance on robust tuning choices and extends the discarding idea to asynchronous experiments and offline testing.
summary.tldr: ADDIS controls online false discoveries while improving detection power when null p-values are conservative.

title: ADDIS: an adaptive discarding algorithm for online FDR control with conservative nulls

abstract: A proper understanding of the striking generalization abilities of deep neural networks presents an enduring puzzle. Recently, there has been a growing body of numerically-grounded theoretical work that has contributed important insights to the theory of learning in deep neural nets. There has also been a recent interest in extending these analyses to understanding how multitask learning can further improve the generalization capacity of deep neural nets. These studies deal almost exclusively with regression tasks which are amenable to existing analytical techniques. We develop an analytic theory of the nonlinear dynamics of generalization of deep neural networks trained to solve classification tasks using softmax outputs and cross-entropy loss, addressing both single task and multitask settings. We do so by adapting techniques from the statistical physics of disordered systems, accounting for both finite size datasets and correlated outputs induced by the training dynamics. We discuss the validity of our theoretical results in comparison to a comprehensive suite of numerical experiments. Our analysis provides theoretical support for the intuition that the performance of multitask learning is determined by the noisiness of the tasks and how well their input features align with each other. Highly related, clean tasks benefit each other, whereas unrelated, clean tasks can be detrimental to individual task performance.

paragraphs: Training related tasks together can improve generalization, but the benefit depends on the relationship between those tasks. This paper develops an analytic theory of how generalization evolves in deep neural classifiers. It covers both single-task and multitask training with softmax outputs and cross-entropy loss, extending a line of analysis largely focused on regression.

The authors adapt methods from the statistical physics of disordered systems to study nonlinear learning dynamics. Their treatment accounts for finite datasets and correlations between outputs that arise during training. They compare the theoretical results with a comprehensive collection of numerical experiments to assess how well the analysis describes observed behavior.

The analysis supports the idea that task noise and alignment between input features determine multitask performance. Highly related, clean tasks can benefit one another, whereas unrelated, clean tasks can harm individual-task performance. This explains why adding another task is not automatically useful: even clean supervision can be detrimental when the tasks’ features do not align in a helpful way.
summary.tldr: A statistical-physics analysis links multitask classifier generalization to task noise and feature alignment, explaining both benefits and detrimental interactions.

title: Generalization in multitask deep neural classifiers: a statistical physics approach

abstract: We propose to represent shapes as the deformation and combination of learnt elementary 3D structures. We demonstrate this decomposition in learnt elementary 3D structures is highly interpretable and leads to clear improvements in 3D shape generation and matching. More precisely, we present two complementary approaches to learn elementary structures in a deep learning framework: (i) continuous surface deformation learning and (ii) 3D structure points learning. Both approaches can be extended to abstract structures of higher dimensions for improved results. We evaluate our method on two very different tasks: ShapeNet objects reconstruction and dense correspondences estimation between human scans. Qualitatively our approach provides interpretable and repeatable results. Quantitatively, we show an important 16% boost for 3D object generation via surface deformation, as well as a clear 6% improvement over state of the art correspondence results on the FAUST inter challenge.

The authors argue that this decomposition provides an interpretable account of shapes while improving both shape generation and matching between shapes.

They develop two complementary approaches within a deep learning framework. One learns continuous surface deformations, while the other learns structures expressed through three-dimensional points. Both approaches can also extend to abstract structures in higher dimensions, which the authors report can improve results. The shared idea is to learn useful underlying structures and then adapt them to represent particular shapes.

Evaluation covers object reconstruction on ShapeNet and dense correspondence estimation between human scans. The results are described as interpretable and repeatable in qualitative comparisons. Quantitatively, the authors report a 16% improvement for object generation through surface deformation and a 6% improvement over state-of-the-art correspondence results on the FAUST inter challenge. These findings support the representation across two substantially different geometric tasks.
summary.tldr: Learning elementary structures that can be deformed and combined improves both 3D object generation and matching between human scans.

title: Learning elementary structures for 3D shape generation and matching

abstract: Personalized interventions in social services, education, and healthcare leverage individual-level causal effect predictions in order to give the best treatment to each individual or to prioritize program interventions for the individuals most likely to benefit. While the sensitivity of these domains compels us to evaluate the fairness of such policies, we show that actually auditing their disparate impacts per standard observational metrics, such as true positive rates, is impossible since ground truths are unknown. Whether our data is experimental or observational, an individual's actual outcome under an intervention different than that received can never be known, only predicted based on features. We prove how we can nonetheless point-identify these quantities under the additional assumption of monotone treatment response, which may be reasonable in many applications. We further provide a sensitivity analysis for this assumption via sharp partial-identification bounds under violations of monotonicity of varying strengths. We show how to use our results to audit personalized interventions using partially-identified ROC and xROC curves and demonstrate this in a case study of a French job training dataset.

paragraphs: Personalized intervention policies use predictions about who would benefit from treatment to decide whom to help. Auditing their fairness creates a special difficulty: an individual's outcome under the treatment they did not receive is unobserved. Consequently, even experimental data cannot directly reveal the individual benefit labels needed to calculate standard fairness measures such as true positive rates.

The paper establishes this identification problem and then studies what additional assumptions make an audit possible. Under monotone treatment response, an assumption that rules out treatment changing outcomes in the adverse direction, the authors show that the fairness quantities can be uniquely identified. That conclusion depends on the assumption; it does not remove the underlying absence of individual counterfactual outcomes.

The authors also derive sharp bounds when monotonicity is allowed to fail to varying degrees. These bounds support a sensitivity analysis rather than requiring unquestioned acceptance of monotonicity. Partially identified ROC and xROC curves turn the results into auditing tools, illustrated with French job training data.
summary.tldr: The paper shows why auditing personalized interventions requires causal assumptions and provides exact identification under monotonicity plus bounds when it fails.

title: Assessing Disparate Impact of Personalized Interventions: Identifiability and Bounds

abstract: In regression tasks, aleatoric uncertainty is commonly addressed by considering a parametric distribution of the output variable, which is based on strong assumptions such as symmetry, unimodality or by supposing a restricted shape. These assumptions are too limited in scenarios where complex shapes, strong skews or multiple modes are present. In this paper, we propose a generic deep learning framework that learns an Uncountable Mixture of Asymmetric Laplacians (UMAL), which will allow us to estimate heterogeneous distributions of the output variable and shows its connections to quantile regression. Despite having a fixed number of parameters, the model can be interpreted as an infinite mixture of components, which yields a flexible approximation for heterogeneous distributions. Apart from synthetic cases, we apply this model to room price forecasting and to predict financial operations in personal bank accounts. We demonstrate that UMAL produces proper distributions, which allows us to extract richer insights and to sharpen decision-making.

This paper introduces an Uncountable Mixture of Asymmetric Laplacians, or UMAL, to represent heterogeneous output distributions more flexibly.

The framework uses deep learning and connects its construction to quantile regression. Although it has a fixed number of parameters, it can be interpreted as an infinite mixture of components. This provides a way to model richer aleatoric uncertainty without explicitly assigning a separate parameter set to infinitely many components.

The authors evaluate synthetic cases, room-price forecasting, and prediction of financial operations in personal bank accounts. They report proper predictive distributions that support richer interpretation and decisions. The abstract gives no numerical comparison, calibration measure, or decision-outcome result, so it establishes the modeling approach and demonstrated applications rather than a quantified improvement in downstream decisions.
summary.tldr: UMAL models complex regression uncertainty with an effectively infinite mixture and finitely many parameters.

title: Modelling heterogeneous distributions with an Uncountable Mixture of Asymmetric Laplacians

abstract: We investigate whether post-hoc model explanations are effective for diagnosing model errors--model debugging. In response to the challenge of explaining a model's prediction, a vast array of explanation methods have been proposed. Despite increasing use, it is unclear if they are effective. To start, we categorize \textit{bugs}, based on their source, into: ~\textit{data, model, and test-time} contamination bugs. For several explanation methods, we assess their ability to: detect spurious correlation artifacts (data contamination), diagnose mislabeled training examples (data contamination), differentiate between a (partially) re-initialized model and a trained one (model contamination), and detect out-of-distribution inputs (test-time contamination). We find that the methods tested are able to diagnose a spurious background bug, but not conclusively identify mislabeled training examples. In addition, a class of methods, that modify the back-propagation algorithm are invariant to the higher layer parameters of a deep network; hence, ineffective for diagnosing model contamination. We complement our analysis with a human subject study, and find that subjects fail to identify defective models using attributions, but instead rely, primarily, on model predictions. Taken together, our results provide guidance for practitioners and researchers turning to explanations as tools for model debugging.

In response to the challenge of explaining a model's prediction, a vast array of explanation methods have been proposed. Despite increasing use, it is unclear if they are effective. To start, we categorize \textit{bugs}, based on their source, into: ~\textit{data, model, and test-time} contamination bugs. For several explanation methods, we assess their ability to: detect spurious correlation artifacts (data contamination), diagnose mislabeled training examples (data contamination), differentiate between a (partially) re-initialized model and a trained one (model contamination), and detect out-of-distribution inputs (test-time contamination). We find that the methods tested are able to diagnose a spurious background bug, but not conclusively identify mislabeled training examples. In addition, a class of methods, that modify the back-propagation algorithm are invariant to the higher layer parameters of a deep network; hence, ineffective for diagnosing model contamination. We complement our analysis with a human subject study, and find that subjects fail to identify defective models using attributions, but instead rely, primarily, on model predictions. Taken together, our results provide guidance for practitioners and researchers turning to explanations as tools for model debugging.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether explanations produced after a prediction actually help diagnose model defects. It organizes bugs by their source: contaminated training data, problems in the model itself, and contamination at test time. This turns the broad question of explanation usefulness into specific debugging tasks with different kinds of failure to detect.

The tests examine spurious correlations, mislabeled training examples, partially reinitialized networks, and inputs outside the training distribution. The tested explanation methods identify a spurious background bug, but do not conclusively identify mislabeled examples. The authors also find that a class of methods that alter back-propagation is insensitive to higher-layer parameters, making those methods ineffective for diagnosing the studied model contamination.

A human-subject study adds a practical perspective. Participants fail to identify defective models using attribution explanations and instead rely primarily on predictions. Taken together, the results show why successful debugging in one setting does not establish usefulness across other defects. The paper provides task-specific evidence for judging explanations as debugging tools, rather than treating an explanation's availability as evidence of diagnostic value.
summary.tldr: Debugging tests reveal that the evaluated explanation methods detect some data artifacts but miss other defects and can be insensitive to model changes.

title: Debugging Tests for Model Explanations

abstract: Routing games are amongst the most studied classes of games in game theory. Their most well-known property is that learning dynamics typically converge to equilibria implying approximately optimal performance (low Price of Anarchy). We perform a stress test for these classic results by studying the ubiquitous learning dynamics, Multiplicative Weights Update (MWU), in different classes of congestion games, uncovering intricate non-equilibrium phenomena. We study MWU using the actual game costs without applying cost normalization to $[0,1]$. Although this non-standard assumption leads to large regret, it captures realistic agents' behaviors. Namely, as the total demand increases, agents respond more aggressively to unbearably large costs. We start with the illustrative case of non-atomic routing games with two paths of linear cost, and show that every system has a carrying capacity, above which it becomes unstable. If the equilibrium flow is a symmetric $50-50\%$ split, the system exhibits one period-doubling bifurcation. Although the Price of Anarchy is equal to one, in the large population limit the time-average social cost for all but a zero measure set of initial conditions converges to its worst possible value. For asymmetric equilibrium flows, increasing the demand eventually forces the system into Li-Yorke chaos with positive topological entropy and periodic orbits of all possible periods. Remarkably, in all non-equilibrating regimes, the time-average flows on the paths converge {\it exactly} to the equilibrium flows, a property akin to no-regret learning in zero-sum games. We extend our results to games with arbitrarily many strategies, polynomial cost functions, non-atomic as well as atomic routing games, and heterogenous users.

title: The route to chaos in routing games: When is price of anarchy too optimistic?

abstract: We study minimax methods for off-policy evaluation (OPE) using value functions and marginalized importance weights. Despite that they hold promises of overcoming the exponential variance in traditional importance sampling, several key problems remain: (1) They require function approximation and are generally biased. For the sake of trustworthy OPE, is there anyway to quantify the biases? (2) They are split into two styles (“weight-learning” vs “value-learning”). Can we unify them? In this paper we answer both questions positively. By slightly altering the derivation of previous methods (one from each style), we unify them into a single value interval that comes with a special type of double robustness: when either the value-function or the importance-weight class is well specified, the interval is valid and its length quantifies the misspecification of the other class. Our interval also provides a unified view of and new insights to some recent methods, and we further explore the implications of our results on exploration and exploitation in off-policy policy optimization with insufficient data coverage.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy's value using data obtained under another policy. Minimax approaches based on value functions or marginalized importance weights offer a route around the exponential variance of traditional importance sampling. However, their use of function approximation can introduce bias, raising the question of how to assess the trustworthiness of their estimates.

The paper unifies methods that learn weights and methods that learn values into a single value interval. It does so by modifying the derivations of representative approaches from both groups. Rather than treating their estimates as separate answers, the construction connects them through bounds on the policy's value.

The interval has a specific double-robustness property: it is valid when either the value-function class or the importance-weight class is well specified. Its length then measures misspecification in the other class. This condition is central to the guarantee. The authors also use the framework to reinterpret recent methods and explore implications for balancing exploration and exploitation when off-policy data provide insufficient coverage.
summary.tldr: A unified off-policy value interval remains valid when either the value-function or importance-weight class is well specified and quantifies misspecification in the other.

title: Minimax Value Interval for Off-Policy Evaluation and Policy Optimization

abstract: We introduce a novel self-supervised pretext task for learning representations from audio-visual content. Prior work on audio-visual representation learning leverages correspondences at the video level. Approaches based on audio-visual correspondence (AVC) predict whether audio and video clips originate from the same or different video instances. Audio-visual temporal synchronization (AVTS) further discriminates negative pairs originated from the same video instance but at different moments in time. While these approaches learn high-quality representations for downstream tasks such as action recognition, they completely disregard the spatial cues of audio and visual signals naturally occurring in the real world. To learn from these spatial cues, we tasked a network to perform contrastive audio-visual spatial alignment of 360\degree video and spatial audio. The ability to perform spatial alignment is enhanced by reasoning over the full spatial content of the 360\degree video using a transformer architecture to combine representations from multiple viewpoints. The advantages of the proposed pretext task are demonstrated on a variety of audio and visual downstream tasks, including audio-visual correspondence, spatial alignment, action recognition and video semantic segmentation. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/pedro-morgado/AVSpatialAlignment.

paragraphs: Audio and video provide related information about both when and where events occur. This paper uses their spatial relationship as a self-supervised learning task. Earlier approaches described in the abstract match clips by video identity or temporal synchronization, leaving spatial cues unused even though those approaches can learn useful representations.

The proposed task trains a network to perform contrastive spatial alignment between 360-degree video and spatial audio. Learning therefore depends on how the two modalities correspond across space. A transformer combines representations from multiple viewpoints, allowing the network to reason over the full visual surroundings and improving its ability to perform the alignment task.

The authors demonstrate advantages across several downstream tasks: audio–visual correspondence, spatial alignment, action recognition, and video semantic segmentation. These evaluations connect the training task to both audio and visual uses of the learned representations. The stated findings support spatial alignment as an additional source of self-supervision, showing that information about where audiovisual content occurs can help representation learning.
summary.tldr: Spatial alignment between 360-degree video and spatial audio supplies a self-supervised task that improves representations for multiple downstream tasks.

title: Learning Representations from Audio-Visual Spatial Alignment

abstract: The ability to record activities from hundreds of neurons simultaneously in the brain has placed an increasing demand for developing appropriate statistical techniques to analyze such data. Recently, deep generative models have been proposed to fit neural population responses. While these methods are flexible and expressive, the downside is that they can be difficult to interpret and identify. To address this problem, we propose a method that integrates key ingredients from latent models and traditional neural encoding models. Our method, pi-VAE, is inspired by recent progress on identifiable variational auto-encoder, which we adapt to make appropriate for neuroscience applications. Specifically, we propose to construct latent variable models of neural activity while simultaneously modeling the relation between the latent and task variables (non-neural variables, e.g. sensory, motor, and other externally observable states). The incorporation of task variables results in models that are not only more constrained, but also show qualitative improvements in interpretability and identifiability. We validate pi-VAE using synthetic data, and apply it to analyze neurophysiological datasets from rat hippocampus and macaque motor cortex. We demonstrate that pi-VAE not only fits the data better, but also provides unexpected novel insights into the structure of the neural codes.

Deep generative models can fit complex neural responses, but their hidden representations can be difficult to interpret and identify. This paper introduces pi-VAE to bring additional structure to those latent representations.

The method combines ideas from latent-variable models and traditional neural encoding models. Alongside neural activity, it models the relationship between latent variables and observable task variables, such as sensory or motor states. These additional relationships constrain the model and connect its hidden representation to measurable aspects of the task. The authors adapt ideas from identifiable variational autoencoders for neuroscience applications.

It validates pi-VAE on synthetic data and applies it to recordings from rat hippocampus and macaque motor cortex. The authors report better data fits and new insights into neural-code structure. The contribution is a way to combine expressive population modeling with task information that helps make the learned representation scientifically interpretable.
summary.tldr: pi-VAE links latent neural activity to observable task variables, improving interpretability and identifiability while providing better fits in the reported analyses.

title: Learning identifiable and interpretable latent models of high-dimensional neural activity using pi-VAE

abstract: The scalability of Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is today limited by communication bottlenecks. We propose a novel SGD variant: \underline{C}ommunication-efficient \underline{S}GD with \underline{E}rror \underline{R}eset, or \underline{CSER}. The key idea in CSER is first a new technique called ``error reset'' that adapts arbitrary compressors for SGD, producing bifurcated local models with periodic reset of resulting local residual errors. Second we introduce partial synchronization for both the gradients and the models, leveraging advantages from them. We prove the convergence of CSER for smooth non-convex problems. Empirical results show that when combined with highly aggressive compressors, the CSER algorithms accelerate the distributed training by nearly $10\times$ for CIFAR-100, and by $4.5\times$ for ImageNet.

We propose a novel SGD variant: \underline{C}ommunication-efficient \underline{S}GD with \underline{E}rror \underline{R}eset, or \underline{CSER}. The key idea in CSER is first a new technique called ``error reset'' that adapts arbitrary compressors for SGD, producing bifurcated local models with periodic reset of resulting local residual errors. paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent spreads training across workers, but communication can limit its scalability. CSER addresses that bottleneck by combining compressed communication with a mechanism for handling the residual errors that compression creates. Its aim is to accelerate distributed training while retaining a convergence guarantee for the stated class of optimization problems.

The first component, called error reset, adapts arbitrary compressors for SGD. It allows local models to diverge and periodically resets the resulting local residual errors. The second component partially synchronizes both gradients and models. By including both forms of synchronization, the method draws on information about local update directions as well as the models being updated.

The authors prove convergence for smooth non-convex problems. In experiments using highly aggressive compressors, CSER accelerates distributed training by nearly ten times on CIFAR-100 and by 4.5 times on ImageNet. These are reported empirical speedups for the evaluated settings. Together, the theoretical and experimental results show how error handling and partial synchronization can make aggressive communication compression useful for distributed SGD.
summary.tldr: CSER combines compression, periodic error resets, and partial synchronization to accelerate distributed SGD, with convergence proved for smooth non-convex problems.

title: CSER: Communication-efficient SGD with Error Reset

abstract: Sparse models are desirable for many applications across diverse domains as they can perform automatic variable selection, aid interpretability, and provide regularization. When fitting sparse models in a Bayesian framework, however, analytically obtaining a posterior distribution over the parameters of interest is intractable for all but the simplest cases. As a result practitioners must rely on either sampling algorithms such as Markov chain Monte Carlo or variational methods to obtain an approximate posterior. Mean field variational inference is a particularly simple and popular framework that is often amenable to analytically deriving closed-form parameter updates. When all distributions in the model are members of exponential families and are conditionally conjugate, optimization schemes can often be derived by hand. Yet, I show that using standard mean field variational inference can fail to produce sensible results for models with sparsity-inducing priors, such as the spike-and-slab. Fortunately, such pathological behavior can be remedied as I show that mixtures of exponential family distributions with non-overlapping support form an exponential family. In particular, any mixture of an exponential family of diffuse distributions and a point mass at zero to model sparsity forms an exponential family. Furthermore, specific choices of these distributions maintain conditional conjugacy. I use two applications to motivate these results: one from statistical genetics that has connections to generalized least squares with a spike-and-slab prior on the regression coefficients; and sparse probabilistic principal component analysis. The theoretical results presented here are broadly applicable beyond these two examples.

title: Flexible mean field variational inference using mixtures of non-overlapping exponential families

abstract: In this work we produce a framework for constructing universal function approximators on graph isomorphism classes. We prove how this framework comes with a collection of theoretically desirable properties and enables novel analysis. We show how this allows us to achieve state-of-the-art performance on four different well-known datasets in graph classification and separate classes of graphs that other graph-learning methods cannot. Our approach is inspired by persistent homology, dependency parsing for NLP, and multivalued functions. The complexity of the underlying algorithm is O(#edges x #nodes) and code is publicly available (https://github.com/bruel-gabrielsson/universal-function-approximation-on-graphs).

We prove how this framework comes with a collection of theoretically desirable properties and enables novel analysis. We show how this allows us to achieve state-of-the-art performance on four different well-known datasets in graph classification and separate classes of graphs that other graph-learning methods cannot. Our approach is inspired by persistent homology, dependency parsing for NLP, and multivalued functions. The complexity of the underlying algorithm is O(#edges x #nodes) and code is publicly available (https://github.com/bruel-gabrielsson/universal-function-approximation-on-graphs).

paragraphs: Learning a function of a graph should account for its structure rather than depend on arbitrary names assigned to its nodes. This paper develops a framework for universal function approximation on graph isomorphism classes, which group together graphs that are structurally equivalent. The framework therefore targets graph-level functions defined over structural identities.

The approach draws inspiration from persistent homology, dependency parsing in language processing, and multivalued functions. The authors prove a collection of desirable theoretical properties and use the framework to enable additional analysis. They also show that it can distinguish classes of graphs that other graph-learning methods cannot separate, connecting approximation power to structural discrimination.

On four established graph classification datasets, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. The underlying algorithm has complexity proportional to the number of edges multiplied by the number of nodes. The paper thus combines an expressiveness framework, concrete graph-separation results, and empirical classification performance, while specifying how its computational cost scales with graph size.
summary.tldr: A framework for universal approximation on graph isomorphism classes distinguishes graph classes missed by other methods and achieves leading results on four classification datasets.

title: Universal Function Approximation on Graphs

abstract: We study minimax optimal reinforcement learning in episodic factored Markov decision processes (FMDPs), which are MDPs with conditionally independent transition components. Assuming the factorization is known, we propose two model-based algorithms. The first one achieves minimax optimal regret guarantees for a rich class of factored structures, while the second one enjoys better computational complexity with a slightly worse regret. A key new ingredient of our algorithms is the design of a bonus term to guide exploration. We complement our algorithms by presenting several structure dependent lower bounds on regret for FMDPs that reveal the difficulty hiding in the intricacy of the structures.

paragraphs: Factored Markov decision processes describe transitions through components that are conditionally independent. This structure can help organize a reinforcement learning problem, but the particular pattern of dependencies affects its difficulty. The paper studies episodic learning in this setting, assuming that the factorization is already known to the learner.

The authors propose two model-based algorithms with different statistical and computational tradeoffs. The first obtains minimax-optimal regret guarantees for a rich class of factored structures, meaning its worst-case regret matches the best achievable order within that class. The second has better computational complexity while accepting a slightly weaker regret guarantee.

A key ingredient is a newly designed exploration bonus that guides the algorithms' information gathering. The paper also establishes several lower bounds that depend on the factored structure, explaining how structural intricacy can make learning harder. These bounds help assess the algorithms against the difficulty of the problem itself and show why a single generic description of factorization does not fully capture learning complexity.
summary.tldr: With known transition factorization, two model-based algorithms trade computational efficiency against regret, achieving minimax optimality for a rich class of structures.

title: Towards Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning in Factored Markov Decision Processes

abstract: We consider the blackbox transfer-based targeted adversarial attack threat model in the realm of deep neural network (DNN) image classifiers. Rather than focusing on crossing decision boundaries at the output layer of the source model, our method perturbs representations throughout the extracted feature hierarchy to resemble other classes. We design a flexible attack framework that allows for multi-layer perturbations and demonstrates state-of-the-art targeted transfer performance between ImageNet DNNs. We also show the superiority of our feature space methods under a relaxation of the common assumption that the source and target models are trained on the same dataset and label space, in some instances achieving a $10\times$ increase in targeted success rate relative to other blackbox transfer methods. Finally, we analyze why the proposed methods outperform existing attack strategies and show an extension of the method in the case when limited queries to the blackbox model are allowed.

paragraphs: A targeted transfer attack constructs an adversarial image using a source classifier and aims to make another, blackbox classifier assign a chosen class. This paper investigates how to make such attacks transfer more effectively. Its focus is the hierarchy of internal image representations learned by deep neural networks.

The proposed framework perturbs representations at multiple layers so that they resemble other classes. This broadens the attack objective beyond changing the source model's final output decision. The framework supports flexible combinations of layer-level perturbations and achieves state-of-the-art targeted transfer performance between the ImageNet networks evaluated by the authors.

The paper also relaxes the usual assumption that source and target models share their training dataset and label space. Feature-space methods remain superior in those evaluations, with some instances showing a tenfold increase in targeted success rate relative to other transfer methods. The authors analyze why the methods outperform existing strategies and extend the approach to a setting permitting limited blackbox queries. These findings identify internal representations as useful targets for transferable adversarial perturbations.
summary.tldr: Perturbing multiple internal feature layers improves targeted attack transfer, including some settings with different source and target datasets or labels.

title: Perturbing Across the Feature Hierarchy to Improve Standard and Strict Blackbox Attack Transferability

abstract: We introduce the forward-backward (FB) representation of the dynamics of a reward-free Markov decision process. It provides explicit near-optimal policies for any reward specified a posteriori. During an unsupervised phase, we use reward-free interactions with the environment to learn two representations via off-the-shelf deep learning methods and temporal difference (TD) learning. In the test phase, a reward representation is estimated either from reward observations or an explicit reward description (e.g., a target state). The optimal policy for thatreward is directly obtained from these representations, with no planning. We assume access to an exploration scheme or replay buffer for the first phase.The corresponding unsupervised loss is well-principled: if training is perfect, the policies obtained are provably optimal for any reward function. With imperfect training, the sub-optimality is proportional to the unsupervised approximation error. The FB representation learns long-range relationships between states and actions, via a predictive occupancy map, without having to synthesize states as in model-based approaches.This is a step towards learning controllable agents in arbitrary black-box stochastic environments. This approach compares well to goal-oriented RL algorithms on discrete and continuous mazes, pixel-based MsPacman, and the FetchReach virtual robot arm. We also illustrate how the agent can immediately adapt to new tasks beyond goal-oriented RL.

paragraphs: The forward-backward representation aims to learn environment dynamics before a task's reward is specified. During an unsupervised phase, reward-free interactions train two representations using deep learning and temporal-difference learning. This phase assumes access to an exploration scheme or replay buffer. The learned representation captures long-range state-action relationships through a predictive occupancy map.

When a reward becomes available, the method estimates its representation from reward observations or an explicit description, such as a target state. It then obtains a policy directly from the representations, without planning. The guarantee depends on training quality: perfect training yields provably optimal policies for any reward function, while imperfect training produces suboptimality proportional to the unsupervised approximation error.

The approach compares well with goal-oriented reinforcement-learning algorithms on discrete and continuous mazes, pixel-based MsPacman, and the FetchReach virtual robot arm. The authors also demonstrate immediate adaptation to new tasks beyond goal-oriented learning. The central contribution is reusable control knowledge: the initial representation can support rewards introduced afterward without synthesizing states as in model-based approaches or requiring a planning stage for each new task.
summary.tldr: Forward-backward representations turn reward-free experience into policies for later-specified rewards, with optimality guarantees tied to representation accuracy.

title: Learning One Representation to Optimize All Rewards

abstract: We introduce DMTet, a deep 3D conditional generative model that can synthesize high-resolution 3D shapes using simple user guides such as coarse voxels. It marries the merits of implicit and explicit 3D representations by leveraging a novel hybrid 3D representation. Compared to the current implicit approaches, which are trained to regress the signed distance values, DMTet directly optimizes for the reconstructed surface, which enables us to synthesize finer geometric details with fewer artifacts. Unlike deep 3D generative models that directly generate explicit representations such as meshes, our model can synthesize shapes with arbitrary topology. The core of DMTet includes a deformable tetrahedral grid that encodes a discretized signed distance function and a differentiable marching tetrahedra layer that converts the implicit signed distance representation to the explicit surface mesh representation. This combination allows joint optimization of the surface geometry and topology as well as generation of the hierarchy of subdivisions using reconstruction and adversarial losses defined explicitly on the surface mesh. Our approach significantly outperforms existing work on conditional shape synthesis from coarse voxel inputs, trained on a dataset of complex 3D animal shapes. Project page: https://nv-tlabs.github.io/DMTet/.

The results support combining flexible shape structure with training objectives applied to the actual generated surface.
summary.tldr: DMTet combines a deformable implicit representation with differentiable mesh extraction to generate detailed 3D shapes with flexible topology.

title: Deep Marching Tetrahedra: a Hybrid Representation for High-Resolution 3D Shape Synthesis

abstract: An in-depth scene understanding usually requires recognizing all the objects and their relations in an image, encoded as a scene graph. Most existing approaches for scene graph generation first independently recognize each object and then predict their relations independently. Though these approaches are very efficient, they ignore the dependency between different objects as well as between their relations. In this paper, we propose a principled approach to jointly predict the entire scene graph by fully capturing the dependency between different objects and between their relations. Specifically, we establish a unified conditional random field (CRF) to model the joint distribution of all the objects and their relations in a scene graph. We carefully design the potential functions to enable relational reasoning among different objects according to knowledge graph embedding methods. We further propose an efficient and effective algorithm for inference based on mean-field variational inference, in which we first provide a warm initialization by independently predicting the objects and their relations according to the current model, followed by a few iterations of relational reasoning. Experimental results on both the relationship retrieval and zero-shot relationship retrieval tasks prove the efficiency and efficacy of our proposed approach.

This paper proposes predicting the scene graph jointly, allowing object and relationship predictions to inform one another within a single probabilistic model.

The model is a conditional random field over all objects and relations in the graph. Its potential functions are designed using knowledge graph embedding methods to support relational reasoning. This gives the system a structured way to account for connections among predictions, rather than treating each object or relation as an isolated recognition task.

To make inference efficient, the authors begin with independent predictions from the current model as a warm initialization. They then apply a few rounds of relational reasoning using mean-field variational inference. Experiments on relationship retrieval and zero-shot relationship retrieval support the approach's efficiency and effectiveness. The method therefore combines an inexpensive starting point with subsequent joint refinement, using dependencies to improve the overall interpretation of a scene.
summary.tldr: A joint probabilistic model refines object and relationship predictions together to generate scene graphs efficiently.

title: Joint Modeling of Visual Objects and Relations for Scene Graph Generation

abstract: Understanding the generalization of deep neural networks is one of the most important tasks in deep learning. Although much progress has been made, theoretical error bounds still often behave disparately from empirical observations. In this work, we develop margin-based generalization bounds, where the margins are normalized with optimal transport costs between independent random subsets sampled from the training distribution. In particular, the optimal transport cost can be interpreted as a generalization of variance which captures the structural properties of the learned feature space. Our bounds robustly predict the generalization error, given training data and network parameters, on large scale datasets. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the concentration and separation of features play crucial roles in generalization, supporting empirical results in the literature.

paragraphs: Generalization theory seeks to explain how well a trained network will perform on new data, yet theoretical bounds often track observed performance poorly. This paper develops bounds that account for the geometry of the network's learned features. It combines classification margins with optimal transport costs calculated between independent random subsets drawn from the training distribution.

The transport cost normalizes the margins, giving them a scale informed by the feature space rather than treating margin size in isolation. The authors interpret this cost as a generalization of variance that captures structural properties of the representation. This links prediction confidence, expressed through margins, to how the learned features are distributed.

The theoretical analysis identifies feature concentration and separation as important factors in generalization. Empirically, the resulting bounds robustly predict generalization error on large-scale datasets using training data and network parameters. The findings support evaluating both the organization of learned features and the margins they produce, helping connect a theoretical account of generalization with patterns observed in trained networks.
summary.tldr: Optimal-transport-normalized margin bounds connect feature geometry to generalization and empirically predict error on large-scale datasets.

title: Measuring Generalization with Optimal Transport

abstract: Adder neural network (AdderNet) replaces the original convolutions with massive multiplications by cheap additions while achieving comparable performance thus yields a series of energy-efficient neural networks. Compared with convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the training of AdderNets is much more sophisticated including several techniques for adjusting gradient and batch normalization. In addition, variances of both weights and activations in resulting adder networks are very enormous which limits its performance and the potential for applying to other tasks. To enhance the stability and robustness of AdderNets, we first thoroughly analyze the variance estimation of weight parameters and output features of an arbitrary adder layer. Then, we develop a weight normalization scheme for adaptively optimizing the weight distribution of AdderNets during the training procedure, which can reduce the perturbation on running mean and variance in batch normalization layers. Meanwhile, the proposed weight normalization can also be utilized to enhance the adversarial robustness of resulting networks. Experiments conducted on several benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach for generating AdderNets with higher performance.

This paper studies those statistical properties as a route to making AdderNets more stable and useful.

The authors analyze variance estimates for the weights and output features of an arbitrary adder layer. Based on that analysis, they develop an adaptive weight-normalization scheme that adjusts the weight distribution during training. The scheme can reduce disturbances in the running mean and variance maintained by batch-normalization layers, addressing a concrete source of training instability.

The proposed normalization can also enhance adversarial robustness. Experiments across several benchmarks show higher-performing AdderNets using the approach. The contribution therefore connects layer-level variance analysis with practical training improvements and robustness benefits. It supports the idea that controlling weight distributions is consequential for addition-based networks, where unusually large weight and activation variances can otherwise restrict performance and the potential for broader use.
summary.tldr: Adaptive weight normalization improves AdderNet training stability, performance, and adversarial robustness.

title: Towards Stable and Robust AdderNets

abstract: The null space of the $k$-th order Laplacian $\mathbf{\mathcal L}_k$, known as the {\em $k$-th homology vector space}, encodes the non-trivial topology of a manifold or a network. Understanding the structure of the homology embedding can thus disclose geometric or topological information from the data. The study of the null space embedding of the graph Laplacian $\mathbf{\mathcal L}_0$ has spurred new research and applications, such as spectral clustering algorithms with theoretical guarantees and estimators of the Stochastic Block Model. In this work, we investigate the geometry of the $k$-th homology embedding and focus on cases reminiscent of spectral clustering. Namely, we analyze the {\em connected sum} of manifolds as a perturbation to the direct sum of their homology embeddings. We propose an algorithm to factorize the homology embedding into subspaces corresponding to a manifold's simplest topological components. The proposed framework is applied to the {\em shortest homologous loop detection} problem, a problem known to be NP-hard in general. Our spectral loop detection algorithm scales better than existing methods and is effective on diverse data such as point clouds and images.

paragraphs: The null space of a higher-order Laplacian encodes nontrivial topological structure in a manifold or network. This paper investigates the geometry of the resulting homology embedding. Its motivation parallels spectral clustering, where understanding a graph Laplacian’s null-space representation has enabled useful algorithms and theoretical analysis.

The authors study a connected sum of manifolds by treating its homology embedding as a perturbation of the direct sum of the component embeddings. This viewpoint leads to an algorithm that decomposes the embedding into subspaces associated with simpler topological components. The aim is to make the embedding’s internal structure reveal how the underlying topology is assembled.

They apply the framework to detecting shortest homologous loops, a problem that is NP-hard in general. The resulting spectral loop-detection algorithm scales better than existing methods and works effectively on varied data, including point clouds and images. These results demonstrate an algorithmic use for the decomposition without implying that the general computational difficulty of shortest-loop detection has disappeared.
summary.tldr: Decomposing higher-order homology embeddings exposes simpler topological components and supports scalable spectral loop detection.

title: The decomposition of the higher-order homology embedding constructed from the $k$-Laplacian

abstract: The study of Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) has been in the spotlight in recent times as they may lead to real-world applications of near-term quantum devices. However, their performance depends on the structure of the used variational ansatz, which requires balancing the depth and expressivity of the corresponding circuit. At the same time, near-term restrictions limit the depth of the circuit we can expect to run. Thus, the optimization of the VQE ansatz requires maximizing the expressivity of the circuit while maintaining low depth. In recent years, various methods for VQE structure optimization have been introduced but the capacities of machine learning to aid with this problem have not yet been extensively investigated. In this work, we propose a reinforcement learning algorithm that autonomously explores the space of possible ansatzes, identifying economic circuits which still yield accurate ground energy estimates. The algorithm uses a feedback-driven curriculum learning method that autonomously adapts the complexity of the learning problem to the current performance of the learning algorithm and it incrementally improves the accuracy of the result while minimizing the circuit depth. We showcase the performance of our algorithm on the problem of estimating the ground-state energy of lithium hydride (LiH) in various configurations. In this well-known benchmark problem, we achieve chemical accuracy and state-of-the-art results in terms of circuit depth.

That structure must balance expressive power with circuit depth, because near-term devices restrict how deep a circuit can practically be. The paper addresses the choice of circuit architecture as a learning problem.

The authors propose a reinforcement learning algorithm that autonomously searches possible circuit structures for compact circuits that still produce accurate energy estimates. A feedback-driven curriculum adjusts the difficulty of the learning problem according to the algorithm’s current performance. On this benchmark, it achieves chemical accuracy and state-of-the-art results for circuit depth. The findings show that reinforcement learning can discover economical ansatzes for the studied problem. The curriculum is central to the approach because it adapts the learning challenge as the search develops, supporting the joint pursuit of accurate estimates and shallow circuits.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning search with an adaptive curriculum finds shallow quantum circuits that achieve chemical accuracy on lithium hydride energy estimation.

title: Reinforcement learning for optimization of variational quantum circuit architectures

abstract: Flatness of the loss curve is conjectured to be connected to the generalization ability of machine learning models, in particular neural networks. While it has been empirically observed that flatness measures consistently correlate strongly with generalization, it is still an open theoretical problem why and under which circumstances flatness is connected to generalization, in particular in light of reparameterizations that change certain flatness measures but leave generalization unchanged. We investigate the connection between flatness and generalization by relating it to the interpolation from representative data, deriving notions of representativeness, and feature robustness. The notions allow us to rigorously connect flatness and generalization and to identify conditions under which the connection holds. Moreover, they give rise to a novel, but natural relative flatness measure that correlates strongly with generalization, simplifies to ridge regression for ordinary least squares, and solves the reparameterization issue.

paragraphs: Flat regions of a model’s training loss are often associated empirically with good generalization. Explaining that connection is difficult because some measurements of flatness change when a model is reparameterized, even though its predictive behavior and generalization remain the same. This paper seeks a more principled relationship between these quantities.

The authors connect flatness to interpolation from representative data and to robustness of features. They develop notions of representativeness that allow a rigorous connection and identify conditions under which it holds. This makes the role of the data and features explicit, rather than treating a flat loss surface alone as an unconditional explanation for generalization.

The analysis produces a relative flatness measure that addresses the reparameterization issue and correlates strongly with generalization. For ordinary least squares, the resulting construction simplifies to ridge regression, linking the proposal to a familiar regularization method. The contribution combines a conditional theoretical account with a measure designed to avoid an important ambiguity in earlier flatness notions. It clarifies when flatness can be informative about performance beyond the training data.
summary.tldr: Relative flatness connects loss geometry to generalization under identified conditions while addressing reparameterization and recovering ridge regression for ordinary least squares.

title: Relative Flatness and Generalization

abstract: Bayesian models have many desirable properties, most notable is their ability to generalize from limited data and to properly estimate the uncertainty in their predictions. However, these benefits come at a steep computational cost as Bayesian inference, in most cases, is computationally intractable. One popular approach to alleviate this problem is using a Monte-Carlo estimation with an ensemble of models sampled from the posterior. However, this approach still comes at a significant computational cost, as one needs to store and run multiple models at test time. In this work, we investigate how to best distill an ensemble's predictions using an efficient model. First, we argue that current approaches are limited as they are constrained to classification and the Dirichlet distribution. Second, in many limited data settings, all ensemble members achieve nearly zero training loss, namely, they produce near-identical predictions on the training set which results in sub-optimal distilled models. To address both problems, we propose a novel and general distillation approach, named Functional Ensemble Distillation (FED), and we investigate how to best distill an ensemble in this setting. We find that learning the distilled model via a simple augmentation scheme in the form of mixup augmentation significantly boosts the performance. We evaluated our method on several tasks and showed that it achieves superior results in both accuracy and uncertainty estimation compared to current approaches.

paragraphs: Ensembles sampled from a Bayesian posterior can help estimate uncertainty and generalize from limited data, but storing and running many models remains expensive. Functional Ensemble Distillation asks how to transfer an ensemble's predictions into an efficient model. The aim is to retain useful predictive behavior while reducing the burden of using the ensemble at test time.

The authors identify two obstacles. Existing distillation approaches are constrained to classification and the Dirichlet distribution. Moreover, when data are scarce, ensemble members can all fit the training set almost perfectly. Their predictions then look nearly identical on those examples, leaving the distillation process with little information about how the members differ.

The proposed FED approach is designed to be more general, and the paper investigates how to train it effectively in this setting. A simple mixup augmentation scheme substantially improves the distilled model's performance. Across several evaluated tasks, FED achieves better accuracy and uncertainty estimation than existing approaches. The results highlight that the examples used to teach a distilled model matter alongside the distillation formulation itself.
summary.tldr: Functional Ensemble Distillation uses a general distillation approach and mixup augmentation to improve efficient models' accuracy and uncertainty estimates.

title: Functional Ensemble Distillation

abstract: In this work we consider a variant of adversarial online learning where in each round one picks $B$ out of $N$ arms and incurs cost equal to the $\textit{minimum}$ of the costs of each arm chosen. We propose an algorithm called Follow the Perturbed Multiple Leaders (FPML) for this problem, which we show (by adapting the techniques of Kalai and Vempala [2005]) achieves expected regret $\mathcal{O}(T^{\frac{1}{B+1}}\ln(N)^{\frac{B}{B+1}})$ over time horizon $T$ relative to the $\textit{single}$ best arm in hindsight. This introduces a trade-off between the budget $B$ and the single-best-arm regret, and we proceed to investigate several applications of this trade-off. First, we observe that algorithms which use standard regret minimizers as subroutines can sometimes be adapted by replacing these subroutines with FPML, and we use this to generalize existing algorithms for Online Submodular Function Maximization [Streeter and Golovin, 2008] in both the full feedback and semi-bandit feedback settings. Next, we empirically evaluate our new algorithms on an online black-box hyperparameter optimization problem. Finally, we show how FPML can lead to new algorithms for Linear Programming which require stronger oracles at the benefit of fewer oracle calls.

paragraphs: The paper studies an online decision problem in which an algorithm selects B options from N available options each round. Its cost is the lowest cost among those selected. Performance is compared with the single best option chosen in hindsight, so the central question is how a larger selection budget improves regret against that benchmark.

The proposed Follow the Perturbed Multiple Leaders algorithm achieves expected regret O(T^(1/(B+1)) · ln(N)^(B/(B+1))) over T rounds. Increasing B reduces the exponent governing growth with time. This makes the resource trade-off explicit: the algorithm can obtain a better regret bound by selecting more options each round under the minimum-cost rule.

The authors show that some methods using conventional regret minimizers can instead use this algorithm as a subroutine. They apply the idea to online submodular maximization with full and semi-bandit feedback and evaluate the resulting algorithms on online black-box hyperparameter optimization. They also derive linear-programming algorithms that exchange stronger oracles for fewer oracle calls, extending the same resource-versus-iteration theme.
summary.tldr: Selecting more options per round improves regret against the best single option, with applications to online optimization and linear programming.

title: Trading Off Resource Budgets For Improved Regret Bounds

abstract: Automated machine learning has been widely explored to reduce human efforts in designing neural architectures and looking for proper hyperparameters. In the domain of neural initialization, however, similar automated techniques have rarely been studied. Most existing initialization methods are handcrafted and highly dependent on specific architectures. In this paper, we propose a differentiable quantity, named GradCoisne, with theoretical insights to evaluate the initial state of a neural network. Specifically, GradCosine is the cosine similarity of sample-wise gradients with respect to the initialized parameters. By analyzing the sample-wise optimization landscape, we show that both the training and test performance of a network can be improved by maximizing GradCosine under gradient norm constraint. Based on this observation, we further propose the neural initialization optimization (NIO) algorithm. Generalized from the sample-wise analysis into the real batch setting, NIO is able to automatically look for a better initialization with negligible cost compared with the training time. With NIO, we improve the classification performance of a variety of neural architectures on CIFAR10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Moreover, we find that our method can even help to train large vision Transformer architecture without warmup.

paragraphs: Neural-network initialization is often chosen using handcrafted rules tied to particular architectures. This paper explores automating that choice. It introduces GradCosine, a differentiable measure of how closely gradients from individual training samples point in the same direction at the initialized parameters.

The authors analyze the optimization landscape at the sample level and show that maximizing GradCosine under a gradient-norm constraint can improve training and test performance. The norm constraint is part of the stated result. They turn this observation into neural initialization optimization, or NIO, extending the analysis into a practical batch-based procedure for finding a better starting point.

These results support using gradient agreement to guide initialization, while the warmup finding remains an observed capability rather than a universal replacement for warmup.
summary.tldr: NIO automatically improves initialization by promoting sample-gradient alignment under a gradient-norm constraint, with classification gains in experiments.

title: Towards Theoretically Inspired Neural Initialization Optimization

abstract: Understanding how the dynamics of neural networks is shaped by the computations they perform is a fundamental question in neuroscience. Recently, the framework of efficient coding proposed a theory of how spiking neural networks can compute low-dimensional stimulus signals with high efficiency. Efficient spiking networks are based on time-dependent minimization of a loss function related to information coding with spikes. To inform the understanding of the function and dynamics of biological networks in the brain, however, the mathematical models have to be informed by biology and obey the same constraints as biological networks. Currently, spiking network models of efficient coding have been extended to include some features of biological plausibility, such as architectures with excitatory and inhibitory neurons. However, biological realism of efficient coding theories is still limited to simple cases and does not include single neuron and network properties that are known to be key in biological circuits. Here, we revisit the theory of efficient coding with spikes to develop spiking neural networks that are closer to biological circuits. Namely, we find a biologically plausible spiking model realizing efficient coding in the case of a generalized leaky integrate-and-fire network with excitatory and inhibitory units, equipped with fast and slow synaptic currents, local homeostatic currents such as spike-triggered adaptation, hyperpolarization-activated rebound current, heterogeneous firing thresholds and resets, heterogeneous postsynaptic potentials, and structured, low-rank connectivity. We show how the rank of E-E connectivity matrix shapes network responses.

Recently, the framework of efficient coding proposed a theory of how spiking neural networks can compute low-dimensional stimulus signals with high efficiency. Efficient spiking networks are based on time-dependent minimization of a loss function related to information coding with spikes. To inform the understanding of the function and dynamics of biological networks in the brain, however, the mathematical models have to be informed by biology and obey the same constraints as biological networks. Currently, spiking network models of efficient coding have been extended to include some features of biological plausibility, such as architectures with excitatory and inhibitory neurons. However, biological realism of efficient coding theories is still limited to simple cases and does not include single neuron and network properties that are known to be key in biological circuits. Here, we revisit the theory of efficient coding with spikes to develop spiking neural networks that are closer to biological circuits. Namely, we find a biologically plausible spiking model realizing efficient coding in the case of a generalized leaky integrate-and-fire network with excitatory and inhibitory units, equipped with fast and slow synaptic currents, local homeostatic currents such as spike-triggered adaptation, hyperpolarization-activated rebound current, heterogeneous firing thresholds and resets, heterogeneous postsynaptic potentials, and structured, low-rank connectivity. We show how the rank of E-E connectivity matrix shapes network responses.

paragraphs: Efficient coding offers a way to connect what a neural network computes with how its activity evolves. In spiking networks, the idea is to represent low-dimensional stimulus signals efficiently by minimizing a time-dependent loss associated with coding information through spikes. To explain biological circuits, however, such models also need to respect properties of real neurons and their connections.

This paper revisits efficient coding to construct a more biologically plausible generalized leaky integrate-and-fire network. The model includes excitatory and inhibitory neurons, fast and slow synaptic currents, and local currents associated with adaptation and rebound. It also allows neurons to differ in their firing thresholds, resets, and postsynaptic potentials, alongside structured connectivity of low rank.

The contribution is a model that realizes efficient coding while incorporating this richer collection of biological features. The authors also show how the rank of connections among excitatory neurons shapes network responses. This links a specific structural property of the network to its dynamics within an efficient-coding account.
summary.tldr: The paper builds efficient-coding spiking networks with richer biological features and connects excitatory connectivity rank to network responses.

title: Biologically plausible solutions for spiking networks with efficient coding

abstract: Several goal-oriented problems in the real-world can be naturally expressed as Stochastic Shortest Path problems (SSPs). However, the computational complexity of solving SSPs makes finding solutions to even moderately sized problems intractable. State-of-the-art SSP solvers are unable to learn generalized solutions or policies that would solve multiple problem instances with different object names and/or quantities. This paper presents an approach for learning \emph{Generalized Policy Automata} (GPA): non-deterministic partial policies that can be used to catalyze the solution process. GPAs are learned using relational, feature-based abstractions, which makes them applicable on broad classes of related problems with different object names and quantities. Theoretical analysis of this approach shows that it guarantees completeness and hierarchical optimality. Empirical analysis shows that this approach effectively learns broadly applicable policy knowledge in a few-shot fashion and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art SSP solvers on test problems whose object counts are far greater than those used during training.

paragraphs: Stochastic shortest path problems describe goal-directed decisions with uncertain outcomes. Solving them can become computationally difficult even at moderate sizes. The paper targets a further challenge: reusing planning knowledge across related problems whose objects have different names or whose object counts differ.

The proposed Generalized Policy Automata are nondeterministic partial policies that help accelerate the solution process. They are learned through relational, feature-based abstractions, so the learned guidance is expressed through reusable properties and relationships. Because the policies are partial, their role is to assist planning across a problem family rather than prescribe every decision in every possible state.

The theoretical analysis establishes completeness and hierarchical optimality for the approach. Hierarchical optimality is the stated guarantee, and should not be read as an unrestricted claim of global optimality. Empirically, the method learns broadly applicable policy knowledge from few examples and substantially outperforms the compared solvers on test instances with many more objects than the training instances. This supports abstraction as a way to carry useful planning structure into larger problems.
summary.tldr: Relational policy automata learn reusable partial planning guidance that transfers to larger stochastic shortest path problems.

title: Learning Generalized Policy Automata for Relational Stochastic Shortest Path Problems

abstract: Computational inference of aesthetics is an ill-defined task due to its subjective nature. Many datasets have been proposed to tackle the problem by providing pairs of images and aesthetic scores based on human ratings. However, humans are better at expressing their opinion, taste, and emotions by means of language rather than summarizing them in a single number. In fact, photo critiques provide much richer information as they reveal how and why users rate the aesthetics of visual stimuli. In this regard, we propose the Reddit Photo Critique Dataset (RPCD), which contains tuples of image and photo critiques. RPCD consists of 74K images and 220K comments and is collected from a Reddit community used by hobbyists and professional photographers to improve their photography skills by leveraging constructive community feedback. The proposed dataset differs from previous aesthetics datasets mainly in three aspects, namely (i) the large scale of the dataset and the extension of the comments criticizing different aspects of the image, (ii) it contains mostly UltraHD images, and (iii) it can easily be extended to new data as it is collected through an automatic pipeline. To the best of our knowledge, in this work, we propose the first attempt to estimate the aesthetic quality of visual stimuli from the critiques. To this end, we exploit the polarity of the sentiment of criticism as an indicator of aesthetic judgment. We demonstrate how sentiment polarity correlates positively with the aesthetic judgment available for two aesthetic assessment benchmarks. Finally, we experiment with several models by using the sentiment scores as a target for ranking images. Dataset and baselines are available https://github.com/mediatechnologycenter/aestheval.

It contains 74,000 images and 220,000 comments from a photography community offering constructive criticism.

These properties make it a resource for connecting detailed language about photographs with the visual material being assessed, while acknowledging that aesthetic judgment is subjective.

They use sentiment polarity as an indicator of judgment and find a positive correlation with aesthetic judgments in two assessment benchmarks. They then train several models to rank images using sentiment scores as targets. The findings support sentiment as a useful source of aesthetic supervision, with the reported relationship being a positive correlation rather than an equivalence between sentiment and aesthetic quality.
summary.tldr: A large photo-critique dataset supports learning aesthetic rankings from language, with critique sentiment positively correlated with benchmark aesthetic judgments.

title: Understanding Aesthetics with Language: A Photo Critique Dataset for Aesthetic Assessment

abstract: As a challenging multi-player card game, DouDizhu has recently drawn much attention for analyzing competition and collaboration in imperfect-information games. In this paper, we propose PerfectDou, a state-of-the-art Doudizhu AI system that summits the game, in an actor-critic framework with a proposed technique named perfect information distillation.In detail, we adopt a perfect-training-imperfection-execution framework that allows the agents to utilize the global information to guide the training of the policies as if it is a perfect information game and the trained policies can be used to play the imperfect information game during the actual gameplay. Correspondingly, we characterize card and game features for DouDizhu to represent the perfect and imperfect information. To train our system, we adopt proximal policy optimization with generalized advantage estimation in a parallel training paradigm. In experiments we show how and why PerfectDou beats all existing programs, and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
