paragraphs: DouDizhu is a multiplayer card game involving both competition and collaboration under incomplete information. PerfectDou addresses this setting with an actor–critic learning system. Its central technique, perfect information distillation, uses access to global game information during training to guide policies that must later play with the limited information available during actual gameplay.

The training and execution stages therefore operate under different information conditions. During training, global information helps teach the policy as though the game were fully observable. During execution, the trained policy remains usable in the imperfect-information game. The authors also design card and game features to represent both the complete and incomplete information available in these respective settings.

The system trains with proximal policy optimization and generalized advantage estimation in a parallel training setup. The experiments report that PerfectDou outperforms existing programs and achieves state-of-the-art performance in the study. The result supports using richer training information to improve policies for hidden-information play, while keeping the actual gameplay policy compatible with the information restrictions of the game.
summary.tldr: PerfectDou uses full game information during training to teach policies that achieve strong DouDizhu performance under actual hidden-information play.

title: PerfectDou: Dominating DouDizhu with Perfect Information Distillation

abstract: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have recently been highly successful at imputing and acquiring heterogeneous missing data. However, within this specific application domain, existing VAE methods are restricted by using only one layer of latent variables and strictly Gaussian posterior approximations. To address these limitations, we present HH-VAEM, a Hierarchical VAE model for mixed-type incomplete data that uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with automatic hyper-parameter tuning for improved approximate inference. Our experiments show that HH-VAEM outperforms existing baselines in the tasks of missing data imputation and supervised learning with missing features. Finally, we also present a sampling-based approach for efficiently computing the information gain when missing features are to be acquired with HH-VAEM. Our experiments show that this sampling-based approach is superior to alternatives based on Gaussian approximations.

paragraphs: Incomplete datasets raise two related questions: how to fill in missing values, and which missing features would be most useful to acquire. This paper studies both for mixed-type data. It identifies restrictions in existing VAE approaches for this application: a single layer of latent variables and strictly Gaussian approximations to the posterior.

HH-VAEM replaces that setup with a hierarchical VAE and uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for improved approximate inference. Automatic tuning handles the sampling method's hyperparameters. The combination expands the latent structure used to model incomplete data and changes how the model approximates uncertainty about unobserved quantities.

Experiments show improvements over existing baselines in missing-value imputation and supervised learning with missing features. The paper also introduces a sampling-based method for efficiently estimating information gain when deciding which missing feature to acquire. That method outperforms alternatives based on Gaussian approximations in the experiments. The findings connect richer inference to both reconstructing absent information and selecting additional observations that are expected to be informative.
summary.tldr: HH-VAEM combines hierarchical latent variables and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to improve missing-data inference and information-based feature acquisition.

title: Missing Data Imputation and Acquisition with Deep Hierarchical Models and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: We present a minimax optimal learner for the problem of learning predictors robust to adversarial examples at test-time. Interestingly, we find that this requires new algorithmic ideas and approaches to adversarially robust learning. In particular, we show, in a strong negative sense, the suboptimality of the robust learner proposed by Montasser, Hanneke, and Srebro [2019] and a broader family of learners we identify as local learners. Our results are enabled by adopting a global perspective, specifically, through a key technical contribution: the the global one-inclusion graph, which may be of independent interest, that generalizes the classical one-inclusion graph due to Haussler, Littlestone, and Warmuth [1994]. Finally, as a byproduct, we identify a dimension characterizing qualitatively and quantitatively what classes of predictors $\mathcal{H}$ are robustly learnable. This resolves an open problem due to Montasser et al. [2019], and closes a (potentially) infinite gap between the established upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of adversarially robust learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn predictors that remain reliable when test inputs are adversarially modified. It presents a learner that is minimax optimal: it achieves the best worst-case learning performance in the setting studied. Reaching this result requires a different algorithmic perspective from earlier approaches to robust learning.

The authors establish strong suboptimality results for an earlier robust learner and a broader family they call local learners. Their alternative takes a global view through a new mathematical construction, the global one-inclusion graph. This extends a classical tool for learning theory and enables the analysis behind the optimal learner.

A further result identifies a dimension that characterizes which predictor classes can be learned robustly and quantifies their sample requirements. This connects the possibility of robust learning with the amount of data it needs. The characterization resolves a previously open question and closes a gap between known upper and lower sample-complexity bounds that could potentially have been infinite.
summary.tldr: A global graph construction enables minimax-optimal adversarially robust learning and a dimension characterizing robust learnability and sample complexity.

title: Adversarially Robust Learning: A Generic Minimax Optimal Learner and Characterization

abstract: Recently there is a large amount of work devoted to the study of Markov chain stochastic gradient methods (MC-SGMs) which mainly focus on their convergence analysis for solving minimization problems. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive generalization analysis of MC-SGMs for both minimization and minimax problems through the lens of algorithmic stability in the framework of statistical learning theory. For empirical risk minimization (ERM) problems, we establish the optimal excess population risk bounds for both smooth and non-smooth cases by introducing on-average argument stability. For minimax problems, we develop a quantitative connection between on-average argument stability and generalization error which extends the existing results for uniform stability (Lei et al., 2021). We further develop the first nearly optimal convergence rates for convex-concave problems both in expectation and with high probability, which, combined with our stability results, show that the optimal generalization bounds can be attained for both smooth and non-smooth cases. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first generalization analysis of SGMs when the gradients are sampled from a Markov process.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic gradient methods whose gradients are sampled through a Markov process. Earlier analyses largely examined whether these methods converge during optimization. The authors instead also ask how their learned solutions generalize, covering both minimization and minimax learning problems through algorithmic stability.

Their key tool is on-average argument stability, which tracks the average sensitivity of the learned solution to changes in training data. For empirical risk minimization, it yields optimal excess population-risk bounds in both smooth and nonsmooth cases. For minimax problems, the authors establish a quantitative relationship between this stability notion and generalization error, extending earlier results based on uniform stability.

Combining those optimization results with stability establishes attainable optimal generalization bounds for smooth and nonsmooth cases. The contribution thus connects optimization progress with statistical performance when gradient samples have the dependence induced by a Markov process.
summary.tldr: A stability analysis establishes generalization guarantees for stochastic gradient methods with Markov-dependent samples, including minimization and convex-concave minimax problems.

title: Stability and Generalization for Markov Chain Stochastic Gradient Methods

abstract: We show the universality of depth-2 group convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) in a unified and constructive manner based on the ridgelet theory. Despite widespread use in applications, the approximation property of (G)CNNs has not been well investigated. The universality of (G)CNNs has been shown since the late 2010s. Yet, our understanding on how (G)CNNs represent functions is incomplete because the past universality theorems have been shown in a case-by-case manner by manually/carefully assigning the network parameters depending on the variety of convolution layers, and in an indirect manner by converting/modifying the (G)CNNs into other universal approximators such as invariant polynomials and fully-connected networks. In this study, we formulate a versatile depth-2 continuous GCNN $S[\gamma]$ as a nonlinear mapping between group representations, and directly obtain an analysis operator, called the ridgelet trasform, that maps a given function $f$ to the network parameter $\gamma$ so that $S[\gamma]=f$. The proposed GCNN covers typical GCNNs such as the cyclic convolution on multi-channel images, networks on permutation-invariant inputs (Deep Sets), and $\mathrm{E}(n)$-equivariant networks. The closed-form expression of the ridgelet transform can describe how the network parameters are organized to represent a function. While it has been known only for fully-connected networks, this study is the first to obtain the ridgelet transform for GCNNs. By discretizing the closed-form expression, we can systematically generate a constructive proof of the $cc$-universality of finite GCNNs. In other words, our universality proofs are more unified and constructive than previous proofs.

This connects an explicit continuous representation with finite-network approximation guarantees. The significance lies in the description of how parameters are organized to represent a function, alongside the unification of several network types within one analysis. The authors identify this as the first ridgelet-transform construction for group convolutional neural networks.
summary.tldr: A ridgelet transform provides an explicit, unified route from target functions to universality proofs for depth-two group convolutional networks.

title: Universality of Group Convolutional Neural Networks Based on Ridgelet Analysis on Groups

abstract: We study robust reinforcement learning (RL) with the goal of determining a well-performing policy that is robust against model mismatch between the training simulator and the testing environment. Previous policy-based robust RL algorithms mainly focus on the tabular setting under uncertainty sets that facilitate robust policy evaluation, but are no longer tractable when the number of states scales up. To this end, we propose two novel uncertainty set formulations, one based on double sampling and the other on an integral probability metric. Both make large-scale robust RL tractable even when one only has access to a simulator. We propose a robust natural actor-critic (RNAC) approach that incorporates the new uncertainty sets and employs function approximation. We provide finite-time convergence guarantees for the proposed RNAC algorithm to the optimal robust policy within the function approximation error. Finally, we demonstrate the robust performance of the policy learned by our proposed RNAC approach in multiple MuJoCo environments and a real-world TurtleBot navigation task.

paragraphs: A policy trained in a simulator may encounter different dynamics when deployed. Robust reinforcement learning seeks policies that perform well despite this model mismatch. The paper addresses a scalability obstacle: earlier policy-based robust methods mainly use tabular representations and uncertainty sets that become intractable as the number of states grows.

The authors introduce two uncertainty-set formulations, one based on double sampling and another on an integral probability metric. Both are designed to make large-scale robust learning tractable when access is limited to a simulator. Their robust natural actor-critic algorithm, RNAC, incorporates these formulations and uses function approximation to represent quantities needed for learning.

The paper provides finite-time convergence guarantees toward an optimal robust policy, with accuracy limited by function approximation error. That qualification connects the guarantee to the capabilities of the chosen representation. Experiments in multiple MuJoCo environments and a real-world TurtleBot navigation task demonstrate robust performance. Together, the results offer a theoretical and practical route beyond tabular robust learning for simulator-trained policies.
summary.tldr: RNAC combines tractable uncertainty sets with function approximation to learn robust policies, with convergence guarantees up to approximation error.

title: Natural Actor-Critic for Robust Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation

abstract: A desirable data selection algorithm can efficiently choose the most informative samples to maximize the utility of limited annotation budgets. However, current approaches, represented by active learning methods, typically follow a cumbersome pipeline that iterates the time-consuming model training and batch data selection repeatedly. In this paper, we challenge this status quo by designing a distinct data selection pipeline that utilizes existing general-purpose models to select data from various datasets with a single-pass inference without the need for additional training or supervision. A novel free data selection (FreeSel) method is proposed following this new pipeline. Specifically, we define semantic patterns extracted from inter-mediate features of the general-purpose model to capture subtle local information in each image. We then enable the selection of all data samples in a single pass through distance-based sampling at the fine-grained semantic pattern level. FreeSel bypasses the heavy batch selection process, achieving a significant improvement in efficiency and being 530x faster than existing active learning methods. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of FreeSel on various computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: When annotation budgets are limited, choosing informative examples can be as important as choosing a learning algorithm. Many active-learning methods repeatedly alternate between training a model and selecting another batch of data. This paper proposes a different pipeline: use an existing general-purpose model to select examples through a single inference pass, without additional training or supervision for selection.

The resulting method, FreeSel, extracts semantic patterns from intermediate model features. These patterns capture subtle local information within each image. It then performs distance-based sampling at the level of those fine-grained patterns to select the data in one pass. The selection process therefore uses information already available inside the general-purpose model instead of repeatedly retraining a selector.

The authors report that FreeSel is 530 times faster than existing active-learning methods in their comparison, and experiments support its effectiveness across several computer-vision tasks. The efficiency gain comes from bypassing the repeated batch-selection pipeline. The term free refers to avoiding additional training and supervision in this approach; the method still performs inference and sampling to choose examples.
summary.tldr: FreeSel selects informative images using existing model features in a single inference pass, avoiding repeated training and batch selection.

title: Towards Free Data Selection with General-Purpose Models

abstract: We introduce a novel policy learning method that integrates analytical gradients from differentiable environments with the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. To incorporate analytical gradients into the PPO framework, we introduce the concept of an α-policy that stands as a locally superior policy. By adaptively modifying the α value, we can effectively manage the influence of analytical policy gradients during learning. To this end, we suggest metrics for assessing the variance and bias of analytical gradients, reducing dependence on these gradients when high variance or bias is detected. Our proposed approach outperforms baseline algorithms in various scenarios, such as function optimization, physics simulations, and traffic control environments. Our code can be found online: https://github.com/SonSang/gippo.

paragraphs: Differentiable environments make analytical gradients available for learning a policy, providing information about how changes in behavior affect outcomes. This paper integrates that information with Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO. Its central concern is how to use these gradients while adjusting their influence when their estimates are unreliable.

The method introduces an α-policy, described as a locally superior policy, to bring analytical gradients into the PPO framework. Changing α controls how strongly those gradients affect learning. The authors also propose measures of gradient variance and bias, reducing reliance on analytical gradients when either measure indicates a problem. The local qualification matters: the construction does not assert that this policy is globally optimal.

Evaluations cover function optimization, physics simulations, and traffic control environments, with the proposed method outperforming baseline algorithms in the reported scenarios. The contribution is an adaptive connection between PPO and information available from differentiable environments. Its findings support modulating that extra information according to estimated reliability instead of assigning it an unchanging role throughout training.
summary.tldr: The method augments PPO with analytical environment gradients and adaptively reduces their influence when estimated bias or variance is high.

title: Gradient Informed Proximal Policy Optimization

abstract: Understanding the behavior of non-human primates is crucial for improving animal welfare, modeling social behavior, and gaining insights into distinctively human and phylogenetically shared behaviors. However, the lack of datasets on non-human primate behavior hinders in-depth exploration of primate social interactions, posing challenges to research on our closest living relatives. To address these limitations, we present ChimpACT, a comprehensive dataset for quantifying the longitudinal behavior and social relations of chimpanzees within a social group. Spanning from 2015 to 2018, ChimpACT features videos of a group of over 20 chimpanzees residing at the Leipzig Zoo, Germany, with a particular focus on documenting the developmental trajectory of one young male, Azibo. ChimpACT is both comprehensive and challenging, consisting of 163 videos with a cumulative 160,500 frames, each richly annotated with detection, identification, pose estimation, and fine-grained spatiotemporal behavior labels. We benchmark representative methods of three tracks on ChimpACT: (i) tracking and identification, (ii) pose estimation, and (iii) spatiotemporal action detection of the chimpanzees. Our experiments reveal that ChimpACT offers ample opportunities for both devising new methods and adapting existing ones to solve fundamental computer vision tasks applied to chimpanzee groups, such as detection, pose estimation, and behavior analysis, ultimately deepening our comprehension of communication and sociality in non-human primates.

These complementary labels support analysis of who appears, how they move, and what they do within the observed social group.

Their experiments identify opportunities to adapt existing vision methods and develop new ones for chimpanzee groups. The main contribution is therefore a richly annotated longitudinal resource and a set of benchmarks that can support more detailed computational study of primate communication and sociality.
summary.tldr: ChimpACT provides richly annotated longitudinal videos and benchmarks for studying chimpanzee identity, pose, behavior, and social relationships.

title: ChimpACT: A Longitudinal Dataset for Understanding Chimpanzee Behaviors

abstract: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) aims to recover independent latent variables from observed mixtures thereof. Causal Representation Learning (CRL) aims instead to infer causally related (thus often statistically _dependent_) latent variables, together with the unknown graph encoding their causal relationships. We introduce an intermediate problem termed _Causal Component Analysis (CauCA)_. CauCA can be viewed as a generalization of ICA, modelling the causal dependence among the latent components, and as a special case of CRL. In contrast to CRL, it presupposes knowledge of the causal graph, focusing solely on learning the unmixing function and the causal mechanisms. Any impossibility results regarding the recovery of the ground truth in CauCA also apply for CRL, while possibility results may serve as a stepping stone for extensions to CRL. We characterize CauCA identifiability from multiple datasets generated through different types of interventions on the latent causal variables. As a corollary, this interventional perspective also leads to new identifiability results for nonlinear ICA—a special case of CauCA with an empty graph—requiring strictly fewer datasets than previous results. We introduce a likelihood-based approach using normalizing flows to estimate both the unmixing function and the causal mechanisms, and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive synthetic experiments in the CauCA and ICA setting.

paragraphs: Observed data can mix together hidden factors that influence one another. Independent Component Analysis seeks independent factors, while causal representation learning also tries to discover their causal relationships. This paper introduces Causal Component Analysis, an intermediate problem that assumes the causal graph is already known and learns how to separate the observations and recover the causal mechanisms.

The authors characterize when those hidden components can be identified using multiple datasets produced by interventions on the latent variables. The known-graph assumption makes the problem more focused: impossibility results also constrain the broader causal representation learning problem, while successful recovery results may help develop solutions for it. An empty causal graph gives nonlinear ICA as a special case.

This intervention-based analysis yields new nonlinear ICA identifiability results requiring strictly fewer datasets than previous results. The paper also develops a likelihood-based estimator using normalizing flows to learn both the unmixing function and causal mechanisms. Synthetic experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in the CauCA and ICA settings, connecting the recovery analysis to a practical estimation approach.
summary.tldr: Causal Component Analysis studies recovering interacting hidden factors when their causal graph is known, with intervention-based guarantees and a flow-based estimator.

title: Causal Component Analysis

abstract: Existing methods for adapting Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to scene changes require extensive data capture and model retraining, which is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of efficiently adapting NeRFs to real-world scene changes over time using a few new images while retaining the memory of unaltered areas, focusing on the continual learning aspect of NeRFs. To this end, we propose CL-NeRF, which consists of two key components: a lightweight expert adaptor for adapting to new changes and evolving scene representations and a conflict-aware knowledge distillation learning objective for memorizing unchanged parts. We also present a new benchmark for evaluating Continual Learning of NeRFs with comprehensive metrics. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that CL-NeRF can synthesize high-quality novel views of both changed and unchanged regions with high training efficiency, surpassing existing methods in terms of reducing forgetting and adapting to changes. Code and benchmark will be made available.

paragraphs: A scene representation must adapt when the physical scene changes, while preserving what it already knows about areas that remain the same. Existing approaches for updating neural radiance fields can require substantial new image capture and retraining. CL-NeRF studies continual updates using only a few new images, making adaptation and memory preservation joint objectives.

The method combines two components with distinct roles. A lightweight expert adaptor handles new changes and the evolving scene representation. A conflict-aware knowledge distillation objective helps retain information about unchanged regions. Together, these components address the tension between incorporating new observations and forgetting previously learned parts of the scene.

The authors also introduce a benchmark and evaluation metrics for continual learning of neural radiance fields. Their experiments report high-quality views from new viewpoints in both changed and unchanged regions, alongside efficient training. Compared with existing methods, CL-NeRF improves adaptation and reduces forgetting. The findings support treating scene updates as an ongoing learning problem with explicit mechanisms for both change and retention.
summary.tldr: CL-NeRF updates evolving scenes from a few new images while using an adaptor and knowledge distillation to reduce forgetting.

title: CL-NeRF: Continual Learning of Neural Radiance Fields for Evolving Scene Representation

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to multiobjective algorithms aimed at modeling the Pareto set using neural networks. Whereas previous methods mainly focused on identifying a finite number of solutions, our approach allows for the direct modeling of the entire Pareto set. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between learning the complete Pareto set and maximizing the associated hypervolume, which enables the convergence analysis of hypervolume (as a new metric) for Pareto set learning. Specifically, our new analysis framework reveals the connection between the learned Pareto solution and its representation in a polar coordinate system. We evaluate our proposed approach on various benchmark problems and real-world problems, and the encouraging results make it a potentially viable alternative to existing multiobjective algorithms. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/xzhang2523/hvpsl/tree/master}.

paragraphs: Multiobjective optimization involves finding useful tradeoffs between competing objectives. The Pareto set describes solutions for which improving one objective requires sacrificing another. Many approaches identify a finite collection of such solutions. This paper instead uses a neural network to directly model the entire set, aiming to represent the broader structure of available tradeoffs.

The authors establish an equivalence between learning the complete Pareto set and maximizing its associated hypervolume. This supplies a geometric objective for learning and enables an analysis of convergence through hypervolume. Their framework also relates a learned Pareto solution to its representation in polar coordinates, connecting the network's outputs to the geometry underlying the optimization problem.

The method is evaluated on benchmark problems and real-world problems, with encouraging results. The authors position it as a potentially viable alternative to existing multiobjective algorithms. Its significance lies in combining a representation of the complete tradeoff set with a geometric learning criterion that can be analyzed, extending the focus beyond selecting isolated candidate solutions.
summary.tldr: The paper connects neural modeling of the complete Pareto set to hypervolume maximization, enabling geometric convergence analysis.

title: Hypervolume Maximization: A Geometric View of Pareto Set Learning

abstract: It is extremely difficult to train a superhuman Artificial Intelligence (AI) for games of similar size to StarCraft II. AlphaStar is the first AI that beat human professionals in the full game of StarCraft II, using a league training framework that is inspired by a game-theoretic approach. In this paper, we improve AlphaStar's league training in two significant aspects. We train goal-conditioned exploiters, whose abilities of spotting weaknesses in the main agent and the entire league are greatly improved compared to the unconditioned exploiters in AlphaStar. In addition, we endow the agents in the league with the new ability of opponent modeling, which makes the agent more responsive to the opponent's real-time strategy. Based on these improvements, we train a better and superhuman AI with orders of magnitude less resources than AlphaStar (see Table 1 for a full comparison). Considering the iconic role of StarCraft II in game AI research, we believe our method and results on StarCraft II provide valuable design principles on how one would utilize the general league training framework for obtaining a least-exploitable strategy in various, large-scale, real-world games.

paragraphs: League training develops game-playing agents through competition within a population. This paper improves the league framework used by AlphaStar for StarCraft II, focusing on two related problems: discovering weaknesses in trained strategies and responding to an opponent's strategy during play. Both matter when a strong agent can still have exploitable vulnerabilities.

The first change is to train goal-conditioned exploiters: agents guided by goals while seeking weaknesses in the main agent and the broader league. The authors report that these exploiters uncover weaknesses substantially better than AlphaStar's unconditioned versions. The second change adds opponent modeling, allowing league agents to respond more directly to the opponent's current strategy.

Together, these changes produce an AI reported to be stronger and superhuman while using orders of magnitude fewer resources than AlphaStar. The result supports the practical value of improving both the challenges generated during training and the information used during play. The authors also suggest these design principles could help league training pursue less exploitable strategies in other large games.
summary.tldr: Goal-conditioned exploiters and opponent modeling improve StarCraft II league training, producing a reported superhuman agent with far fewer resources than AlphaStar.

title: A Robust and Opponent-Aware League Training Method for StarCraft II

abstract: As a nonlinear dimension reduction technique, the diffusion map (DM) has been widely used. In DM, kernels play an important role for capturing the nonlinear relationship of data. However, only symmetric kernels can be used now, which prevents the use of DM in directed graphs, trophic networks, and other real-world scenarios where the intrinsic and extrinsic geometries in data are asymmetric. A promising technique is the magnetic transform which converts an asymmetric matrix to a Hermitian one. However, we are facing essential problems, including how diffusion distance could be preserved and how divergence could be avoided during diffusion process. Via theoretical proof, we successfully establish a diffusion representation framework with the magnetic transform, named MagDM. The effectiveness and robustness for dealing data endowed with asymmetric proximity are demonstrated on three synthetic datasets and two trophic networks.

paragraphs: Diffusion maps reduce dimensionality by using a kernel to describe nonlinear relationships among data points. The paper addresses a restriction of the existing framework: its reliance on symmetric kernels. Directional relationships in graphs and trophic networks do not naturally fit that requirement, because proximity in one direction need not match proximity in the reverse direction.

The authors develop MagDM around a magnetic transform, which converts an asymmetric matrix into a Hermitian matrix. Simply performing that conversion leaves important mathematical questions unresolved. A diffusion representation must retain a meaningful diffusion distance and avoid divergence as diffusion proceeds. The paper supplies a theoretical foundation for a framework using the transform to address these issues.

Experiments on three synthetic datasets and two trophic networks demonstrate effectiveness and robustness for data with asymmetric proximity. The contribution extends the diffusion representation framework to accommodate directional structure. This matters for settings where asymmetry carries information that a method restricted to symmetric relationships cannot directly represent.
summary.tldr: MagDM uses a theoretically grounded magnetic transform to extend diffusion representations to asymmetric relationships.

title: Diffusion Representation for Asymmetric Kernels via Magnetic Transform

abstract: We investigate a novel safe reinforcement learning problem with step-wise violation constraints. Our problem differs from existing works in that we focus on stricter step-wise violation constraints and do not assume the existence of safe actions, making our formulation more suitable for safety-critical applications that need to ensure safety in all decision steps but may not always possess safe actions, e.g., robot control and autonomous driving.We propose an efficient algorithm SUCBVI, which guarantees $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{ST})$ or gap-dependent $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(S/\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{gap}} + S^2AH^2)$ step-wise violation and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^3SAT})$ regret. Lower bounds are provided to validate the optimality in both violation and regret performance with respect to the number of states $S$ and the total number of steps $T$. Moreover, we further study an innovative safe reward-free exploration problem with step-wise violation constraints. For this problem, we design algorithm SRF-UCRL to find a near-optimal safe policy, which achieves nearly state-of-the-art sample complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}((\frac{S^2AH^2}{\varepsilon}+\frac{H^4SA}{\varepsilon^2})(\log(\frac{1}{\delta})+S))$, and guarantees $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{ST})$ violation during exploration. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our algorithms in safety performance and corroborate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with safety constraints applied at individual decision steps. Its formulation does not assume that a safe action is always available, reflecting situations where avoiding every violation may be impossible. The goal is to control violations while still learning to obtain reward, rather than relying on a permanently available safe choice.

The proposed SUCBVI algorithm has theoretical bounds on both step-wise violation and regret. Its violation bound scales as the square root of the number of states times the total interaction steps, with logarithmic factors suppressed; the authors also provide a gap-dependent alternative. Lower bounds establish optimal dependence on state count and total steps for both violation and regret.

The paper additionally considers safe exploration before a reward function is supplied. Its SRF-UCRL algorithm seeks a near-optimal safe policy with nearly state-of-the-art sample complexity while controlling violations during exploration. Experiments support the theoretical results and report better safety performance. These guarantees bound violations during learning; they do not assert that every individual action is violation-free.
summary.tldr: Two reinforcement-learning algorithms bound step-wise safety violations without assuming safe actions always exist.

title: Provably Safe Reinforcement Learning with Step-wise Violation Constraints

abstract: We introduce ViCA-NeRF, the *first* view-consistency-aware method for 3D editing with text instructions. In addition to the implicit neural radiance field (NeRF) modeling, our key insight is to exploit two sources of regularization that *explicitly* propagate the editing information across different views, thus ensuring multi-view consistency. For *geometric regularization*, we leverage the depth information derived from NeRF to establish image correspondences between different views. For *learned regularization*, we align the latent codes in the 2D diffusion model between edited and unedited images, enabling us to edit key views and propagate the update throughout the entire scene. Incorporating these two strategies, our ViCA-NeRF operates in two stages. In the initial stage, we blend edits from different views to create a preliminary 3D edit. This is followed by a second stage of NeRF training, dedicated to further refining the scene's appearance. Experimental results demonstrate that ViCA-NeRF provides more flexible, efficient (3 times faster) editing with higher levels of consistency and details, compared with the state of the art. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Dongjiahua/VICA-NeRF

paragraphs: Text-guided editing of a three-dimensional scene must keep the requested changes consistent when the scene is viewed from different directions. ViCA-NeRF addresses this by explicitly sharing editing information across views, alongside the scene representation supplied by a neural radiance field. The method combines geometric relationships with learned image representations to coordinate the edits.

Its geometric regularization uses depth from the NeRF to establish correspondences between views. Its learned regularization aligns latent codes from a two-dimensional diffusion model between edited and unedited images. Together, these mechanisms allow edits made to key views to propagate throughout the scene, linking appearance changes to both scene geometry and learned visual information.

The process has two stages: blending edits from multiple views into a preliminary three-dimensional result, then training the NeRF further to refine its appearance. Experiments report more flexible editing, greater consistency and detail, and a threefold speed improvement over the state of the art. These results support explicit cross-view propagation as a way to improve both the coherence and efficiency of scene editing.
summary.tldr: ViCA-NeRF propagates text-guided edits across views using geometry and diffusion-model representations, improving reported consistency, detail, and speed.

title: ViCA-NeRF: View-Consistency-Aware 3D Editing of Neural Radiance Fields

abstract: We focus on the task of approximating the optimal value function in deep reinforcement learning. This iterative process is comprised of solving a sequence of optimization problems where the loss function changes per iteration. The common approach to solving this sequence of problems is to employ modern variants of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm such as Adam. These optimizers maintain their own internal parameters such as estimates of the first-order and the second-order moments of the gradient, and update them over time. Therefore, information obtained in previous iterations is used to solve the optimization problem in the current iteration. We demonstrate that this can contaminate the moment estimates because the optimization landscape can change arbitrarily from one iteration to the next one. To hedge against this negative effect, a simple idea is to reset the internal parameters of the optimizer when starting a new iteration. We empirically investigate this resetting idea by employing various optimizers in conjunction with the Rainbow algorithm. We demonstrate that this simple modification significantly improves the performance of deep RL on the Atari benchmark.

paragraphs: Learning an optimal value function in deep reinforcement learning involves solving a sequence of optimization problems. The loss changes between iterations, but commonly used optimizers carry information forward. Adam and related methods maintain internal estimates of gradient moments, so previous optimization problems influence how the current problem is solved.

The paper shows why this history can become problematic: the optimization landscape can change arbitrarily between iterations, contaminating the moment estimates. The proposed response is simple—reset the optimizer's internal parameters when a new iteration begins. The intervention concerns the optimizer's accumulated state, which is the source of the potentially outdated information.

The authors investigate this idea empirically with several optimizers used alongside the Rainbow algorithm. They report significant improvements on the Atari benchmark. The findings suggest that retaining optimizer history across changing objectives can be harmful in this setting and that a small procedural change can improve performance. The evidence supports resetting within the studied deep reinforcement learning setup, rather than establishing that optimizer memory is generally undesirable for every learning problem.
summary.tldr: Resetting optimizer state between changing value-learning objectives significantly improves Rainbow-based Atari performance in the reported experiments.

title: Resetting the Optimizer in Deep RL: An Empirical Study

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve problems more accurately and interpretably when instructed to work out the answer step by step using a "chain-of-thought" (CoT) prompt. One can also improve LLMs' performance on a specific task by supervised fine-tuning, i.e., by using gradient ascent on some tunable parameters to maximize the average log-likelihood of correct answers from a labeled training set. Naively combining CoT with supervised tuning requires supervision not just of the correct answers, but also of detailed rationales that lead to those answers; these rationales are expensive to produce by hand. Instead, we propose a fine-tuning strategy that tries to maximize the \emph{marginal} log-likelihood of generating a correct answer using CoT prompting, approximately averaging over all possible rationales. The core challenge is sampling from the posterior over rationales conditioned on the correct answer; we address it using a simple Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm inspired by the self-taught reasoner (STaR), memoized wake-sleep, Markovian score climbing, and persistent contrastive divergence. This algorithm also admits a novel control-variate technique that drives the variance of our gradient estimates to zero as the model improves. Applying our technique to GSM8K and the tasks in BIG-Bench Hard, we find that this MCMC-EM fine-tuning technique typically improves the model's accuracy on held-out examples more than STaR or prompt-tuning with or without CoT.

paragraphs: Step-by-step prompting can improve language-model problem solving, but directly supervising those steps requires costly written rationales. This paper proposes training from correct answers while treating the rationale as an unobserved variable. The objective approximately averages over possible rationales when maximizing the likelihood of producing the correct answer.

The main technical challenge is sampling rationales conditioned on that answer. The authors use a Markov chain Monte Carlo expectation-maximization algorithm, drawing inspiration from STaR and several latent-variable learning methods. They also introduce a control-variate technique that reduces noise in gradient estimates, with variance tending to zero as the model improves.

On GSM8K and BIG-Bench Hard tasks, this training method typically improves held-out accuracy more than STaR or prompt-tuning with or without chain-of-thought. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is typical across the evaluation, rather than universal. The approach offers a way to improve reasoning-oriented performance without requiring people to annotate detailed rationales, using probabilistic inference to connect possible reasoning paths with known correct answers.
summary.tldr: MCMC-EM fine-tuning treats rationales as latent variables and typically improves reasoning-task accuracy without manually labeled reasoning steps.

title: Training Chain-of-Thought via Latent-Variable Inference

abstract: Recent curriculum Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shown notable progress in solving complex tasks by proposing sequences of surrogate tasks. However, the previous approaches often face challenges when they generate curriculum goals in a high-dimensional space. Thus, they usually rely on manually specified goal spaces. To alleviate this limitation and improve the scalability of the curriculum, we propose a novel curriculum method that automatically defines the semantic goal space which contains vital information for the curriculum process, and suggests curriculum goals over it. To define the semantic goal space, our method discretizes continuous observations via vector quantized-variational autoencoders (VQ-VAE) and restores the temporal relations between the discretized observations by a graph. Concurrently, ours suggests uncertainty and temporal distance-aware curriculum goals that converges to the final goals over the automatically composed goal space. We demonstrate that the proposed method allows efficient explorations in an uninformed environment with raw goal examples only. Also, ours outperforms the state-of-the-art curriculum RL methods on data efficiency and performance, in various goal-reaching tasks even with ego-centric visual inputs.

title: CQM: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning with a Quantized World Model

abstract: Representation learning based on multi-task pretraining has become a powerful approach in many domains. In particular, task-aware representation learning aims to learn an optimal representation for a specific target task by sampling data from a set of source tasks, while task-agnostic representation learning seeks to learn a universal representation for a class of tasks. In this paper, we propose a general and versatile algorithmic and theoretic framework for \emph{active representation learning}, where the learner optimally chooses which source tasks to sample from. This framework, along with a tractable meta algorithm, allows most arbitrary target and source task spaces (from discrete to continuous), covers both task-aware and task-agnostic settings, and is compatible with deep representation learning practices. We provide several instantiations under this framework, from bilinear and feature-based nonlinear to general nonlinear cases. In the bilinear case, by leveraging the non-uniform spectrum of the task representation and the calibrated source-target relevance, we prove that the sample complexity to achieve $\varepsilon$-excess risk on target scales with $(k^*)^2 ||v^*||_2^2 \varepsilon^{-2}$ where $k^*$ is the effective dimension of the target and $||v^*||_2^2 \in (0,1]$ represents the connection between source and target space. Compared to the passive one, this can save up to $\frac{1}{d_W}$ of sample complexity, where $d_W$ is the task space dimension. Finally, we demonstrate different instantiations of our meta algorithm in synthetic datasets and robotics problems, from pendulum simulations to real-world drone flight datasets. On average, our algorithms outperform baselines by 20%-70%.

paragraphs: Learning across multiple tasks raises a practical question: which tasks should supply the training data? This paper studies active representation learning, where the learner chooses source tasks to support either one specific target task or a broader family of tasks. The aim is to spend samples where they contribute most to a useful shared representation.

The authors introduce a general framework and a tractable meta algorithm that accommodate task spaces ranging from discrete collections to continuous spaces. They give versions for bilinear, feature-based nonlinear, and general nonlinear settings. This breadth connects the task-selection problem to different forms of representation learning, including practices involving deep models.

For the bilinear setting, the sample-complexity result depends on the target's effective dimension and the relationship between source and target tasks. It identifies circumstances in which active selection can require substantially fewer samples than passive selection. Experiments cover synthetic data, pendulum simulations, and real drone flight datasets, with reported average improvements of 20%–70% over baselines. The theoretical savings belong to the specified bilinear setting, while the experiments illustrate broader practical applications.
summary.tldr: Actively choosing source tasks can make representation learning more sample-efficient, with theoretical guarantees in a bilinear setting and gains in robotics experiments.

title: Active representation learning for general task space with applications in robotics

abstract: Visual-Language Alignment (VLA) has gained a lot of attention since CLIP's groundbreaking work. Although CLIP performs well, the typical direct latent feature alignment lacks clarity in its representation and similarity scores. On the other hand, lexical representation, a vector whose element represents the similarity between the sample and a word from the vocabulary, is a natural sparse representation and interpretable, providing exact matches for individual words.However, lexical representations are difficult to learn due to no ground-truth supervision and false-discovery issues, and thus requires complex design to train effectively.In this paper, we introduce LexVLA, a more interpretable VLA framework by learning a unified lexical representation for both modalities without complex design. We use DINOv2 as our visual model for its local-inclined features and Llama 2, a generative language model, to leverage its in-context lexical prediction ability.To avoid the false discovery, we propose an overuse penalty to refrain the lexical representation from falsely frequently activating meaningless words.We demonstrate that these two pre-trained uni-modal models can be well-aligned by fine-tuning on the modest multi-modal dataset and avoid intricate training configurations. On cross-modal retrieval benchmarks, LexVLA, trained on the CC-12M multi-modal dataset, outperforms baselines fine-tuned on larger datasets (e.g., YFCC15M) and those trained from scratch on even bigger datasets (e.g., 1.1B data, including CC-12M).We conduct extensive experiments to analyze LexVLA. Codes are available at https://github.com/Clementine24/LexVLA.

paragraphs: LexVLA aims to make image-text alignment easier to interpret. Instead of comparing representations whose dimensions have unclear meanings, it represents each input through its similarities to vocabulary words. This gives the representation a lexical meaning, so individual word matches can help explain how images and text align.

Learning these representations is difficult without direct supervision and can produce meaningless word activations. LexVLA combines DINOv2's visual features with Llama 2's ability to predict lexical content in context. An overuse penalty discourages words from activating frequently without useful meaning. The two pretrained models are aligned through multimodal fine-tuning without an intricate training setup.

On cross-modal retrieval benchmarks, LexVLA trained on CC-12M outperforms the compared models fine-tuned on larger datasets and models trained from scratch on much larger collections. This finding supports the combination of lexical interpretability and competitive retrieval performance in the evaluated setting. The result also highlights how pretrained single-modality models can be brought into a shared word-based representation through multimodal alignment.
summary.tldr: LexVLA aligns images and text through interpretable vocabulary-based representations and outperforms larger-data comparators on reported retrieval benchmarks.

title: Unified Lexical Representation for Interpretable Visual-Language Alignment

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been very successful at tackling complex control problems, such as AlphaGo or fusion control. However, current research mainly emphasizes solution quality, often achieved by using large models trained on large amounts of data, and does not account for the financial, environmental, and societal costs associated with developing and deploying such models. Modern neural networks are often overparameterized and a significant number of parameters can be pruned without meaningful loss in performance, resulting in more efficient use of the model's capacity lottery ticket. We present a methodology for identifying sub-networks within a larger network in reinforcement learning (RL). We call such sub-networks, neural pathways. We show empirically that even very small learned sub-networks, using less than 5% of the large network's parameters, can provide very good quality solutions. We also demonstrate the training of multiple pathways within the same networks in a multitask setup, where each pathway is encouraged to tackle a separate task. We evaluate empirically our approach on several continuous control tasks, in both online and offline training

paragraphs: Strong reinforcement-learning results often rely on large networks and substantial training data. This paper asks how much of a network's capacity is actually needed for good control. It develops a method for finding useful subnetworks inside a larger model, calling these smaller computational structures neural pathways. The motivation is to use model capacity more efficiently.

The authors empirically show that learned pathways containing less than 5% of the original network's parameters can still produce very good solutions. This finding supports searching for compact parts of a large model that retain useful control behavior. It gives a concrete parameter-efficiency result without requiring every component of the larger network to participate in the resulting solution.

The approach also supports a multitask setting in which several pathways are trained within one network, with each encouraged to handle a separate task. Evaluations cover multiple continuous-control problems under both online and offline training. The results suggest that pathway discovery can support compact task solutions and task-specific use of shared network capacity.
summary.tldr: Learned neural pathways using less than 5% of a larger network's parameters can deliver strong reinforcement-learning solutions in the evaluated control tasks.

title: Efficient Reinforcement Learning by Discovering Neural Pathways

abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models may implicitly learn world models. How should we assess this possibility? We formalize this question for the case where the underlying reality is governed by a deterministic finite automaton. This includes problems as diverse as simple logical reasoning, geographic navigation, game-playing, and chemistry. We propose new evaluation metrics for world model recovery inspired by the classic Myhill-Nerode theorem from language theory. We illustrate their utility in three domains: game playing, logic puzzles, and navigation. In all domains, the generative models we consider do well on existing diagnostics for assessing world models, but our evaluation metrics reveal their world models to be far less coherent than they appear. Such incoherence creates fragility: using a generative model to solve related but subtly different tasks can lead to failures. Building generative models that meaningfully capture the underlying logic of the domains they model would be immensely valuable; our results suggest new ways to assess how close a given model is to that goal.

paragraphs: A generative model can perform well on familiar tasks without necessarily capturing a coherent account of the rules behind them. This paper asks how to assess claims that a model has learned an implicit world model. It formalizes the question for environments whose underlying behavior is governed by a deterministic finite automaton.

Within that setting, the authors develop evaluation metrics inspired by the Myhill-Nerode theorem from language theory. They apply the metrics to game playing, logic puzzles, and navigation. The goal is to assess recovery of the underlying world structure, extending evaluation beyond the diagnostics already used to support world-model claims.

Across all three domains, the evaluated generative models perform well on existing diagnostics, but the new metrics reveal substantially less coherent world models. The authors connect this incoherence to fragility: related tasks with subtle changes can lead to failures. The contribution is therefore an evaluation framework that exposes gaps between apparent competence and structural understanding in the studied automaton-based setting.
summary.tldr: New automaton-based evaluations reveal incoherent implicit world models that existing diagnostics miss in game playing, logic, and navigation.

title: Evaluating the World Model Implicit in a Generative Model

abstract: This paper presents a method for estimating the hallucination rate for in-context learning (ICL) with generative AI. In ICL, a conditional generative model (CGM) is prompted with a dataset and a prediction question and asked to generate a response. One interpretation of ICL assumes that the CGM computes the posterior predictive of an unknown Bayesian model, which implicitly defines a joint distribution over observable datasets and latent mechanisms. This joint distribution factorizes into two components: the model prior over mechanisms and the model likelihood of datasets given a mechanism. With this perspective, we define a \textit{hallucination} as a generated response to the prediction question with low model likelihood given the mechanism. We develop a new method that takes an ICL problem and estimates the probability that a CGM will generate a hallucination. Our method only requires generating prediction questions and responses from the CGM and evaluating its response log probability. We empirically evaluate our method using large language models for synthetic regression and natural language ICL tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies hallucination in in-context learning, where a generative model receives a dataset and a prediction question. Its starting point is a Bayesian interpretation: the model behaves as though it predicts using an unknown probabilistic model connecting observed datasets with hidden mechanisms. That interpretation supplies a specific meaning for hallucination.

Under this perspective, a hallucination is a generated answer with low likelihood given the underlying mechanism. The authors develop a method for estimating the probability of such an answer for a particular in-context learning problem. The method requires generating prediction questions and responses from the model and evaluating the log probabilities of its responses.

The authors empirically evaluate the estimator using language models on synthetic regression and natural-language in-context learning tasks. The contribution is a way to estimate a hallucination rate through model generation and probability evaluation within the stated probabilistic framework. Because the definition is tied to likelihood under a mechanism, its interpretation depends on that framework rather than automatically covering every everyday use of the word hallucination.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework estimates in-context hallucination rates using generated questions, responses, and response log probabilities.

title: Estimating the Hallucination Rate of Generative AI

abstract: Understanding how the collective activity of neural populations relates to computation and ultimately behavior is a key goal in neuroscience. To this end, statistical methods which describe high-dimensional neural time series in terms of low-dimensional latent dynamics have played a fundamental role in characterizing neural systems. Yet, what constitutes a successful method involves two opposing criteria: (1) methods should be expressive enough to capture complex nonlinear dynamics, and (2) they should maintain a notion of interpretability often only warranted by simpler linear models. In this paper, we develop an approach that balances these two objectives: the Gaussian Process Switching Linear Dynamical System (gpSLDS). Our method builds on previous work modeling the latent state evolution via a stochastic differential equation whose nonlinear dynamics are described by a Gaussian process (GP-SDEs). We propose a novel kernel function which enforces smoothly interpolated locally linear dynamics, and therefore expresses flexible -- yet interpretable -- dynamics akin to those of recurrent switching linear dynamical systems (rSLDS). Our approach resolves key limitations of the rSLDS such as artifactual oscillations in dynamics near discrete state boundaries, while also providing posterior uncertainty estimates of the dynamics. To fit our models, we leverage a modified learning objective which improves the estimation accuracy of kernel hyperparameters compared to previous GP-SDE fitting approaches. We apply our method to synthetic data and data recorded in two neuroscience experiments and demonstrate favorable performance in comparison to the rSLDS.

paragraphs: Neural population recordings contain many signals that change together over time. Researchers describe this activity through a smaller set of hidden variables and study how those variables evolve. The challenge is to capture complicated nonlinear behavior while keeping the resulting description understandable. This paper introduces the Gaussian Process Switching Linear Dynamical System, or gpSLDS, to balance those goals.

The method builds on models that use a Gaussian process to describe nonlinear dynamics within a stochastic differential equation. Its central contribution is a new kernel, which controls the structure of those dynamics. The kernel makes the dynamics locally linear while blending smoothly between these local descriptions. This combines the interpretability of linear models with flexibility to describe more complex evolution.

Smooth blending addresses artificial oscillations that can occur near discrete state boundaries in recurrent switching linear dynamical systems. The method also provides posterior uncertainty estimates for the dynamics. A modified training objective improves estimation of kernel hyperparameters compared with previous fitting approaches for Gaussian-process stochastic differential equations. On synthetic data and recordings from two neuroscience experiments, the authors report favorable performance relative to recurrent switching linear dynamical systems. These results support the approach as a way to combine flexible dynamics, interpretable local structure, and uncertainty estimates.
summary.tldr: gpSLDS models neural dynamics by smoothly blending locally linear descriptions, combining flexibility, interpretability, and uncertainty estimates with favorable reported performance against recurrent switching linear dynamical systems.

title: Modeling Latent Neural Dynamics with Gaussian Process Switching Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: The recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) show promising results on the novel view synthesis (NVS) task. With its superior rendering performance and high-fidelity rendering quality, 3DGS is excelling at its previous NeRF counterparts. The most recent 3DGS method focuses either on improving the instability of rendering efficiency or reducing the model size. On the other hand, the training efficiency of 3DGS on large-scale scenes has not gained much attention. In this work, we propose DoGaussian, a method that trains 3DGS distributedly. Our method first decomposes a scene into $K$ blocks and then introduces the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) into the training procedure of 3DGS. During training, our DoGaussian maintains one global 3DGS model on the master node and $K$ local 3DGS models on the slave nodes. The $K$ local 3DGS models are dropped after training and we only query the global 3DGS model during inference. The training time is reduced by scene decomposition, and the training convergence and stability are guaranteed through the consensus on the shared 3D Gaussians. Our method accelerates the training of 3DGS by $6+$ times when evaluated on large-scale scenes while concurrently achieving state-of-the-art rendering quality. Our code is publicly available at [https://github.com/AIBluefisher/DOGS](https://github.com/AIBluefisher/DOGS).

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting offers fast, high-quality rendering of scenes from new viewpoints, but training on large scenes remains a separate efficiency challenge. This paper introduces DoGaussian, a distributed training method that divides a scene into blocks. The aim is to accelerate learning while retaining a coherent scene model suitable for rendering after training.

The method maintains one global model on a master node and separate local models for the scene blocks on worker nodes. It incorporates the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers to coordinate training through agreement on shared 3D Gaussians. This consensus mechanism connects the local computations and provides the stated guarantees for training convergence and stability.

After training, the local models are discarded, and inference uses only the global model. The distributed arrangement therefore serves the training process without requiring all the local models for subsequent rendering. On the evaluated large-scale scenes, the approach accelerates training by more than six times while achieving state-of-the-art rendering quality. The results show that coordinated scene decomposition can improve training speed alongside strong visual reconstruction.
summary.tldr: DoGaussian coordinates distributed scene-block training through Gaussian consensus, achieving over sixfold training acceleration on evaluated large scenes.

title: DOGS: Distributed-Oriented Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale 3D Reconstruction Via Gaussian Consensus

abstract: The metric backbone of a weighted graph is the union of all-pairs shortest paths. It is obtained by removing all edges $(u,v)$ that are not the shortest path between $u$ and $v$. In networks with well-separated communities, the metric backbone tends to preserve many inter-community edges, because these edges serve as bridges connecting two communities, but tends to delete many intra-community edges because the communities are dense. This suggests that the metric backbone would dilute or destroy the community structure of the network. However, this is not borne out by prior empirical work, which instead showed that the metric backbone of real networks preserves the community structure of the original network well. In this work, we analyze the metric backbone of a broad class of weighted random graphs with communities, and we formally prove the robustness of the community structure with respect to the deletion of all the edges that are not in the metric backbone. An empirical comparison of several graph sparsification techniques confirms our theoretical finding and shows that the metric backbone is an efficient sparsifier in the presence of communities.

paragraphs: A weighted graph’s metric backbone retains the edges belonging to shortest paths and removes edges for which a shorter route exists between their endpoints. This creates an apparent problem for community structure. Dense communities offer many alternative internal routes, while edges between communities often serve as bridges, so pruning appears likely to weaken the distinction between communities.

Earlier empirical work nevertheless found that metric backbones preserve community structure well in real networks. This paper investigates that discrepancy mathematically. The authors analyze a broad class of weighted random graphs with communities and prove that their community structure is robust to removing every edge outside the metric backbone.

They also compare graph sparsification techniques empirically, finding support for the theoretical result and showing that the metric backbone is an efficient sparsifier when communities are present. The result explains why preferentially deleting many within-community edges need not destroy the larger grouping structure. Its formal guarantee concerns the analyzed random-graph class, while the empirical comparison provides complementary evidence about the sparsification method.
summary.tldr: The paper proves community robustness under metric-backbone pruning for a broad weighted random-graph class and supports it empirically.

title: Why the Metric Backbone Preserves Community Structure

abstract: As a widely explored multi-modal task, Temporal Sentence Grounding in videos (TSG) endeavors to retrieve a specific video segment matched with a given query text from a video. The traditional paradigm for TSG generally assumes that relevant segments always exist within a given video. However, this assumption is restrictive and unrealistic in real-world applications where the existence of a query-related segment is uncertain, easily resulting in erroneous grounding. Motivated by the research gap and practical application, this paper introduces a new task, named Temporal Sentence Grounding with Relevance Feedback (TSG-RF) in videos, which accommodates the possibility that a video may or may not include a segment related to the query. This task entails localizing precise video segments that semantically align with the query text when such content is present, while delivering definitive feedback on the non-existence of related segments when absent. Moreover, we propose a novel Relation-aware Temporal Sentence Grounding (RaTSG) network for addressing this challenging task. This network first reformulates the TSG-RF task as a foreground-background detection problem by investigating whether the query-related semantics exist in both frame and video levels. Then, a multi-granularity relevance discriminator is exploited to produce precise video-query relevance feedback and a relation-aware segment grounding module is employed to selectively conduct the grounding process, dynamically adapting to the presence or absence of query-related segments in videos. To validate our RaTSG network, we reconstruct two popular TSG datasets, establishing a rigorous benchmark for TSG-RF. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed RaTSG for the TSG-RF task. Our source code is available at https://github.com/HuiGuanLab/RaTSG.

This task entails localizing precise video segments that semantically align with the query text when such content is present, while delivering definitive feedback on the non-existence of related segments when absent. This network first reformulates the TSG-RF task as a foreground-background detection problem by investigating whether the query-related semantics exist in both frame and video levels. Then, a multi-granularity relevance discriminator is exploited to produce precise video-query relevance feedback and a relation-aware segment grounding module is employed to selectively conduct the grounding process, dynamically adapting to the presence or absence of query-related segments in videos. To validate our RaTSG network, we reconstruct two popular TSG datasets, establishing a rigorous benchmark for TSG-RF. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed RaTSG for the TSG-RF task. Our source code is available at https://github.com/HuiGuanLab/RaTSG.

paragraphs: Temporal sentence grounding locates the part of a video that matches a written query. Traditional formulations assume that a matching segment exists, which can lead to an erroneous result when the requested content is absent. This paper introduces a task that explicitly includes both possibilities: locate relevant content when present, and report its absence otherwise.

The proposed RaTSG network treats this as a foreground-background detection problem, checking for query-related meaning at both frame and whole-video levels. A relevance discriminator combines information at multiple granularities to assess whether the video matches the query. A relation-aware grounding module then selectively performs localization according to the presence or absence of relevant segments.

The researchers reconstruct two established temporal-grounding datasets to create a benchmark for this expanded task. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RaTSG in that setting. The contribution changes both the evaluation problem and the model behavior, making the decision that a video contains no relevant segment an explicit part of video retrieval.
summary.tldr: RaTSG locates video segments matching a query and provides relevance feedback when the requested content is absent.

title: Temporal Sentence Grounding with Relevance Feedback in Videos

abstract: Atmospheric turbulence, caused by random fluctuations in the atmosphere's refractive index, introduces complex spatio-temporal distortions in imagery captured at long range. Video Atmospheric Turbulence Mitigation (ATM) aims to restore videos affected by these distortions. However, existing video ATM methods, both supervised and self-supervised, struggle to maintain temporally consistent mitigation across frames, leading to visually incoherent results. This limitation arises from the stochastic nature of atmospheric turbulence, which varies across space and time. Inspired by the observation that atmospheric turbulence induces high-frequency temporal variations, we propose ConVRT, a novel framework for consistent video restoration through turbulence. ConVRT introduces a neural video representation that explicitly decouples spatial and temporal information into a spatial content field and a temporal deformation field, enabling targeted regularization of the network's temporal representation capability. By leveraging the low-pass filtering properties of the regularized temporal representations, ConVRT effectively mitigates turbulence-induced temporal frequency variations and promotes temporal consistency. Furthermore, our training framework seamlessly integrates supervised pre-training on synthetic turbulence data with self-supervised learning on real-world videos, significantly improving the temporally consistent mitigation of ATM methods on diverse real-world data. More information can be found on our project page: https://convrt-2024.github.io/

paragraphs: Atmospheric turbulence distorts long-range video through fluctuations in how the atmosphere refracts light. Restoring individual frames does not necessarily produce a coherent video, because the distortions vary across space and time. This paper introduces ConVRT to improve consistency across frames while mitigating those turbulence effects.

ConVRT builds on the observation that turbulence introduces high-frequency temporal variation. Its neural video representation separates spatial content from temporal deformation, allowing the temporal part to be regularized specifically. The regularized representation acts as a low-pass filter, suppressing the rapid temporal variations associated with turbulence and promoting more stable restored sequences.

The training framework combines supervised pretraining on synthetic turbulence with self-supervised learning on real-world videos. This links learning from controlled synthetic examples to restoration of actual recordings. The authors report significantly improved temporal consistency across diverse real-world data. The key contribution is the connection between a physical observation about turbulence and a representation whose temporal behavior can be directly controlled, making coherence across frames an explicit part of restoration.
summary.tldr: ConVRT separates video content from temporal deformation to suppress turbulence-related variation and improve consistency across restored frames.

title: Temporally Consistent Atmospheric Turbulence Mitigation with Neural Representations

abstract: Realistic audio synthesis that captures accurate acoustic phenomena is essential for creating immersive experiences in virtual and augmented reality. Synthesizing the sound received at any position relies on the estimation of impulse response (IR), which characterizes how sound propagates in one scene along different paths before arriving at the listener position. In this paper, we present Acoustic Volume Rendering (AVR), a novel approach that adapts volume rendering techniques to model acoustic impulse responses. While volume rendering has been successful in modeling radiance fields for images and neural scene representations, IRs present unique challenges as time-series signals. To address these challenges, we introduce frequency-domain volume rendering and use spherical integration to fit the IR measurements. Our method constructs an impulse response field that inherently encodes wave propagation principles and achieves state of-the-art performance in synthesizing impulse responses for novel poses. Experiments show that AVR surpasses current leading methods by a substantial margin. Additionally, we develop an acoustic simulation platform, AcoustiX, which provides more accurate and realistic IR simulations than existing simulators. Code for AVR and AcoustiX are available at https://zitonglan.github.io/avr.
