This paradigm presents two fundamental technical challenges. First, the prediction-decision misalignment: Conventional ML methods focus solely on prediction accuracy without considering downstream optimization objectives, leading to improved predictive metrics that fail to translate to better decisions. Second, the bias-variance dilemma: Observational data suffers from multiple biases (e.g., selection bias, position bias), while experimental data (e.g., randomized controlled trials), though unbiased, is typically scarce and costly --- resulting in high-variance estimates. We propose **Bi**-level **D**ecision-**F**ocused **C**ausal **L**earning (**Bi-DFCL**) that systematically addresses these challenges. First, we develop an unbiased estimator of OR decision quality using experimental data, which guides ML model training through surrogate loss functions that bridge discrete optimization gradients. Second, we establish a bi-level optimization framework that jointly leverages observational and experimental data, solved via implicit differentiation. This novel formulation enables our unbiased OR estimator to correct learning directions from biased observational data, achieving optimal bias-variance tradeoff. Extensive evaluations on public benchmarks, industrial marketing datasets, and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate the effectiveness of Bi-DFCL, showing statistically significant improvements over state-of-the-art. Currently, Bi-DFCL has been deployed across several marketing scenarios at Meituan, one of the largest online food delivery platforms in the world.

paragraphs: Marketing allocation systems often predict how individuals will respond to an action and then use an optimizer to decide where to spend resources. Better predictions do not necessarily produce better allocations. The data also pose a tension: observational records contain biases, while randomized experimental data are costly and scarce, making estimates from them variable.

Bi-DFCL links model training directly to the quality of the resulting allocation decisions. It constructs an unbiased estimator of decision quality from experimental data and uses surrogate losses to connect that signal to discrete optimization. A two-level optimization framework then combines observational and experimental information, with implicit differentiation used to solve the resulting learning problem.

The experimental signal corrects learning directions supplied by biased observational data, addressing the prediction-decision mismatch and the bias-variance tradeoff together. The authors report statistically significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on public benchmarks, industrial datasets, and online A/B tests. They also report deployment in several Meituan marketing scenarios, showing that the framework has been applied beyond benchmark evaluation.
summary.tldr: Bi-DFCL combines observational and experimental data to train causal models around the quality of downstream marketing decisions.

title: Bi-Level Decision-Focused Causal Learning for Large-Scale Marketing Optimization: Bridging Observational and Experimental Data

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks promise brain-inspired and energy-efficient computation by transmitting information through binary (0/1) spikes. Yet, their performance still lags behind that of artificial neural networks, often assumed to result from information loss caused by sparse and binary activations. In this work, we challenge this long-standing assumption and reveal a previously overlooked frequency bias: **spiking neurons inherently suppress high-frequency components and preferentially propagate low-frequency information.** This frequency-domain imbalance, we argue, is the root cause of degraded feature representation in SNNs. Empirically, on Spiking Transformers, adopting Avg-Pooling (low-pass) for token mixing lowers performance to 76.73% on Cifar-100, whereas replacing it with Max-Pool (high-pass) pushes the top-1 accuracy to 79.12%. Accordingly, we introduce **Max-Former** that restores high-frequency signals through two frequency-enhancing operators: (1) extra Max-Pool in patch embedding, and (2) Depth-Wise Convolution in place of self-attention. Notably, **Max-Former** attains 82.39% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet using only 63.99M parameters, surpassing Spikformer (74.81%, 66.34M) by +7.58%. Extending our insight beyond transformers, our **Max-ResNet-18** achieves state-of-the-art performance on convolution-based benchmarks: 97.17% on CIFAR-10 and 83.06% on CIFAR-100. We hope this simple yet effective solution inspires future research to explore the distinctive nature of spiking neural networks. Code is available: https://github.com/bic-L/MaxFormer.

title: Spiking Neural Networks Need High-Frequency Information

abstract: We utilise a sampler originating from nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, termed here Jarzynski-adjusted Langevin algorithm (JALA), to build statistical estimation methods in latent variable models. We achieve this by leveraging Jarzynski’s equality and developing algorithms based on a weighted version of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) with recursively updated weights. Adapting this for latent variable models, we develop a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method that provides the maximum marginal likelihood estimate of the parameters, termed JALA-EM. Under suitable regularity assumptions on the marginal likelihood, we provide a nonasymptotic analysis of the JALA-EM scheme implemented with stochastic gradient descent and show that it provably converges to the maximum marginal likelihood estimate. We demonstrate the performance of JALA-EM on a variety of latent variable models and show that it performs comparably to existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Importantly, the ability to recursively estimate marginal likelihoods—an uncommon feature among scalable methods—makes our approach particularly suited for model selection, which we validate through dedicated experiments.

paragraphs: Latent variable models describe observations using variables that are not directly observed. Estimating their parameters requires accounting for those hidden variables. This paper adapts a sampling method from nonequilibrium statistical mechanics to build an estimation procedure that also tracks marginal likelihoods.

The Jarzynski-adjusted Langevin algorithm combines the unadjusted Langevin algorithm with weights updated recursively using Jarzynski's equality. The authors adapt this construction into JALA-EM, a sequential Monte Carlo method for maximum marginal likelihood estimation. The method therefore combines competitive estimation performance with an additional quantity useful for comparing candidate models.
summary.tldr: JALA-EM uses recursively weighted Langevin sampling to fit latent variable models and estimate marginal likelihoods for model selection.

title: Learning Latent Variable Models via Jarzynski-adjusted Langevin Algorithm

abstract: Label Distribution Learning (LDL) has emerged as a powerful framework for estimating complete conditional label distributions, providing crucial reliability for risk-sensitive decision-making tasks. While existing LDL algorithms exhibit competent performance under the conventional LDL performance evaluation methods, two key limitations remain: (1) current algorithms systematically underperform on the samples with low-entropy label distributions, which can be particularly valuable for decision making, and (2) the conventional performance evaluation methods are inherently biased due to the numerical imbalance of samples. In this paper, through empirical and theoretical analyses, we find that excessive cohesion between anchor vectors contributes significantly to the observed entropy bias phenomenon in LDL algorithms. Accordingly, we propose an inter-anchor angular regularization term that mitigates cohesion among anchor vectors by penalizing over-small angles. Besides, to alleviate the numerical imbalance of high-entropy samples in test set, we propose an entropy-calibrated aggregation strategy that obtains the overall model performance by evaluating performance on the low-entropy and high-entropy subsets of the overall test set separately. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on various real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how probability is spread across possible labels. A low-entropy target distribution concentrates that probability on relatively few labels, making such examples particularly useful for some decisions. The paper finds that existing methods systematically perform worse on these examples, while conventional aggregate evaluations can obscure the problem because different kinds of examples occur in unequal numbers.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors identify excessive similarity among anchor vectors as a significant contributor to this entropy bias. They introduce a regularization term that penalizes angles between anchors when those angles become too small. This discourages the anchors from crowding together and addresses a representation-level source of the observed bias.

The paper also changes evaluation by assessing low-entropy and high-entropy test subsets separately before aggregating performance. This makes the overall assessment less dominated by the numerical abundance of high-entropy samples. Experiments on real datasets support the proposal. The combined contribution addresses both how the model learns and how its performance across different target distributions is judged.
summary.tldr: The paper reduces entropy-related bias in label distribution learning through angular regularization and separate evaluation of low- and high-entropy samples.

title: Entropy-Calibrated Label Distribution Learning

abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from neural population activity is crucial for understanding the brain and for applications in brain-machine interfaces. However, such biological data is often scarce, particularly in primates or humans, where high-throughput recording techniques, such as two-photon imaging, remain challenging or impossible to apply. This, in turn, poses a challenge for deep learning decoding techniques. To overcome this, we introduce MEIcoder, a biologically informed decoding method that leverages neuron-specific most exciting inputs (MEIs), a structural similarity index measure loss, and adversarial training. MEIcoder achieves state-of-the-art performance in reconstructing visual stimuli from single-cell activity in primary visual cortex (V1), especially excelling on small datasets with fewer recorded neurons. Using ablation studies, we demonstrate that MEIs are the main drivers of the performance, and in scaling experiments, we show that MEIcoder can reconstruct high-fidelity natural-looking images from as few as 1,000-2,500 neurons and less than 1,000 training data points. We also propose a unified benchmark with over 160,000 samples to foster future research. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of reliable decoding in early visual system and provide practical insights for neuroscience and neuroengineering applications.

paragraphs: MEIcoder reconstructs viewed images from activity recorded in primary visual cortex. The paper focuses on situations where neural recordings and training examples are scarce, a significant obstacle for deep learning decoders. Its approach incorporates neuron-specific most exciting inputs, or MEIs, which describe visual inputs that strongly excite individual neurons.

The decoder combines these MEIs with a structural-similarity loss and adversarial training. This brings information about individual neurons' visual preferences into the reconstruction process. Ablation experiments identify MEIs as the main source of the performance gains, giving evidence that the biologically informed component plays a central role in the method's results.

They also introduce a unified benchmark containing over 160,000 samples. Together, the results support visual decoding in the studied early-visual-system setting and provide a larger shared resource for evaluating future reconstruction methods.
summary.tldr: MEIcoder uses neuron-specific preferred inputs to reconstruct visual stimuli effectively from limited neural recordings and training data.

title: MEIcoder: Decoding Visual Stimuli from Neural Activity by Leveraging Most Exciting Inputs

abstract: When a vision model performs image recognition, which visual attributes drive its predictions? Detecting unintended reliance on specific visual features is critical for ensuring model robustness, preventing overfitting, and avoiding spurious correlations. We introduce an automated framework for detecting such dependencies in trained vision models. At the core of our method is a self-reflective agent that systematically generates and tests hypotheses about visual attributes that a model may rely on. This process is iterative: the agent refines its hypotheses based on experimental outcomes and uses a self-evaluation protocol to assess whether its findings accurately explain model behavior. When inconsistencies arise, the agent self-reflects over its findings and triggers a new cycle of experimentation. We evaluate our approach on a novel benchmark of 130 models designed to exhibit diverse visual attribute dependencies across 18 categories. Our results show that the agent's performance consistently improves with self-reflection, with a significant performance increase over non-reflective baselines. We further demonstrate that the agent identifies real-world visual attribute dependencies in state-of-the-art models, including CLIP's vision encoder and the YOLOv8 object detector.

paragraphs: An image recognition model can make successful predictions while relying on visual attributes that its designers did not intend it to use. This paper introduces an automated framework for investigating those dependencies in trained vision models. The aim is to discover which attributes influence predictions, helping expose reliance that could undermine robustness or reflect spurious correlations.

The framework uses an agent that repeatedly proposes hypotheses about a model’s behavior and tests them. Experimental outcomes inform the next hypotheses, while a self-evaluation procedure checks whether the emerging explanation fits the observed behavior. When the explanation contains inconsistencies, the agent reflects on its findings and starts another experimental cycle.

The authors evaluate this process on a new benchmark containing 130 models with dependencies spanning 18 categories. Self-reflection consistently improves performance over versions without reflection. The agent also identifies visual attribute dependencies in CLIP’s vision encoder and YOLOv8. These findings support iterative checking as a useful component of automated model investigation, alongside hypothesis generation and testing.
summary.tldr: A self-reflective agent improves automated discovery of the visual attributes that influence trained vision models.

title: Automated Detection of Visual Attribute Reliance with a Self-Reflective Agent

abstract: Conventional wisdom in machine learning privacy research states that memorization directly implies a loss of privacy. In contrast, a well-generalized model only remembers distributional patterns and preserves privacy of its training data. In this work, we show that this relationship is much more complex for LLMs trained for chat, and depends heavily on how knowledge is encoded and manipulated. To this end, we fine-tune language models on synthetically generated biographical information including PIIs, and try to extract them in different ways after instruction fine-tuning. We find counter to conventional wisdom that better verbatim memorization does not necessarily increase data leakage via chat. We also find that it is easier to extract information via chat from an LLM that is better able to manipulate and process knowledge even if it is smaller, and that not all attributes are equally extractable. This suggests that the relationship between privacy, memorization and language understanding of LLMs is very intricate, and that examining memorization in isolation can lead to misleading conclusions.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether a chat model’s ability to memorize training text predicts how much personal information can be extracted from it. The authors challenge a simple connection between stronger memorization and greater leakage. Their focus is on how knowledge is encoded and manipulated after a language model has been adapted for instruction-following conversation.

The study fine-tunes language models on synthetic biographies containing personally identifiable information. After instruction fine-tuning, the authors attempt to extract that information in different ways. They find that better verbatim memorization does not necessarily produce more leakage through chat. They also find that a model better able to process and manipulate knowledge can be easier to extract information from, even when it is smaller.

Different attributes are not equally extractable in these experiments. Together, the findings show why a single memorization measure can give a misleading picture of conversational privacy risk. The supported conclusion is that memorization, knowledge-processing ability, and the information being requested interact in determining leakage in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Experiments with synthetic personal information show that verbatim memorization alone does not reliably characterize leakage through chat.

title: Rethinking the Role of Verbatim Memorization in LLM Privacy

abstract: We present an ultra-efficient post-training method for shortcutting large-scale pre-trained flow matching diffusion models into efficient few-step samplers, enabled by novel velocity field self-distillation. While shortcutting in flow matching, originally introduced by shortcut models, offers flexible trajectory-skipping capabilities, it requires a specialized step-size embedding incompatible with existing models unless retraining from scratch—a process nearly as costly as pretraining itself. Our key contribution is thus imparting a more aggressive shortcut mechanism to standard flow matching models (e.g., Flux), leveraging a unique distillation principle that obviates the need for step-size embedding. Working on the velocity field rather than sample space and learning rapidly from self-guided distillation in an online manner, our approach trains efficiently, e.g., producing a 3-step Flux <1 A100 day. Beyond distillation, our method can be incorporated into the pretraining stage itself, yielding models that inherently learn efficient, few-step flows without compromising quality. This capability also enables, to our knowledge, the first few-shot distillation method (e.g., 10 text-image pairs) for dozen-billion-parameter diffusion models, delivering state-of-the-art performance at almost free cost.

paragraphs: This paper develops a post-training method that converts large pretrained flow-matching diffusion models into samplers requiring only a few steps. Existing shortcut models support skipping along generation trajectories, but depend on specialized step-size embeddings. Adding those embeddings to standard pretrained models would require retraining from scratch at a cost approaching pretraining.

The proposed method avoids that requirement through velocity-field self-distillation. It trains in the space of velocity fields rather than sample outputs and learns online from self-guided distillation. This allows standard models such as Flux to acquire more aggressive shortcuts without a step-size embedding. The authors give a concrete efficiency example: producing a three-step Flux model in less than one A100 GPU-day.

The method can also be incorporated into pretraining so that models learn efficient few-step flows from the outset, with the authors reporting no compromise in quality. They further demonstrate few-shot distillation using, for example, ten text-image pairs for diffusion models with around a dozen billion parameters. The reported state-of-the-art performance supports a substantially cheaper route to few-step generation in these settings.
summary.tldr: Velocity-field self-distillation turns pretrained flow-matching models into few-step samplers without requiring specialized step-size embeddings.

title: Shortcutting Pre-trained Flow Matching Diffusion Models is Almost Free Lunch

abstract: Capturing the interactions between entities in a structured way plays a central role in world models that flexibly adapt to changes in the environment. Recent works motivate the benefits of models that explicitly represent the structure of interactions and formulate the problem as discovering local causal structures. In this work, we demonstrate that reliably capturing these relationships in complex settings remains challenging. To remedy this shortcoming, we postulate that sparsity is a critical ingredient for the discovery of such local structures. To this end we present the SPARse TrANsformer World model (SPARTAN), a Transformer-based world model that learns context-dependent interaction structures between entities in a scene. By applying sparsity regularisation on the attention patterns between object-factored tokens, SPARTAN learns sparse, context-dependent interaction graphs that accurately predict future object states. We further extend our model to adapt to sparse interventions with unknown targets on the dynamics of the environment. This results in a highly interpretable world model that can efficiently adapt to changes. Empirically, we evaluate SPARTAN against the current state-of-the-art in object-centric world models on observation-based environments and demonstrate that our model can learn local causal graphs that accurately reflects the underlying interactions between objects and achieve significantly improved few-shot adaptation to dynamics changes as well as robustness against distractors.

paragraphs: SPARTAN learns how objects interact so that a world model can predict their future states and adapt when dynamics change. The paper identifies reliable discovery of local interaction structure as a challenge in complex environments. It proposes sparsity as a key ingredient for making those learned relationships selective and interpretable.

The model represents objects with separate tokens and regularizes attention to favor sparse connections between them. The resulting interaction graph depends on context, allowing relevant relationships to change with the scene. An extension handles sparse interventions on environmental dynamics even when the affected targets are unknown, supporting adaptation to localized changes.

Evaluations compare SPARTAN with state-of-the-art object-centric world models in observation-based environments. The reported results show learned local causal graphs that reflect underlying object interactions, improved adaptation from few examples after dynamics changes, and greater robustness to distractors. These findings support sparse attention as a useful structural bias for discovering interactions and making world models easier to adapt.
summary.tldr: SPARTAN learns sparse, context-dependent object interactions to improve world-model prediction, adaptation to changed dynamics, and distractor robustness.

title: SPARTAN: A Sparse Transformer World Model Attending to What Matters

abstract: Skill assessment from video entails rating the quality of a person’s physical performance and explaining what could be done better. Today’s models specialize for an individual sport, and suffer from the high cost and scarcity of expert-level supervision across the long tail of sports. Towards closing that gap, we explore transferable video representations for skill assessment. Our CrossTrainer approach discovers skill-attributes—such as balance, control, and hand positioning—whose meaning transcends the boundaries of any given sport, then trains a multimodal language model to generate actionable feedback for a novel video, e.g., “lift hands more to generate more power” as well as its proficiency level, e.g., early expert. We validate the new model on multiple datasets for both cross-sport (transfer) and intra-sport (in-domain) settings, where it achieves gains up to 60% relative to the state of the art. By abstracting out the shared behaviors indicative of human skill, the proposed video representation generalizes substantially better than an array of existing techniques, enriching today’s multimodal large language models.

paragraphs: Assessing physical skill from video involves judging performance quality and explaining how a person could improve. Models specialized for individual sports need expert supervision that can be expensive and scarce. This paper explores whether a representation of shared skill attributes can make assessment transfer more effectively between sports.

CrossTrainer discovers attributes such as balance, control, and hand positioning whose meaning extends across particular activities. It uses this representation to train a multimodal language model that produces both a proficiency assessment and actionable feedback for a new video. The goal is to connect what the model observes to reusable aspects of skilled behavior, so its assessment can draw on more than sport-specific patterns.

The authors evaluate the method on multiple datasets in both within-sport and cross-sport settings. They report gains of up to 60% relative to state-of-the-art methods and substantially stronger generalization than several existing approaches. The maximum gain does not describe every evaluation, but the overall findings support shared skill attributes as useful building blocks for transferable assessment and more informative video-based feedback.
summary.tldr: CrossTrainer learns skill attributes shared across sports to generate transferable proficiency assessments and actionable video feedback.

title: Learning Skill-Attributes for Transferable Assessment in Video

abstract: Recently Burger et al. (2012) and Xie et al. (2012) proposed to use a denoising autoencoder (DAE) for denoising noisy images. They showed that a plain, deep DAE can denoise noisy images as well as the conventional methods such as BM3D and KSVD. Both of them approached image denoising by denoising small, image patches of a larger image and combining them to form a clean image. In this setting, it is usual to use the encoder of the DAE to obtain the latent representation and subsequently apply the decoder to get the clean patch. We propose that a simple sparsification of the latent representation found by the encoder improves denoising performance, when the DAE was trained with sparsity regularization. The experiments confirm that the proposed sparsification indeed helps both denoising a small image patch and denoising a larger image consisting of those patches. Furthermore, it is found out that the proposed method improves even classification performance when test samples are corrupted with noise.

They showed that a plain, deep DAE can denoise noisy images as well as the conventional methods such as BM3D and KSVD. Both of them approached image denoising by denoising small, image patches of a larger image and combining them to form a clean image. In this setting, it is usual to use the encoder of the DAE to obtain the latent representation and subsequently apply the decoder to get the clean patch. We propose that a simple sparsification of the latent representation found by the encoder improves denoising performance, when the DAE was trained with sparsity regularization. The experiments confirm that the proposed sparsification indeed helps both denoising a small image patch and denoising a larger image consisting of those patches. Furthermore, it is found out that the proposed method improves even classification performance when test samples are corrupted with noise.

paragraphs: Denoising autoencoders can clean images by processing small patches and combining the cleaned patches into a larger image. In the usual pipeline, an encoder converts a noisy patch into a latent representation, and a decoder reconstructs a clean patch from that representation. This paper examines a simple modification between those two stages.

The proposed change sparsifies the encoder's latent representation before passing it to the decoder. The stated setting is an autoencoder trained with sparsity regularization, so the intervention builds on a property already encouraged during training. The contribution is an additional operation on the learned representation within the existing patch-denoising pipeline.

Experiments confirm improved denoising both for individual patches and for larger images assembled from those patches. The authors also find improved classification performance when test examples are corrupted by noise. These findings indicate that further sparsifying the representation can help in the studied noisy-input settings, with the denoising claim specifically tied to training that includes sparsity regularization.
summary.tldr: Sparsifying latent representations improves denoising in sparsity-regularized autoencoders and also helps classification on noisy test inputs.

title: Simple Sparsification Improves Sparse Denoising Autoencoders in Denoising Highly Corrupted Images

abstract: Structured prediction is used in areas such as computer vision and natural language processing to predict structured outputs such as segmentations or parse trees. In these settings, prediction is performed by MAP inference or, equivalently, by solving an integer linear program. Because of the complex scoring functions required to obtain accurate predictions, both learning and inference typically require the use of approximate solvers. We propose a theoretical explanation to the striking observation that approximations based on linear programming (LP) relaxations are often tight on real-world instances. In particular, we show that learning with LP relaxed inference encourages integrality of training instances, and that tightness generalizes from train to test data.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with internal organization, such as image segmentations or parse trees. Finding the highest-scoring output can be formulated as an integer linear program. Rich scoring functions make this computation difficult, so both training and prediction often depend on approximate solvers. A common approach replaces the integer problem with a linear programming relaxation.

The paper asks why these relaxations are often tight on real-world instances. Tightness means that the relaxed optimization retains a solution consistent with the original discrete problem. This is valuable because the computational relaxation can then recover the desired discrete solution. The authors propose a theoretical explanation centered on the interaction between learning and approximate inference.

They show that training with LP-relaxed inference encourages integral solutions on training examples and that tightness generalizes from training to test data. This connects observed inference behavior to the learning procedure itself. The result explains why tightness can persist on unseen examples, without turning the empirical observation that relaxations are often tight into a claim that they always are.
summary.tldr: Training with LP-relaxed inference encourages integral solutions, and the paper shows how this tightness can generalize to test examples.

title: Train and Test Tightness of LP Relaxations in Structured Prediction

abstract: We study the fixed design segmented regression problem: Given noisy samples from a piecewise linear function f, we want to recover f up to a desired accuracy in mean-squared error. Previous rigorous approaches for this problem rely on dynamic programming (DP) and, while sample efficient, have running time quadratic in the sample size. As our main contribution, we provide new sample near-linear time algorithms for the problem that - while not being minimax optimal - achieve a significantly better sample-time tradeoff on large datasets compared to the DP approach. Our experimental evaluation shows that, compared with the DP approach, our algorithms provide a convergence rate that is only off by a factor of 2 to 4, while achieving speedups of three orders of magnitude.

As our main contribution, we provide new sample near-linear time algorithms for the problem that - while not being minimax optimal - achieve a significantly better sample-time tradeoff on large datasets compared to the DP approach. Our experimental evaluation shows that, compared with the DP approach, our algorithms provide a convergence rate that is only off by a factor of 2 to 4, while achieving speedups of three orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Segmented regression seeks to recover a function composed of linear pieces from noisy observations. This paper studies the fixed-design version, with recovery accuracy measured by mean-squared error. Earlier approaches with rigorous guarantees use dynamic programming and are efficient in their use of samples, but their running time grows quadratically with the number of observations.

The authors introduce algorithms whose running time is nearly linear in the sample size. Their aim is a better balance between the amount of data required and the computation needed to process it. The algorithms are not minimax optimal, so the contribution explicitly accepts a statistical tradeoff to gain much faster computation on large datasets.

In the experimental comparison, the reported convergence rates differ from those of dynamic programming by factors of two to four, while running times improve by three orders of magnitude. These results illustrate why sample efficiency alone may be an incomplete criterion for choosing a regression method. A moderate loss in convergence rate can accompany a very large practical reduction in computation.
summary.tldr: Nearly linear-time segmented regression algorithms trade some statistical efficiency for large computational gains over dynamic programming.

title: Fast Algorithms for Segmented Regression

abstract: We study the off-policy evaluation problem—estimating the value of a target policy using data collected by another policy—under the contextual bandit model. We consider the general (agnostic) setting without access to a consistent model of rewards and establish a minimax lower bound on the mean squared error (MSE). The bound is matched up to constants by the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) and doubly robust (DR) estimators. This highlights the difficulty of the agnostic contextual setting, in contrast with multi-armed bandits and contextual bandits with access to a consistent reward model, where IPS is suboptimal. We then propose the SWITCH estimator, which can use an existing reward model (not necessarily consistent) to achieve a better bias-variance tradeoff than IPS and DR. We prove an upper bound on its MSE and demonstrate its benefits empirically on a diverse collection of datasets, often outperforming prior work by orders of magnitude.

The bound is matched up to constants by the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) and doubly robust (DR) estimators. We then propose the SWITCH estimator, which can use an existing reward model (not necessarily consistent) to achieve a better bias-variance tradeoff than IPS and DR. paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target decision policy would perform using observations collected by another policy. This paper studies contextual bandits in the general setting where no consistent reward model is available. It establishes a minimax lower bound on mean squared error, characterizing the best possible worst-case accuracy in that setting.

Inverse propensity scoring and doubly robust estimators match this bound up to constants. This means their worst-case behavior is already optimal at that level of precision. The result differs from settings such as multi-armed bandits or contextual bandits with a consistent reward model, where inverse propensity scoring is suboptimal.

The authors then introduce SWITCH, which can use an available reward model even if that model is not consistent. It aims for a better balance between bias and variance than the two established estimators. They prove an upper bound on its error and report benefits across diverse datasets, often with improvements of orders of magnitude over prior work.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes worst-case off-policy evaluation limits and proposes SWITCH to improve the bias-variance tradeoff using an imperfect reward model.

title: Optimal and Adaptive Off-policy Evaluation in Contextual Bandits

abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models. The graphical lasso is one of the most popular methods for estimating Gaussian graphical models. However, it does not achieve the oracle rate of convergence. In this paper, we propose the graphical nonconvex optimization for optimal estimation in Gaussian graphical models, which is then approximated by a sequence of convex programs. Our proposal is computationally tractable and produces an estimator that achieves the oracle rate of convergence. The statistical error introduced by the sequential approximation using a sequence of convex programs is clearly demonstrated via a contraction property. The proposed methodology is then extended to modeling semiparametric graphical models. We show via numerical studies that the proposed estimator outperforms other popular methods for estimating Gaussian graphical models.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimation of high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models, which represent relationships among many variables. Graphical lasso is a popular approach, but the authors identify a statistical shortcoming: it does not achieve the oracle convergence rate. Their goal is to obtain that stronger estimation rate while keeping the computation tractable.

They formulate a nonconvex estimation problem and approximate it through a sequence of convex programs. This separates the desired statistical objective from the sequence of manageable optimization problems used to approach it. The proposed estimator achieves the oracle convergence rate. A contraction property characterizes the statistical error introduced by the sequential approximation, connecting the computational procedure to the accuracy of its output.

The methodology is also extended to semiparametric graphical models. Numerical studies report better estimation performance than other popular methods for Gaussian graphical models. The contribution combines an improved statistical guarantee with a practical route to computation: the convex approximations are analyzed as part of the estimator, rather than treated as an unrelated numerical convenience.
summary.tldr: Sequential convex approximations make a nonconvex graphical-model estimator tractable while achieving the oracle convergence rate.

title: Graphical Nonconvex Optimization via an Adaptive Convex Relaxation

abstract: We introduce Minimal Achievable Sufficient Statistic (MASS) Learning, a machine learning training objective for which the minima are minimal sufficient statistics with respect to a class of functions being optimized over (e.g., deep networks). In deriving MASS Learning, we also introduce Conserved Differential Information (CDI), an information-theoretic quantity that {—} unlike standard mutual information {—} can be usefully applied to deterministically-dependent continuous random variables like the input and output of a deep network. In a series of experiments, we show that deep networks trained with MASS Learning achieve competitive performance on supervised learning, regularization, and uncertainty quantification benchmarks.
originalAbstract: We introduce Minimal Achievable Sufficient Statistic (MASS) Learning, a machine learning training objective for which the minima are minimal sufficient statistics with respect to a class of functions being optimized over (e.g., deep networks). In deriving MASS Learning, we also introduce Conserved Differential Information (CDI), an information-theoretic quantity that {—} unlike standard mutual information {—} can be usefully applied to deterministically-dependent continuous random variables like the input and output of a deep network. In a series of experiments, we show that deep networks trained with MASS Learning achieve competitive performance on supervised learning, regularization, and uncertainty quantification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Minimal Achievable Sufficient Statistic Learning defines a training objective around retaining sufficient information with minimal representation. Its minima are minimal sufficient statistics relative to the class of functions being optimized, such as deep networks. This qualification is central: the notion of minimality is tied to what that function class can achieve.

To derive the objective, the authors introduce Conserved Differential Information, or CDI. This information-theoretic quantity is designed to remain useful when continuous random variables depend deterministically on one another, as a network's output depends on its input. The paper contrasts this usefulness with standard mutual information in that setting, making CDI a foundation for the proposed learning objective.

Experiments assess networks trained with MASS Learning on supervised learning, regularization, and uncertainty quantification benchmarks. The reported performance is competitive across these areas. The contribution therefore combines a representation-learning objective with a quantity that supports its derivation and empirical evidence of practical usefulness. The theoretical characterization concerns the objective's minima; the experimental claim concerns the performance of trained networks.
summary.tldr: MASS Learning targets minimal sufficient representations within a function class using a new information measure suited to deterministic continuous networks.

title: Minimal Achievable Sufficient Statistic Learning

abstract: The best-known and most commonly used technique for distribution-property estimation uses a plug-in estimator, with empirical frequency replacing the underlying distribution. We present novel linear-time-computable estimators that significantly “amplify” the effective amount of data available. For a large variety of distribution properties including four of the most popular ones and for every underlying distribution, they achieve the accuracy that the empirical-frequency plug-in estimators would attain using a logarithmic-factor more samples. Specifically, for Shannon entropy and a broad class of Lipschitz properties including the $L_1$ distance to a fixed distribution, the new estimators use $n$ samples to achieve the accuracy attained by the empirical estimators with $n\log n$ samples. For support-size and coverage, the new estimators use $n$ samples to achieve the performance of empirical frequency with sample size $n$ times the logarithm of the property value. Significantly strengthening the traditional min-max formulation, these results hold not only for the worst distributions, but for each and every underlying distribution. Furthermore, the logarithmic amplification factors are optimal. Experiments on a wide variety of distributions show that the new estimators outperform the previous state-of-the-art estimators designed for each specific property.

paragraphs: Estimating a property of an unknown distribution often starts by replacing its probabilities with observed frequencies. This paper develops estimators that extract more accuracy from the same observations. The amplification is statistical: using a given sample size, the new estimators match the accuracy that empirical-frequency estimators would obtain with substantially more samples.

For Shannon entropy and a broad class of Lipschitz properties, including L1 distance to a fixed distribution, n samples achieve the accuracy of the empirical estimator using n log n samples. For support size and coverage, the amplification factor instead depends logarithmically on the property value. The proposed estimators can also be computed in linear time.

These guarantees hold separately for every underlying distribution, making them stronger than a comparison restricted to worst-case distributions. The authors further establish that the logarithmic amplification factors are optimal. Experiments across many distributions show improvements over earlier estimators tailored to individual properties. The contribution combines computational efficiency with a distribution-by-distribution account of how much more effectively observations can be used.
summary.tldr: Linear-time estimators match empirical-frequency estimators using logarithmically more samples, with optimal amplification guarantees for every underlying distribution.

title: Data Amplification: Instance-Optimal Property Estimation

abstract: Tensor factorization is a fundamental framework to analyze high-order interactions in data. Despite the success of the existing methods, the valuable temporal information are severely underused. The timestamps of the interactions are either ignored or discretized into crude steps. The recent work although formulates event-tensors to keep the timestamps in factorization and can capture mutual excitation effects among the interaction events, it overlooks another important type of temporal influence, inhibition. In addition, it uses a local window to exclude all the long-term dependencies. To overcome these limitations, we propose a self-modulating nonparametric Bayesian factorization model. We use the latent factors to construct mutually governed, general random point processes, which can capture various short-term/long-term, excitation/inhibition effects, so as to encode the complex temporal dependencies into factor representations. In addition, our model couples with a latent Gaussian process to estimate and fuse nonlinear yet static relationships between the entities. For efficient inference, we derive a fully decomposed model evidence lower bound to dispense with the huge kernel matrix and costly summations inside the rate and log rate functions. We then develop an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm. We show the advantage of our method in four real-world applications.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization represents interactions involving multiple entities through latent factors. This paper focuses on interaction events with timestamps, arguing that ignoring time or reducing it to coarse intervals loses useful information. It also identifies limitations in a previous event-based approach that captures excitation but omits inhibition and excludes dependencies beyond a local time window.

The proposed Bayesian model uses latent factors to construct mutually governed random point processes. These processes can represent events that encourage or suppress other events over both short and long timescales. A latent Gaussian process additionally models nonlinear relationships between entities that remain static. The factor representations therefore incorporate temporal influences alongside those static relationships.

For efficient inference, the authors derive a fully decomposed evidence lower bound that avoids a huge kernel matrix and costly sums inside event-rate calculations. They then develop stochastic optimization for the model. Results on four real-world applications show advantages for the method, supporting a representation that accounts for both excitation and inhibition across different timescales.
summary.tldr: The model factorizes timestamped interactions while capturing short- and long-term excitation, inhibition, and static nonlinear relationships.

title: Self-Modulating Nonparametric Event-Tensor Factorization

abstract: Recent interest in invertible models and normalizing flows has resulted in new architectures that ensure invertibility of the network model. Neural ODEs and i-ResNets are two recent techniques for constructing models that are invertible, but it is unclear if they can be used to approximate any continuous invertible mapping. Here, we show that out of the box, both of these architectures are limited in their approximation capabilities. We then show how to overcome this limitation: we prove that any homeomorphism on a $p$-dimensional Euclidean space can be approximated by a Neural ODE or an i-ResNet operating on a $2p$-dimensional Euclidean space. We conclude by showing that capping a Neural ODE or an i-ResNet with a single linear layer is sufficient to turn the model into a universal approximator for non-invertible continuous functions.
originalAbstract: Recent interest in invertible models and normalizing flows has resulted in new architectures that ensure invertibility of the network model. Neural ODEs and i-ResNets are two recent techniques for constructing models that are invertible, but it is unclear if they can be used to approximate any continuous invertible mapping. Here, we show that out of the box, both of these architectures are limited in their approximation capabilities. We then show how to overcome this limitation: we prove that any homeomorphism on a $p$-dimensional Euclidean space can be approximated by a Neural ODE or an i-ResNet operating on a $2p$-dimensional Euclidean space. We conclude by showing that capping a Neural ODE or an i-ResNet with a single linear layer is sufficient to turn the model into a universal approximator for non-invertible continuous functions.

paragraphs: An architecture can guarantee that its transformations are invertible without being able to represent every continuous invertible transformation. This paper investigates that distinction for Neural ODEs and invertible residual networks, or i-ResNets. It shows that both architectures have restrictions on what they can approximate in their original form, despite their built-in invertibility.

The central result gives a way to overcome those restrictions by increasing the space in which the model operates. Any homeomorphism on a p-dimensional Euclidean space—a continuous invertible mapping whose inverse is also continuous—can be approximated by either architecture operating in 2p dimensions. Doubling the dimension is a sufficient construction established by the paper; the result does not assert that doubling is always necessary.

The paper also shows that adding a single linear output layer is sufficient to obtain universal approximation of continuous functions that need not be invertible. Together, these results clarify how extra dimensions and an output layer expand the expressive capabilities of otherwise constrained architectures.
summary.tldr: Higher-dimensional constructions overcome approximation limits of Neural ODEs and i-ResNets, while a linear output layer enables approximation of non-invertible continuous functions.

title: Approximation Capabilities of Neural ODEs and Invertible Residual Networks

abstract: In this paper we present a scalable deep learning framework for finding Markovian Nash Equilibria in multi-agent stochastic games using fictitious play. The motivation is inspired by theoretical analysis of Forward Backward Stochastic Differential Equations and their implementation in a deep learning setting, which is the source of our algorithm’s sample efficiency improvement. By taking advantage of the permutation-invariant property of agents in symmetric games, the scalability and performance is further enhanced significantly. We showcase superior performance of our framework over the state-of-the-art deep fictitious play algorithm on an inter-bank lending/borrowing problem in terms of multiple metrics. More importantly, our approach scales up to 3000 agents in simulation, a scale which, to the best of our knowledge, represents a new state-of-the-art. We also demonstrate the applicability of our framework in robotics on a belief space autonomous racing problem.

The motivation is inspired by theoretical analysis of Forward Backward Stochastic Differential Equations and their implementation in a deep learning setting, which is the source of our algorithm’s sample efficiency improvement. By taking advantage of the permutation-invariant property of agents in symmetric games, the scalability and performance is further enhanced significantly. We showcase superior performance of our framework over the state-of-the-art deep fictitious play algorithm on an inter-bank lending/borrowing problem in terms of multiple metrics. More importantly, our approach scales up to 3000 agents in simulation, a scale which, to the best of our knowledge, represents a new state-of-the-art. We also demonstrate the applicability of our framework in robotics on a belief space autonomous racing problem.

paragraphs: This paper develops a deep-learning framework for finding Markovian Nash equilibria in stochastic games with many agents. Such equilibria concern strategies based on the current state, with each agent responding to the others. The framework uses fictitious play and aims to make equilibrium computation more sample efficient and scalable.

Its design draws on theoretical analysis of forward-backward stochastic differential equations and their implementation with neural networks. The authors identify this connection as the source of improved sample efficiency. For symmetric games, they further exploit permutation invariance: the computation can respect the fact that exchanging agent identities does not change the game’s structure. This improves scalability and performance.

On an interbank lending and borrowing problem, the framework outperforms the compared deep fictitious play method across multiple metrics. It also handles simulations with 3,000 agents, which the authors describe as a new scale to their knowledge. A belief-space autonomous racing example demonstrates applicability in robotics. These results establish performance on the presented applications, including a large simulated multi-agent setting.
summary.tldr: A deep fictitious-play framework improves sample efficiency and exploits game symmetry to compute equilibria in simulations with up to 3,000 agents.

title: Large-Scale Multi-Agent Deep FBSDEs

abstract: The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) performs effective nonlinear dimensionality reduction in a variety of problem settings. However, the black-box neural network decoder function typically employed limits the ability of the decoder function to be constrained and interpreted, making the use of VAEs problematic in settings where prior knowledge should be embedded within the decoder. We present DeVAE, a novel VAE-based model with a derivative-based forward mapping, allowing for greater control over decoder behaviour via specification of the decoder function in derivative space. Additionally, we show how DeVAE can be paired with a sparse clustering prior to create BasisDeVAE and perform interpretable simultaneous dimensionality reduction and feature-level clustering. We demonstrate the performance and scalability of the DeVAE and BasisDeVAE models on synthetic and real-world data and present how the derivative-based approach allows for expressive yet interpretable forward models which respect prior knowledge.

However, the black-box neural network decoder function typically employed limits the ability of the decoder function to be constrained and interpreted, making the use of VAEs problematic in settings where prior knowledge should be embedded within the decoder. We present DeVAE, a novel VAE-based model with a derivative-based forward mapping, allowing for greater control over decoder behaviour via specification of the decoder function in derivative space. Additionally, we show how DeVAE can be paired with a sparse clustering prior to create BasisDeVAE and perform interpretable simultaneous dimensionality reduction and feature-level clustering. We demonstrate the performance and scalability of the DeVAE and BasisDeVAE models on synthetic and real-world data and present how the derivative-based approach allows for expressive yet interpretable forward models which respect prior knowledge.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can compress complex data into a lower-dimensional representation, but their decoder is usually a neural network whose behavior is difficult to interpret or constrain. This becomes a problem when a researcher has prior knowledge about how the low-dimensional representation should relate to the original features. A flexible decoder is useful only if that flexibility can coexist with the required structure.

The paper introduces DeVAE, which specifies the decoder through a derivative-based forward mapping. Describing behavior in derivative space gives greater control over how the output changes as the representation changes. The contribution is therefore a different way to construct the decoder, allowing prior knowledge to shape its behavior while retaining an expressive nonlinear mapping.

BasisDeVAE adds a sparse clustering prior to this construction. It combines dimensionality reduction with clustering at the feature level, making both tasks part of an interpretable model. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate performance and scalability for the proposed models. The stated findings support derivative-based decoding as a way to combine expressive representations, interpretable structure, and respect for prior knowledge.
summary.tldr: DeVAE controls decoder behavior through derivatives, while BasisDeVAE adds interpretable feature clustering alongside dimensionality reduction.

title: BasisDeVAE: Interpretable Simultaneous Dimensionality Reduction and Feature-Level Clustering with Derivative-Based Variational Autoencoders

abstract: We propose XOR-Contrastive Divergence learning (XOR-CD), a provable approach for constrained structure generation, which remains difficult for state-of-the-art neural network and constraint reasoning approaches. XOR-CD harnesses XOR-Sampling to generate samples from the model distribution in CD learning and is guaranteed to generate valid structures. In addition, XOR-CD has a linear convergence rate towards the global maximum of the likelihood function within a vanishing constant in learning exponential family models. Constraint satisfaction enabled by XOR-CD also boosts its learning performance. Our real-world experiments on data-driven experimental design, dispatching route generation, and sequence-based protein homology detection demonstrate the superior performance of XOR-CD compared to baseline approaches in generating valid structures as well as capturing the inductive bias in the training set.

XOR-CD harnesses XOR-Sampling to generate samples from the model distribution in CD learning and is guaranteed to generate valid structures. In addition, XOR-CD has a linear convergence rate towards the global maximum of the likelihood function within a vanishing constant in learning exponential family models. Constraint satisfaction enabled by XOR-CD also boosts its learning performance. paragraphs: Generating structured objects requires learning patterns in data while respecting rules that define valid outputs. XOR-Contrastive Divergence addresses both requirements within a single learning approach. It uses XOR-Sampling to obtain samples from the model distribution during contrastive divergence training, and the resulting method guarantees that generated structures satisfy the constraints.

For exponential-family models, the authors establish a linear convergence rate toward the global maximum of the likelihood function, up to a vanishing constant. This gives the approach a formal optimization guarantee in the stated model family. Constraint satisfaction also improves learning performance, connecting validity of generated structures with the model’s ability to learn from its training data.

Experiments cover data-driven experimental design, dispatching route generation, and sequence-based protein homology detection. Across these applications, the authors report superior performance over the tested baselines in generating valid structures and capturing the training set’s inductive bias. The contribution combines guaranteed validity, a qualified global convergence result, and empirical evidence that explicitly enforcing constraints can support effective learning.
summary.tldr: XOR-CD guarantees valid constrained structures and provides linear convergence toward globally optimal likelihood, up to a vanishing constant, for exponential-family models.

title: XOR-CD: Linearly Convergent Constrained Structure Generation

abstract: The goal of meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) is to build agents that can quickly learn new tasks by leveraging prior experience on related tasks. Learning a new task often requires both exploring to gather task-relevant information and exploiting this information to solve the task. In principle, optimal exploration and exploitation can be learned end-to-end by simply maximizing task performance. However, such meta-RL approaches struggle with local optima due to a chicken-and-egg problem: learning to explore requires good exploitation to gauge the exploration’s utility, but learning to exploit requires information gathered via exploration. Optimizing separate objectives for exploration and exploitation can avoid this problem, but prior meta-RL exploration objectives yield suboptimal policies that gather information irrelevant to the task. We alleviate both concerns by constructing an exploitation objective that automatically identifies task-relevant information and an exploration objective to recover only this information. This avoids local optima in end-to-end training, without sacrificing optimal exploration. Empirically, DREAM substantially outperforms existing approaches on complex meta-RL problems, such as sparse-reward 3D visual navigation. Videos of DREAM: https://ezliu.github.io/dream/
originalAbstract: The goal of meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) is to build agents that can quickly learn new tasks by leveraging prior experience on related tasks. Learning a new task often requires both exploring to gather task-relevant information and exploiting this information to solve the task. In principle, optimal exploration and exploitation can be learned end-to-end by simply maximizing task performance. However, such meta-RL approaches struggle with local optima due to a chicken-and-egg problem: learning to explore requires good exploitation to gauge the exploration’s utility, but learning to exploit requires information gathered via exploration. Optimizing separate objectives for exploration and exploitation can avoid this problem, but prior meta-RL exploration objectives yield suboptimal policies that gather information irrelevant to the task. We alleviate both concerns by constructing an exploitation objective that automatically identifies task-relevant information and an exploration objective to recover only this information. This avoids local optima in end-to-end training, without sacrificing optimal exploration. Empirically, DREAM substantially outperforms existing approaches on complex meta-RL problems, such as sparse-reward 3D visual navigation. Videos of DREAM: https://ezliu.github.io/dream/

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to use experience with related tasks to learn a new task quickly. Doing so requires both gathering useful information and acting on it. Jointly training these behaviors creates a circular dependency: exploration looks useful only when exploitation can use its discoveries, while exploitation cannot improve without informative exploration.

DREAM separates the objectives for these two behaviors while keeping them connected through task relevance. Its exploitation objective identifies the information needed to solve the task. Its exploration objective then seeks only that information. This addresses a weakness of earlier separated objectives, which could reward gathering information that did not actually help task performance.

The paper presents this construction as avoiding the local-optimum problem associated with end-to-end training without sacrificing optimal exploration. Empirically, DREAM substantially outperforms existing approaches on complex meta-learning problems, including sparse-reward navigation in three-dimensional visual environments. The key contribution is an objective design that gives exploration a useful learning target before successful task execution is already established, while tying that target to what exploitation needs.
summary.tldr: DREAM separates exploration and exploitation objectives while directing exploration toward information needed to solve the task.

title: Decoupling Exploration and Exploitation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning without Sacrifices

abstract: With rapid progress in neural text-to-speech (TTS) models, personalized speech generation is now in high demand for many applications. For practical applicability, a TTS model should generate high-quality speech with only a few audio samples from the given speaker, that are also short in length. However, existing methods either require to fine-tune the model or achieve low adaptation quality without fine-tuning. In this work, we propose StyleSpeech, a new TTS model which not only synthesizes high-quality speech but also effectively adapts to new speakers. Specifically, we propose Style-Adaptive Layer Normalization (SALN) which aligns gain and bias of the text input according to the style extracted from a reference speech audio. With SALN, our model effectively synthesizes speech in the style of the target speaker even from a single speech audio. Furthermore, to enhance StyleSpeech’s adaptation to speech from new speakers, we extend it to Meta-StyleSpeech by introducing two discriminators trained with style prototypes, and performing episodic training. The experimental results show that our models generate high-quality speech which accurately follows the speaker’s voice with single short-duration (1-3 sec) speech audio, significantly outperforming baselines.

This paper develops StyleSpeech to synthesize high-quality speech and adapt to unfamiliar voices from limited reference audio. The reported gains over baselines support this combination of style conditioning and adaptation-oriented training.
summary.tldr: StyleSpeech and Meta-StyleSpeech use reference-audio style conditioning to synthesize a speaker's voice from a single one-to-three-second recording.

title: Meta-StyleSpeech : Multi-Speaker Adaptive Text-to-Speech Generation

abstract: Data transformations (e.g. rotations, reflections, and cropping) play an important role in self-supervised learning. Typically, images are transformed into different views, and neural networks trained on tasks involving these views produce useful feature representations for downstream tasks, including anomaly detection. However, for anomaly detection beyond image data, it is often unclear which transformations to use. Here we present a simple end-to-end procedure for anomaly detection with learnable transformations. The key idea is to embed the transformed data into a semantic space such that the transformed data still resemble their untransformed form, while different transformations are easily distinguishable. Extensive experiments on time series show that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in the one-vs.-rest setting and is competitive in the more challenging n-vs.-rest anomaly-detection task. On medical and cyber-security tabular data, our method learns domain-specific transformations and detects anomalies more accurately than previous work.

paragraphs: Self-supervised image learning often creates useful training tasks through transformations such as rotations or cropping. For time series and tabular data, choosing equally useful transformations is less straightforward. This paper addresses that obstacle by learning transformations as part of an end-to-end anomaly-detection procedure.

The method embeds transformed examples into a semantic space with two goals. A transformed example should still resemble its original form, while the effects of different transformations should remain distinguishable. These goals combine preservation of the example's identity with differences that provide a useful learning signal, avoiding the need to specify image-like transformations for every data type.

On time series, the method outperforms existing approaches in the one-versus-rest setting and is competitive in the harder multiple-versus-rest setting. On medical and cybersecurity tabular datasets, it learns domain-specific transformations and detects anomalies more accurately than previous work. The results support learned transformations as a way to extend transformation-based anomaly detection beyond images, while distinguishing stronger and more qualified findings across evaluation settings.
summary.tldr: Learning distinguishable transformations that preserve semantic similarity improves anomaly detection on the reported time-series and tabular-data tasks.

title: Neural Transformation Learning for Deep Anomaly Detection Beyond Images

abstract: While contrastive approaches of self-supervised learning (SSL) learn representations by minimizing the distance between two augmented views of the same data point (positive pairs) and maximizing views from different data points (negative pairs), recent \emph{non-contrastive} SSL (e.g., BYOL and SimSiam) show remarkable performance {\it without} negative pairs, with an extra learnable predictor and a stop-gradient operation. A fundamental question rises: why they do not collapse into trivial representation? In this paper, we answer this question via a simple theoretical study and propose a novel approach, \ourmethod{}, that \emph{directly} sets the linear predictor based on the statistics of its inputs, rather than trained with gradient update. On ImageNet, it performs comparably with more complex two-layer non-linear predictors that employ BatchNorm and outperforms linear predictor by $2.5%$ in 300-epoch training (and $5%$ in 60-epoch). \ourmethod{} is motivated by our theoretical study of the nonlinear learning dynamics of non-contrastive SSL in simple linear networks. Our study yields conceptual insights into how non-contrastive SSL methods learn, how they avoid representational collapse, and how multiple factors, like predictor networks, stop-gradients, exponential moving averages, and weight decay all come into play. Our simple theory recapitulates the results of real-world ablation studies in both STL-10 and ImageNet. Code is released\footnote{\url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/luckmatters/tree/master/ssl}}.

The paper investigates the learning dynamics behind this behavior through a theoretical study of simple linear networks.

Although the networks studied are linear, their learning dynamics are nonlinear. The resulting theory reproduces findings from ablation studies on STL-10 and ImageNet and motivates a method that sets a linear predictor directly from its input statistics instead of training it through gradient updates.

On ImageNet, that predictor performs comparably to more complex two-layer nonlinear predictors using BatchNorm. The abstract reports improvements over a trained linear predictor of 2.5% after 300 epochs and 5% after 60 epochs. The contribution links a simplified account of collapse avoidance to a practical predictor construction supported by experiments.
summary.tldr: A linear-network analysis of non-contrastive learning motivates setting predictors from input statistics and helps explain representation collapse avoidance.

title: Understanding self-supervised learning dynamics without contrastive pairs

abstract: Image-to-image regression is an important learning task, used frequently in biological imaging. Current algorithms, however, do not generally offer statistical guarantees that protect against a model’s mistakes and hallucinations. To address this, we develop uncertainty quantification techniques with rigorous statistical guarantees for image-to-image regression problems. In particular, we show how to derive uncertainty intervals around each pixel that are guaranteed to contain the true value with a user-specified confidence probability. Our methods work in conjunction with any base machine learning model, such as a neural network, and endow it with formal mathematical guarantees{—}regardless of the true unknown data distribution or choice of model. Furthermore, they are simple to implement and computationally inexpensive. We evaluate our procedure on three image-to-image regression tasks: quantitative phase microscopy, accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, and super-resolution transmission electron microscopy of a Drosophila melanogaster brain.

paragraphs: Image-to-image regression produces an output image from an input image, including in biological imaging applications. A predicted image alone does not generally provide statistical protection against mistakes or hallucinated details. This paper develops uncertainty quantification that supplements predictions with mathematically guaranteed information about their accuracy.

The method constructs intervals around individual pixel predictions. These intervals are guaranteed to contain the true values with a confidence probability chosen by the user. The approach works alongside any base machine learning model, including a neural network, and its guarantees do not depend on specifying the true unknown data distribution or choosing a particular prediction model.

The authors describe the procedures as simple to implement and computationally inexpensive. They evaluate them on quantitative phase microscopy, accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, and super-resolution electron microscopy of a fruit-fly brain. The contribution is a way to accompany image predictions with statistically grounded uncertainty across these applications. The stated guarantee is probabilistic coverage through intervals; it does not claim to eliminate errors from the underlying image prediction.
summary.tldr: The paper adds inexpensive pixel-level uncertainty intervals with distribution-free statistical guarantees to image-to-image prediction models.

title: Image-to-Image Regression with Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification and Applications in Imaging

abstract: We study the problem of mean estimation of $\ell_2$-bounded vectors under the constraint of local differential privacy. While the literature has a variety of algorithms that achieve the (asymptotic) optimal rates for this problem, the performance of these algorithms in practice can vary significantly due to varying (and often large) hidden constants. In this work, we investigate the question of designing the randomizer with the smallest variance. We show that PrivUnit (Bhowmick et al. 2018) with optimized parameters achieves the optimal variance among a large family of natural randomizers. To prove this result, we establish some properties of local randomizers, and use symmetrization arguments that allow us to write the optimal randomizer as the optimizer of a certain linear program. These structural results, which should extend to other problems, then allow us to show that the optimal randomizer belongs to the PrivUnit family. We also develop a new variant of PrivUnit based on the Gaussian distribution which is more amenable to mathematical analysis and enjoys the same optimality guarantees. This allows us to establish several useful properties on the exact constants of the optimal error as well as to numerically estimate these constants.

paragraphs: Locally private mean estimation protects each participant’s vector before it reaches the estimator. Several algorithms achieve the same asymptotic rate, yet large hidden constants can produce very different practical errors. This paper focuses on finding the smallest variance for mean estimation of vectors bounded in Euclidean norm.

The authors show that PrivUnit, when its parameters are optimized, achieves optimal variance within a large family of natural randomizers. Structural properties and symmetrization reduce the search for an optimal randomizer to a linear program, from which the PrivUnit form emerges. This gives a finer comparison than matching rates alone.

The paper also develops a Gaussian-based PrivUnit variant with the same optimality guarantees and a more tractable analysis. That variant supports exact-constant properties and numerical estimates of the optimal error. The optimality claim is scoped to the analyzed randomizer family and privacy setting, while the structural techniques may be useful for studying other private-estimation problems.
summary.tldr: Optimized PrivUnit minimizes variance within a broad local-randomizer family, sharpening private mean-estimation guarantees beyond asymptotic rates.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Mean Estimation under Local Differential Privacy

abstract: Normalizing flows map an independent set of latent variables to their samples using a bijective transformation. Despite the exact correspondence between samples and latent variables, their high level relationship is not well understood. In this paper we characterize the geometric structure of flows using principal manifolds and understand the relationship between latent variables and samples using contours. We introduce a novel class of normalizing flows, called principal component flows (PCF), whose contours are its principal manifolds, and a variant for injective flows (iPCF) that is more efficient to train than regular injective flows. PCFs can be constructed using any flow architecture, are trained with a regularized maximum likelihood objective and can perform density estimation on all of their principal manifolds. In our experiments we show that PCFs and iPCFs are able to learn the principal manifolds over a variety of datasets. Additionally, we show that PCFs can perform density estimation on data that lie on a manifold with variable dimensionality, which is not possible with existing normalizing flows.
