paragraphs: Normalizing flows connect independent latent variables to generated samples through an invertible transformation. This exact correspondence does not by itself explain the higher-level relationship between latent variation and sample structure. The paper studies that relationship geometrically, using principal manifolds and contours.

The authors introduce principal component flows, or PCFs, whose contours coincide with their principal manifolds. These models can use any flow architecture and are trained through regularized maximum likelihood. They also introduce an injective variant, iPCF, that is more efficient to train than regular injective flows. The construction connects the organization of the flow’s latent variables to geometric structure in the samples.

Experiments show PCFs and iPCFs learning principal manifolds across several datasets. PCFs can estimate densities on all their principal manifolds, and the authors demonstrate density estimation for data lying on a manifold with variable dimensionality. They identify this capability as unavailable in existing normalizing flows. The contribution therefore combines a geometric characterization with a model class that supports richer manifold-based density estimation.
summary.tldr: Principal component flows align flow contours with principal manifolds and enable density estimation on manifolds of variable dimensionality.

title: Principal Component Flows

abstract: We introduce an approach to counterfactual inference based on merging information from multiple datasets. We consider a causal reformulation of the statistical marginal problem: given a collection of marginal structural causal models (SCMs) over distinct but overlapping sets of variables, determine the set of joint SCMs that are counterfactually consistent with the marginal ones. We formalise this approach for categorical SCMs using the response function formulation and show that it reduces the space of allowed marginal and joint SCMs. Our work thus highlights a new mode of falsifiability through additional variables, in contrast to the statistical one via additional data.

We consider a causal reformulation of the statistical marginal problem: given a collection of marginal structural causal models (SCMs) over distinct but overlapping sets of variables, determine the set of joint SCMs that are counterfactually consistent with the marginal ones. We formalise this approach for categorical SCMs using the response function formulation and show that it reduces the space of allowed marginal and joint SCMs. Our work thus highlights a new mode of falsifiability through additional variables, in contrast to the statistical one via additional data.

paragraphs: Different datasets can describe overlapping pieces of a causal system without observing all its variables together. This paper asks how those pieces can constrain counterfactual inference: reasoning about what would have happened under a different intervention. Its starting point is a collection of structural causal models, each covering a different but overlapping set of variables.

The task is to determine which joint causal models are counterfactually consistent with all the smaller models. The authors formalize this problem for categorical variables using a response-function representation. Requiring the pieces to fit together reduces the possible models at both the marginal and joint levels, making compatibility itself a source of information.

This creates a way to challenge causal explanations by bringing additional variables into the analysis. An explanation that is acceptable for one subset may fail to fit the larger collection consistently. The result highlights how expanding the variables considered can restrict causal possibilities, beyond the familiar strategy of collecting more observations of the same variables.
summary.tldr: Combining overlapping causal models constrains counterfactual explanations and creates opportunities to falsify them through additional variables.

title: Causal Inference Through the Structural Causal Marginal Problem

abstract: This paper proves that robustness implies generalization via data-dependent generalization bounds. As a result, robustness and generalization are shown to be connected closely in a data-dependent manner. Our bounds improve previous bounds in two directions, to solve an open problem that has seen little development since 2010. The first is to reduce the dependence on the covering number. The second is to remove the dependence on the hypothesis space. We present several examples, including ones for lasso and deep learning, in which our bounds are provably preferable. The experiments on real-world data and theoretical models demonstrate near-exponential improvements in various situations. To achieve these improvements, we do not require additional assumptions on the unknown distribution; instead, we only incorporate an observable and computable property of the training samples. A key technical innovation is an improved concentration bound for multinomial random variables that is of independent interest beyond robustness and generalization.

paragraphs: This paper develops bounds connecting a learning algorithm’s robustness with its ability to generalize beyond training examples. The central change is to make that connection depend more effectively on the observed data. The authors use a property of the training samples that can be observed and computed.

The bounds improve earlier results in two ways: they reduce dependence on the covering number and remove dependence on the hypothesis space. The paper provides examples, including lasso and deep learning, where the new bounds are provably preferable. These are improvements in the theoretical assessment of generalization, with the data-dependent formulation supplying the additional information used in that assessment.

Experiments on real-world data and theoretical models show near-exponential improvements in various situations. The authors obtain these gains without adding assumptions about the unknown data distribution. A key ingredient is a sharper concentration bound for multinomial random variables, which may also be useful beyond this application. The results strengthen the mathematical link between robustness and generalization while keeping the improvements tied to the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: New data-dependent bounds strengthen the connection between robustness and generalization without additional assumptions on the unknown distribution.

title: Robustness Implies Generalization via Data-Dependent Generalization Bounds

abstract: The vast majority of the work on adaptive data analysis focuses on the case where the samples in the dataset are independent. Several approaches and tools have been successfully applied in this context, such as differential privacy , max-information , compression arguments , and more. The situation is far less well-understood without the independence assumption. We embark on a systematic study of the possibilities of adaptive data analysis with correlated observations. First, we show that, in some cases, differential privacy guarantees generalization even when there are dependencies within the sample, which we quantify using a notion we call Gibbs-dependence . We complement this result with a tight negative example. % Second, we show that the connection between transcript-compression and adaptive data analysis can be extended to the non-iid setting.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis allows later questions to depend on what earlier analyses revealed. Much of its theoretical foundation assumes that observations in the dataset are independent. This paper examines what remains possible when observations are correlated, making dependence within the sample a central part of the analysis.

The authors show that differential privacy can still guarantee generalization in some dependent-data settings. They quantify dependence through a notion called Gibbs-dependence. This makes the positive result explicitly sensitive to the relationships among observations, rather than treating privacy as an unconditional route to generalization. A tight negative example accompanies the guarantee and helps delineate the reach of the result.

The paper also extends the connection between transcript compression and adaptive analysis beyond independent, identically distributed observations. Here, the transcript represents the record of an adaptive interaction with the data. Together, the results show that two established approaches can remain useful with correlated observations, while demonstrating why dependence must be accounted for when stating their guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper extends privacy and transcript-compression approaches to adaptive analysis with correlated data, with guarantees that account for dependence.

title: Adaptive Data Analysis with Correlated Observations

abstract: Neural Language Models (NLMs) have made tremendous advances during the last years, achieving impressive performance on various linguistic tasks. Capitalizing on this, studies in neuroscience have started to use NLMs to study neural activity in the human brain during language processing. However, many questions remain unanswered regarding which factors determine the ability of a neural language model to capture brain activity (aka its ’brain score’). Here, we make first steps in this direction and examine the impact of test loss, training corpus and model architecture (comparing GloVe, LSTM, GPT-2 and BERT), on the prediction of functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging time-courses of participants listening to an audiobook. We find that (1) untrained versions of each model already explain significant amount of signal in the brain by capturing similarity in brain responses across identical words, with the untrained LSTM outperforming the transformer-based models, being less impacted by the effect of context; (2) that training NLP models improves brain scores in the same brain regions irrespective of the model’s architecture; (3) that Perplexity (test loss) is not a good predictor of brain score; (4) that training data have a strong influence on the outcome and, notably, that off-the-shelf models may lack statistical power to detect brain activations. Overall, we outline the impact of model-training choices, and suggest good practices for future studies aiming at explaining the human language system using neural language models.

paragraphs: Language models are used to predict brain activity during language processing, but their usefulness depends on choices beyond linguistic task performance. This study examines architecture, training corpus, and test loss when predicting functional MRI time courses from people listening to an audiobook. It compares GloVe, LSTM, GPT-2, and BERT representations.

Even untrained models explain significant brain signal by capturing similarities in responses to repeated words. Among those untrained models, the LSTM performs better than the transformer models and is less affected by context. Training improves brain prediction in the same brain regions across architectures, indicating a shared pattern of benefit despite differences in the models' initial behavior.

The study also finds that perplexity is a poor predictor of brain score and that training data strongly influence the outcome. Off-the-shelf models may lack enough statistical power to detect brain activations. These findings mean that a model's language-prediction score alone is insufficient for choosing a brain-prediction model; architecture and training choices materially affect the neuroscience analysis.
summary.tldr: Architecture and training data shape language models' ability to predict brain activity, while perplexity poorly predicts that ability.

title: Neural Language Models are not Born Equal to Fit Brain Data, but Training Helps

abstract: The inductive matrix completion (IMC) problem is to recover a low rank matrix from few observed entries while incorporating prior knowledge about its row and column subspaces. In this work, we make three contributions to the IMC problem: (i) we prove that under suitable conditions, the IMC optimization landscape has no bad local minima; (ii) we derive a simple scheme with theoretical guarantees to estimate the rank of the unknown matrix; and (iii) we propose GNIMC, a simple Gauss-Newton based method to solve the IMC problem, analyze its runtime and derive for it strong recovery guarantees. The guarantees for GNIMC are sharper in several aspects than those available for other methods, including a quadratic convergence rate, fewer required observed entries and stability to errors or deviations from low-rank. Empirically, given entries observed uniformly at random, GNIMC recovers the underlying matrix substantially faster than several competing methods.
originalAbstract: The inductive matrix completion (IMC) problem is to recover a low rank matrix from few observed entries while incorporating prior knowledge about its row and column subspaces. In this work, we make three contributions to the IMC problem: (i) we prove that under suitable conditions, the IMC optimization landscape has no bad local minima; (ii) we derive a simple scheme with theoretical guarantees to estimate the rank of the unknown matrix; and (iii) we propose GNIMC, a simple Gauss-Newton based method to solve the IMC problem, analyze its runtime and derive for it strong recovery guarantees. The guarantees for GNIMC are sharper in several aspects than those available for other methods, including a quadratic convergence rate, fewer required observed entries and stability to errors or deviations from low-rank. Empirically, given entries observed uniformly at random, GNIMC recovers the underlying matrix substantially faster than several competing methods.

paragraphs: Inductive matrix completion seeks to reconstruct a low-rank matrix from a limited set of observed entries, using prior knowledge about its row and column subspaces. The paper addresses both the structure of this optimization problem and the practical task of solving it quickly with reliable recovery.

The authors prove that, under suitable conditions, the optimization landscape contains no bad local minima. They also provide a simple procedure with theoretical guarantees for estimating the unknown matrix's rank. These contributions address two distinct uncertainties: whether local optimization can encounter undesirable minima, and how to choose the rank needed for reconstruction.

Their proposed solver, GNIMC, uses a Gauss-Newton method. Its recovery guarantees improve on other methods in several respects, including quadratic convergence, fewer required observations, and stability when observations contain errors or the matrix deviates from low rank. With entries sampled uniformly at random, experiments show substantially faster recovery than several competitors. The landscape and recovery claims retain their stated conditional character.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional landscape guarantees for inductive matrix completion and introduces a fast Gauss-Newton solver with strong recovery guarantees.

title: Inductive Matrix Completion: No Bad Local Minima and a Fast Algorithm

abstract: A major technique in learning-augmented online algorithms is combining multiple algorithms or predictors. Since the performance of each predictor may vary over time, it is desirable to use not the single best predictor as a benchmark, but rather a dynamic combination which follows different predictors at different times. We design algorithms that combine predictions and are competitive against such dynamic combinations for a wide class of online problems, namely, metrical task systems. Against the best (in hindsight) unconstrained combination of $\ell$ predictors, we obtain a competitive ratio of $O(\ell^2)$, and show that this is best possible. However, for a benchmark with slightly constrained number of switches between different predictors, we can get a $(1+\epsilon)$-competitive algorithm. Moreover, our algorithms can be adapted to access predictors in a bandit-like fashion, querying only one predictor at a time. An unexpected implication of one of our lower bounds is a new structural insight about covering formulations for the $k$-server problem.

paragraphs: A predictor that performs well early in an online task may perform poorly later. This paper studies how to combine predictors while comparing against a benchmark that can switch between them over time. It addresses metrical task systems, a broad class of online problems, where decisions must be made as requests arrive.

Against the best unrestricted combination of l predictors chosen in hindsight, the authors achieve a competitive ratio of order l squared and prove that this dependence is optimal. This quantifies the cost of competing with a benchmark that can freely exploit different predictors at different moments. A strong benchmark creates an unavoidable performance gap.

When the benchmark's number of switches is slightly constrained, the authors obtain a much closer guarantee: a competitive ratio of 1 plus ε. Their algorithms can also query just one predictor at a time, in a bandit-like access model. The results show how restrictions on switching change achievable performance, and one lower bound additionally yields a structural insight into covering formulations of the k-server problem.
summary.tldr: Algorithms can compete with predictors that change over time, with much tighter guarantees when the benchmark's switching is constrained.

title: Mixing Predictions for Online Metric Algorithms

abstract: Attention-based graph neural networks (GNNs), such as graph attention networks (GATs), have become popular neural architectures for processing graph-structured data and learning node embeddings. Despite their empirical success, these models rely on labeled data and the theoretical properties of these models have yet to be fully understood. In this work, we propose a novel attention-based node embedding framework for graphs. Our framework builds upon a hierarchical kernel for multisets of subgraphs around nodes (e.g. neighborhoods) and each kernel leverages the geometry of a smooth statistical manifold to compare pairs of multisets, by “projecting” the multisets onto the manifold. By explicitly computing node embeddings with a manifold of Gaussian mixtures, our method leads to a new attention mechanism for neighborhood aggregation. We provide theoretical insights into generalizability and expressivity of our embeddings, contributing to a deeper understanding of attention-based GNNs. We propose both efficient unsupervised and supervised methods for learning the embeddings. Through experiments on several node classification benchmarks, we demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing attention-based graph models like GATs. Our code is available at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/fisher_information_embedding.

paragraphs: Attention-based graph networks learn node representations by combining information from surrounding graph structure. This paper develops a new foundation for that process, motivated by existing models' reliance on labels and incomplete theoretical understanding. It builds node embeddings from collections of nearby subgraphs, such as neighborhoods, while retaining repeated elements in those collections.

The framework uses a hierarchical kernel to compare these collections through the geometry of a smooth statistical manifold. In the concrete construction, that manifold consists of Gaussian mixtures. Explicitly computing embeddings from this representation yields a new attention mechanism for aggregating neighborhood information, connecting the aggregation rule to the underlying statistical geometry.

The authors provide theoretical insights into the embeddings' expressivity and generalizability, together with efficient supervised and unsupervised learning methods. Experiments on several node classification benchmarks show improvements over existing attention-based graph models, including graph attention networks. The contribution therefore combines an alternative attention construction, learning procedures with and without supervision, and evidence about both theoretical properties and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: A graph embedding framework derives neighborhood attention from statistical geometry and improves node classification in the reported benchmarks.

title: Fisher Information Embedding for Node and Graph Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks have been demonstrated to achieve phenomenal success in many domains, and yet their inner mechanisms are not well understood. In this paper, we investigate the curvature of image manifolds, i.e., the manifold deviation from being flat in its principal directions. We find that state-of-the-art trained convolutional neural networks for image classification have a characteristic curvature profile along layers: an initial steep increase, followed by a long phase of a plateau, and followed by another increase. In contrast, this behavior does not appear in untrained networks in which the curvature flattens. We also show that the curvature gap between the last two layers has a strong correlation with the generalization capability of the network. Moreover, we find that the intrinsic dimension of latent codes is not necessarily indicative of curvature. Finally, we observe that common regularization methods such as mixup yield flatter representations when compared to other methods. Our experiments show consistent results over a variety of deep learning architectures and multiple data sets.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the geometry of image representations inside neural networks. It measures curvature: how much the manifold formed by image representations bends away from being flat along its principal directions. Following this quantity through the layers provides a way to examine how trained networks transform their internal representations.

Across the trained convolutional classifiers studied, curvature follows a characteristic pattern: a sharp early rise, a long plateau, and another rise near the end. Untrained networks do not exhibit this pattern; their curvature instead flattens. The authors also find a strong correlation between generalization ability and the curvature difference between the final two layers.

Two further observations help interpret these measurements. The intrinsic dimension of a representation does not necessarily reveal its curvature, and regularization methods such as mixup produce flatter representations than other methods examined. Results are consistent across multiple architectures and datasets. Together, they identify curvature as a useful descriptive property of learned representations, with an observed relationship to generalization rather than a demonstrated causal mechanism.
summary.tldr: Image classifiers exhibit characteristic changes in representation curvature across layers, with final-layer curvature differences correlated with generalization.

title: Data Representations’ Study of Latent Image Manifolds

abstract: Homotopy optimization is a traditional method to deal with a complicated optimization problem by solving a sequence of easy-to-hard surrogate subproblems. However, this method can be very sensitive to the continuation schedule design and might lead to a suboptimal solution to the original problem. In addition, the intermediate solutions, often ignored by classic homotopy optimization, could be useful for many real-world applications. In this work, we propose a novel model-based approach to learn the whole continuation path for homotopy optimization, which contains infinite intermediate solutions for any surrogate subproblems. Rather than the classic unidirectional easy-to-hard optimization, our method can simultaneously optimize the original problem and all surrogate subproblems in a collaborative manner. The proposed model also supports the real-time generation of any intermediate solution, which could be desirable for many applications. Experimental studies on different problems show that our proposed method can significantly improve the performance of homotopy optimization and provide extra helpful information to support better decision-making.

paragraphs: Homotopy optimization tackles a difficult problem through a sequence of easier surrogate problems. Its effectiveness can depend strongly on how that sequence progresses, and an unsuitable continuation schedule can produce a suboptimal final solution. Traditional approaches also tend to discard intermediate solutions, even when those solutions could help with practical decisions.

This paper proposes learning the entire continuation path with a model. The path represents solutions across the continuous family of surrogate problems, including infinitely many intermediate points. Instead of moving only from easy problems toward harder ones, the approach allows the original problem and its surrogates to be optimized collaboratively. The model also supports generating a selected intermediate solution in real time.

Experiments across different problems show that the approach can substantially improve homotopy optimization performance. The learned path additionally supplies intermediate information that can support decision-making. Its value therefore lies both in improving the optimization process and in making the solutions along that process available for use.
summary.tldr: Learning the whole continuation path lets homotopy optimization improve solutions collaboratively and produce intermediate solutions on demand.

title: Continuation Path Learning for Homotopy Optimization

abstract: Introduced by Hinton et al. in 2012, dropout has stood the test of time as a regularizer for preventing overfitting in neural networks. In this study, we demonstrate that dropout can also mitigate underfitting when used at the start of training. During the early phase, we find dropout reduces the directional variance of gradients across mini-batches and helps align the mini-batch gradients with the entire dataset’s gradient. This helps counteract the stochasticity of SGD and limit the influence of individual batches on model training. Our findings lead us to a solution for improving performance in underfitting models - early dropout: dropout is applied only during the initial phases of training, and turned off afterwards. Models equipped with early dropout achieve lower final training loss compared to their counterparts without dropout. Additionally, we explore a symmetric technique for regularizing overfitting models - late dropout, where dropout is not used in the early iterations and is only activated later in training. Experiments on ImageNet and various vision tasks demonstrate that our methods consistently improve generalization accuracy. Our results encourage more research on understanding regularization in deep learning and our methods can be useful tools for future neural network training, especially in the era of large data. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/dropout.

paragraphs: Dropout is usually associated with preventing a neural network from fitting its training data too closely. This paper shows that its timing can produce a different benefit: using dropout early in training can help models that fit the training data insufficiently. The result makes the training schedule an important part of understanding what dropout does.

During early training, the authors find that dropout reduces variation in gradient directions across mini-batches. Those gradients also become better aligned with the gradient of the entire dataset. This limits how strongly individual batches steer learning. Their early dropout method applies dropout only during the initial training phase, then switches it off; the resulting models reach lower final training loss than counterparts without dropout.

The authors also investigate late dropout for models prone to overfitting, leaving it inactive initially and enabling it later. Experiments on ImageNet and other vision tasks show consistent improvements in generalization accuracy. These findings support choosing when to apply dropout according to the training problem being addressed.
summary.tldr: Applying dropout only early in training can reduce underfitting, while activating it later can help regularize overfitting models.

title: Dropout Reduces Underfitting

abstract: We consider fairness in dimensionality reduction. Nonlinear dimensionality reduction yields low dimensional representations that let users visualize and explore high-dimensional data. However, traditional dimensionality reduction may yield biased visualizations overemphasizing relationships of societal phenomena to sensitive attributes or protected groups. We introduce a framework of fair neighbor embedding, the Fair Neighbor Retrieval Visualizer, which formulates fair nonlinear dimensionality reduction as an information retrieval task whose performance and fairness are quantified by information retrieval criteria. The method optimizes low-dimensional embeddings that preserve high-dimensional data neighborhoods without yielding biased association of such neighborhoods to protected groups. In experiments the method yields fair visualizations outperforming previous methods.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction turns high-dimensional data into a smaller representation that people can visualize and explore. This paper examines how those visualizations can overemphasize relationships between societal phenomena and sensitive attributes or protected groups. Because users explore relationships through the resulting layout, the choice of embedding can shape the associations they see.

The authors introduce the Fair Neighbor Retrieval Visualizer, a framework that treats fair nonlinear dimensionality reduction as an information retrieval task. It evaluates both usefulness and fairness through retrieval criteria. The embedding is optimized to preserve neighborhoods from the original data while avoiding biased associations between those neighborhoods and protected groups.

The reported experiments produce fair visualizations that outperform previous methods. The approach matters because neighborhood preservation and fairness are considered together within the optimization problem. Its target is the representation used for exploration: retaining meaningful local relationships without making protected-group associations disproportionately prominent under the framework's criteria. This gives the fairness objective a direct role in constructing the visual layout.
summary.tldr: Fair Neighbor Embedding optimizes visualizations to preserve data neighborhoods while reducing biased associations with protected groups.

title: Fair Neighbor Embedding

abstract: We introduce a novel class of sample-based explanations we term high-dimensional representers , that can be used to explain the predictions of a regularized high-dimensional model in terms of importance weights for each of the training samples. Our workhorse is a novel representer theorem for general regularized high-dimensional models, which decomposes the model prediction in terms of contributions from each of the training samples: with positive (negative) values corresponding to positive (negative) impact training samples to the model’s prediction. We derive consequences for the canonical instances of $\ell_1$ regularized sparse models and nuclear norm regularized low-rank models. As a case study, we further investigate the application of low-rank models in the context of collaborative filtering, where we instantiate high-dimensional representers for specific popular classes of models. Finally, we study the empirical performance of our proposed methods on three real-world binary classification datasets and two recommender system datasets. We also showcase the utility of high-dimensional representers in explaining model recommendations.

paragraphs: A prediction can be explained by identifying which training examples contribute to it. This paper develops such explanations for regularized high-dimensional models, assigning importance weights to individual training samples. The resulting high-dimensional representers connect a model’s output to the data used to fit it.

The central result is a representer theorem that decomposes a prediction into contributions from training samples. A positive contribution supports the prediction in the positive direction, while a negative contribution acts in the opposite direction. The authors derive specific consequences for sparse models using ℓ1 regularization and low-rank models using nuclear-norm regularization, extending the explanation framework across these two important model structures.

The paper further develops the low-rank case for collaborative filtering and instantiates representers for popular model classes in that setting. Empirical studies cover three real-world binary-classification datasets and two recommender-system datasets. Demonstrations of recommendation explanations show how the decomposition can make a model output understandable through relevant training examples and their signed contributions.
summary.tldr: A new representer theorem explains regularized high-dimensional predictions as signed contributions from individual training examples.

title: Representer Point Selection for Explaining Regularized High-dimensional Models

abstract: Many real-world datasets are represented as 3D point clouds – yet they often lack a predefined reference frame, posing a challenge for machine learning or general data analysis. Traditional methods for determining reference frames and normalizing 3D point clouds often struggle with specific inputs, lack theoretical guarantees, or require massive data. We introduce a new algorithm that overcomes these limitations and guarantees both universality and compatibility with any learnable framework for 3D point cloud analysis. Our algorithm works with any input point cloud and performs consistently regardless of input complexities, unlike data-driven methods that are susceptible to biases or limited training data. Empirically, our algorithm outperforms existing methods in effectiveness and generalizability across diverse benchmark datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/Utah-Math-Data-Science/alignment.

paragraphs: A three-dimensional point cloud describes a collection of spatial locations, but it may arrive without a predefined reference frame. That creates an alignment problem before machine learning or other analysis can proceed. Existing approaches to choosing a frame can struggle with particular inputs, lack guarantees, or depend on large amounts of training data.

The paper introduces an explicit algorithm for constructing a frame and normalizing point clouds. The authors state that it works for any input point cloud and is compatible with any learnable framework for point-cloud analysis. This makes the frame construction a broadly applicable preparation step, rather than a procedure tied to one downstream model.

The contribution combines a universality guarantee with empirical comparisons across diverse benchmark datasets. Those comparisons show better effectiveness and generalizability than existing methods. Its significance is the combination of input coverage and model compatibility: the proposed normalization is intended to handle complicated inputs consistently without relying on a learned frame estimator whose behavior depends on its training data.
summary.tldr: An explicit frame-construction algorithm normalizes arbitrary 3D point clouds with universality guarantees and compatibility across learnable analysis frameworks.

title: An Explicit Frame Construction for Normalizing 3D Point Clouds

abstract: Low-bit integer training emerges as a promising approach to mitigate the heavy burden during network training by quantizing the weights, activations, and gradients. However, existing methods cannot well achieve mixed-precision quantization for low-bit training and are commonly limited to INT8 precision. In this paper, we propose a novel low-bit integer training framework that, for the first time, achieves adaptive mixed-precision allocation (AMPA) for weights, activations, and gradients, and pushes the boundaries to a precision level below INT8. We develop a novel magnitude-based sensitivity measurement with regard to the quantization losses of weight, activation, and gradient quantization and the average gradient magnitudes, which is demonstrated as an upper bound of quantization influence in theory. We further design a layer-wise precision update strategy under observations on the quantization losses and their effects on model performance in low-bit training. Extensive experiments on different backbones and datasets show that, compared to INT8 quantization, the proposed method can achieve more than 38% BitOPs reduction with a tolerable loss below 2% in image classification, image segmentation, and language modeling.

This can reduce computational demands, but choosing how much precision each component needs is difficult. The paper introduces AMPA, a framework that adaptively assigns mixed precision across all three components and supports precision below the commonly used INT8 level.

The authors show theoretically that this measure upper-bounds the influence of quantization. They also design a strategy for updating precision layer by layer, using observations about quantization losses and their effects on model performance during low-bit training.

Experiments across different network backbones and datasets cover image classification, image segmentation, and language modeling. Compared with INT8 quantization, the method achieves more than a 38% reduction in BitOPs with reported performance loss below 2%. These findings support adaptive precision as a way to reduce the bit-level computation required for training while controlling the accompanying performance tradeoff.
summary.tldr: AMPA adaptively allocates low-bit precision during training, reducing BitOPs by more than 38% versus INT8 with reported performance loss below 2%.

title: AMPA: Adaptive Mixed Precision Allocation for Low-Bit Integer Training

abstract: A common method to study deep learning systems is to use simplified model representations—for example, using singular value decomposition to visualize the model’s hidden states in a lower dimensional space. This approach assumes that the results of these simplifications are faithful to the original model. Here, we illustrate an important caveat to this assumption: even if the simplified representations can accurately approximate the full model on the training set, they may fail to accurately capture the model’s behavior out of distribution. We illustrate this by training Transformer models on controlled datasets with systematic generalization splits, including the Dyck balanced-parenthesis languages and a code completion task. We simplify these models using tools like dimensionality reduction and clustering, and then explicitly test how these simplified proxies match the behavior of the original model. We find consistent generalization gaps: cases in which the simplified proxies are more faithful to the original model on the in-distribution evaluations and less faithful on various tests of systematic generalization. This includes cases where the original model generalizes systematically but the simplified proxies fail, and cases where the simplified proxies generalize better. Together, our results raise questions about the extent to which mechanistic interpretations derived using tools like SVD can reliably predict what a model will do in novel situations.

paragraphs: Researchers often simplify neural representations to make them easier to inspect, for example by projecting hidden states into fewer dimensions. This paper examines whether those simplified representations remain faithful when a model encounters unfamiliar inputs. Its central concern is that accurately approximating training behavior may not establish how well a proxy describes generalization.

The authors train Transformers on controlled datasets with systematic generalization splits, including balanced-parenthesis languages and code completion. They then create simplified proxies using dimensionality reduction and clustering. By explicitly comparing proxy behavior with the original models, they test fidelity both within the familiar distribution and on systematic generalization tasks.

The experiments find consistent gaps between these settings. Sometimes the original model generalizes systematically while its simplified proxy fails; sometimes the proxy generalizes better than the original. Either direction creates a mismatch for interpretation. The findings therefore question whether mechanistic conclusions drawn from tools such as singular value decomposition can reliably predict behavior in novel situations merely because the simplification matches familiar examples.
summary.tldr: Simplified Transformer representations can match familiar behavior yet misrepresent generalization, with proxies sometimes performing worse or better than the original model.

title: Interpretability Illusions in the Generalization of Simplified Models

abstract: In this work, we investigate how to leverage pre-trained visual-language models (VLM) for online Reinforcement Learning (RL). In particular, we focus on sparse reward tasks with pre-defined textual task descriptions. We first identify the problem of reward misalignment when applying VLM as a reward in RL tasks. To address this issue, we introduce a lightweight fine-tuning method, named Fuzzy VLM reward-aided RL (FuRL), based on reward alignment and relay RL. Specifically, we enhance the performance of SAC/DrQ baseline agents on sparse reward tasks by fine-tuning VLM representations and using relay RL to avoid local minima. Extensive experiments on the Meta-world benchmark tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Code is available at: https://github.com/fuyw/FuRL.

paragraphs: FuRL investigates how pretrained visual-language models can help agents learn online when task rewards are sparse. The setting includes a predefined textual description of the task. Such descriptions make visual-language models a potential source of reward guidance, but the paper identifies a problem: their rewards can be misaligned with the reinforcement learning objective.

The proposed method combines reward alignment with relay reinforcement learning. It uses lightweight fine-tuning of visual-language representations to improve their usefulness as a reward signal. Relay reinforcement learning provides the other part of the method, helping the agent avoid local minima during learning. The two components address the quality of the guidance and the learning behavior that uses it.

Experiments on Meta-world tasks show improvements to SAC and DrQ agents in the sparse-reward setting. The findings support adapting pretrained visual-language representations when using them to guide online reinforcement learning. In the reported experiments, the combined method makes that guidance more effective for agents learning from otherwise infrequent task rewards.
summary.tldr: FuRL combines lightweight visual-language reward alignment with relay reinforcement learning to improve agents on sparse-reward tasks.

title: FuRL: Visual-Language Models as Fuzzy Rewards for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In traditional federated learning, a single global model cannot perform equally well for all clients. Therefore, the need to achieve the client-level fairness in federated system has been emphasized, which can be realized by modifying the static aggregation scheme for updating the global model to an adaptive one, in response to the local signals of the participating clients. Our work reveals that existing fairness-aware aggregation strategies can be unified into an online convex optimization framework, in other words, a central server’s sequential decision making process. To enhance the decision making capability, we propose simple and intuitive improvements for suboptimal designs within existing methods, presenting $\texttt{AAggFF}$. Considering practical requirements, we further subdivide our method tailored for the cross-device and the cross-silo settings, respectively. Theoretical analyses guarantee sublinear regret upper bounds for both settings: $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T \log{K}})$ for the cross-device setting, and $\mathcal{O}(K \log{T})$ for the cross-silo setting, with $K$ clients and $T$ federation rounds. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the federated system equipped with $\texttt{AAggFF}$ achieves better degree of client-level fairness than existing methods in both practical settings.

summary.tldr: AAggFF treats fairness-aware federated aggregation as sequential optimization, providing regret guarantees and improved empirical client-level fairness.

title: Pursuing Overall Welfare in Federated Learning through Sequential Decision Making

abstract: Stepwise inference protocols, such as scratchpads and chain-of-thought, help language models solve complex problems by decomposing them into a sequence of simpler subproblems. To unravel the underlying mechanisms of stepwise inference we propose to study autoregressive Transformer models on a synthetic task that embodies the multi-step nature of problems where stepwise inference is generally most useful. Specifically, we define a graph navigation problem wherein a model is tasked with traversing a path from a start to a goal node on the graph. We find we can empirically reproduce and analyze several phenomena observed at scale: (i) the stepwise inference reasoning gap, the cause of which we find in the structure of the training data; (ii) a diversity-accuracy trade-off in model generations as sampling temperature varies; (iii) a simplicity bias in the model’s output; and (iv) compositional generalization and a primacy bias with in-context exemplars. Overall, our work introduces a grounded, synthetic framework for studying stepwise inference and offers mechanistic hypotheses that can lay the foundation for a deeper understanding of this phenomenon.

paragraphs: Stepwise inference methods, including scratchpads and chain-of-thought, help language models tackle problems through intermediate steps. This paper introduces a synthetic graph-navigation task to study how that behavior arises. An autoregressive Transformer must traverse a path from a starting node to a goal, giving researchers a controlled setting with an explicitly multistep structure.

Within this setting, the authors reproduce several phenomena associated with larger models. They trace the observed stepwise reasoning gap to the structure of the training data and examine how changing sampling temperature trades accuracy against output diversity. They also identify a preference for simpler outputs.

The study additionally observes compositional generalization and a primacy bias when examples are supplied in context, meaning that earlier exemplars receive preferential influence. These findings make the synthetic task useful for examining multiple aspects of stepwise inference within one framework. The paper offers mechanistic hypotheses grounded in that setting, providing a basis for further understanding rather than claiming a complete explanation of reasoning in large language models.
summary.tldr: A synthetic graph-navigation task reproduces several stepwise-inference phenomena and supports mechanistic hypotheses about Transformer behavior.

title: Towards an Understanding of Stepwise Inference in Transformers: A Synthetic Graph Navigation Model

abstract: We propose a new approach to non-parametric density estimation that is based on regularizing a Sobolev norm of the density. This method is statistically consistent, and makes the inductive bias of the model clear and interpretable. While there is no closed analytic form for the associated kernel, we show that one can approximate it using sampling. The optimization problem needed to determine the density is non-convex, and standard gradient methods do not perform well. However, we show that with an appropriate initialization and using natural gradients, one can obtain well performing solutions. Finally, while the approach provides pre-densities (i.e. not necessarily integrating to 1), which prevents the use of log-likelihood for cross validation, we show that one can instead adapt Fisher divergence based score matching methods for this task. We evaluate the resulting method on the comprehensive recent anomaly detection benchmark suite, ADBench, and find that it ranks second best, among more than 15 algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper proposes nonparametric density estimation using a Sobolev-norm regularizer. The regularization makes the model’s preference for particular density shapes explicit and interpretable, and the method is statistically consistent. Although the associated kernel lacks a closed analytic expression, the authors show how to approximate it through sampling.

Fitting the model requires solving a nonconvex optimization problem on which ordinary gradient methods perform poorly. The authors obtain effective solutions by combining an appropriate initialization with natural-gradient optimization. This is a practical part of the contribution: the proposed statistical formulation needs a suitable optimization procedure to produce useful estimates.

The outputs are pre-densities, so they are not guaranteed to integrate to one. That prevents using log-likelihood for cross-validation in the proposed setup. The paper instead adapts score-matching methods based on Fisher divergence for model selection. On the ADBench anomaly-detection suite, the resulting method ranks second among more than fifteen algorithms, providing empirical support for the full combination of regularization, optimization, and validation choices.
summary.tldr: Sobolev-regularized pre-density estimation combines natural gradients and score-based validation, ranking second among more than fifteen methods on ADBench.

title: Sobolev Space Regularised Pre Density Models

abstract: Deep learning based methods for image reconstruction are state-of-the-art for a variety of imaging tasks. However, neural networks often perform worse if the training data differs significantly from the data they are applied to. For example, a model trained for accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on one scanner performs worse on another scanner. In this work, we investigate the impact of the training data on a model’s performance and robustness for accelerated MRI. We find that models trained on the combination of various data distributions, such as those obtained from different MRI scanners and anatomies, exhibit robustness equal or superior to models trained on the best single distribution for a specific target distribution. Thus training on such diverse data tends to improve robustness. Furthermore, training on such a diverse dataset does not compromise in-distribution performance, i.e., a model trained on diverse data yields in-distribution performance at least as good as models trained on the more narrow individual distributions. Our results suggest that training a model for imaging on a variety of distributions tends to yield a more effective and robust model than maintaining separate models for individual distributions.

paragraphs: Neural networks used for accelerated MRI reconstruction can perform worse when their deployment data differs from their training data. A change of scanner is one example. This paper investigates whether the composition of training data can improve robustness, focusing on mixtures of distributions from different scanners and anatomies.

The authors find that models trained on diverse mixtures achieve robustness equal to or better than models trained on the best single distribution for a particular target. In the reported results, broader training also does not reduce performance on the individual distributions included in training. The mixed-data models perform at least as well there as models trained on the narrower distributions separately.

These findings suggest that combining data sources can improve robustness without imposing an observed tradeoff in familiar settings. They also support using a broadly trained reconstruction model instead of maintaining a separate model for each distribution. The conclusion is an empirical tendency established in the study, rather than a universal guarantee for every possible data mixture.
summary.tldr: Training MRI reconstruction models on diverse scanners and anatomies improves reported robustness without sacrificing in-distribution performance.

title: Robustness of Deep Learning for Accelerated MRI: Benefits of Diverse Training Data

abstract: Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) has recently gained much attention due to its flexible framework for handling un-normalized measures and its robustness properties. In this work, we explore learning (structured) sparse transport plans in the UOT setting, i.e., transport plans have an upper bound on the number of non-sparse entries in each column (structured sparse pattern) or in the whole plan (general sparse pattern). We propose novel sparsity-constrained UOT formulations building on the recently explored maximum mean discrepancy based UOT. We show that the proposed optimization problem is equivalent to the maximization of a weakly submodular function over a uniform matroid or a partition matroid. We develop efficient gradient-based discrete greedy algorithms and provide the corresponding theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we observe that our proposed greedy algorithms select a diverse support set and we illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in various applications.

We show that the proposed optimization problem is equivalent to the maximization of a weakly submodular function over a uniform matroid or a partition matroid. Empirically, we observe that our proposed greedy algorithms select a diverse support set and we illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in various applications.

paragraphs: Unbalanced optimal transport supports comparisons between measures whose total mass need not be normalized. This paper adds explicit sparsity constraints to transportation plans. It considers both a cap on the number of nonzero entries in each column and a cap on the number across the entire plan, giving control over where transportation connections can appear.

The proposed formulations build on maximum-mean-discrepancy-based unbalanced transport. The authors show that their optimization problems are equivalent to maximizing a weakly submodular function under either uniform or partition matroid constraints. These mathematical structures express the permitted selections of nonzero entries and make the problem accessible to discrete greedy optimization.

The paper develops efficient gradient-based greedy algorithms and provides theoretical guarantees for them. Empirically, the algorithms select diverse support sets, meaning the chosen nonzero locations cover varied connections. Applications illustrate the approach’s effectiveness. The main contribution is a bridge between sparse transport design and structured discrete optimization, allowing explicit limits on the plan’s support to be incorporated into a principled algorithm.
summary.tldr: Sparse unbalanced transport can be formulated as weakly submodular maximization, enabling greedy algorithms with theoretical guarantees.

title: Submodular framework for structured-sparse optimal transport

abstract: Transformers have emerged as the backbone of large language models (LLMs). However, generation remains inefficient due to the need to store in memory a cache of key–value representations for past tokens, whose size scales linearly with the input sequence length and batch size. As a solution, we propose Dynamic Memory Compression (DMC), a method for on-line key–value cache compression at inference time. Most importantly, the model learns to apply different compression ratios in different heads and layers. We retrofit pre-trained LLMs such as Llama 2 (7B, 13B and 70B) into DMC Transformers, achieving up to $\sim 3.7 \times$ throughput increase during auto-regressive inference on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. DMC is applied via continued pre-training on a negligible percentage of the original data without adding any extra parameters. We find that DMC preserves the original downstream performance with up to 4$\times$ cache compression, outperforming up-trained grouped-query attention (GQA) and key–value eviction policies (H$_2$O, TOVA). GQA and DMC can be even combined to obtain compounded gains. As a result DMC fits longer contexts and larger batches within any given memory budget. We release the DMC code and models at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/tree/DMC.

paragraphs: Language models store key and value representations of past tokens so they can reuse them during generation. This cache grows with sequence length and batch size, creating a memory burden. Dynamic Memory Compression addresses that burden by compressing the cache online while the model generates text.

The model learns different compression ratios for different attention heads and layers. Existing pretrained models are adapted through continued pretraining on a very small fraction of the original data, without adding parameters. The authors retrofit Llama 2 models with 7, 13, and 70 billion parameters, demonstrating that the approach can be applied to already trained language models.

The reported results include up to approximately 3.7 times greater autoregressive throughput on an NVIDIA H100 and preserved downstream performance with up to fourfold cache compression. DMC outperforms the evaluated adapted grouped-query attention and cache eviction approaches. It can also be combined with grouped-query attention for additional gains. Reducing cache size makes room for longer contexts and larger batches within a given memory budget.
summary.tldr: DMC teaches pretrained language models to compress their attention caches adaptively, preserving tested performance with up to fourfold compression.

title: Dynamic Memory Compression: Retrofitting LLMs for Accelerated Inference

abstract: We study the densest subgraph problem and give algorithms via multiplicative weights update and area convexity that converge in $O\left(\frac{\log m}{\epsilon^{2}}\right)$ and $O\left(\frac{\log m}{\epsilon}\right)$ iterations, respectively, both with nearly-linear time per iteration. Compared with the work by Bahmani et al. (2014), our MWU algorithm uses a very different and much simpler procedure for recovering the dense subgraph from the fractional solution and does not employ a binary search. Compared with the work by Boob et al. (2019), our algorithm via area convexity improves the iteration complexity by a factor $\Delta$—the maximum degree in the graph, and matches the fastest theoretical runtime currently known via flows (Chekuri et al., 2022) in total time. Next, we study the dense subgraph decomposition problem and give the first practical iterative algorithm with linear convergence rate $O\left(mn\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ via accelerated random coordinate descent. This significantly improves over $O\left(\frac{m\sqrt{mn\Delta}}{\epsilon}\right)$ time of the FISTA-based algorithm by Harb et al. (2022). In the high precision regime $\epsilon\ll\frac{1}{n}$ where we can even recover the exact solution, our algorithm has a total runtime of $O\left(mn\log n\right)$, matching the state of the art exact algorithm via parametric flows (Gallo et al., 1989). Empirically, we show that this algorithm is very practical and scales to very large graphs, and its performance is competitive with widely used methods that have significantly weaker theoretical guarantees.

title: Multiplicative Weights Update, Area Convexity and Random Coordinate Descent for Densest Subgraph Problems

abstract: Models trained on data composed of different groups or domains can suffer from severe performance degradation under distribution shifts. While recent methods have largely focused on optimizing the worst-group objective, this often comes at the expense of good performance on other groups. To address this problem, we introduce an optimization scheme to achieve good performance across groups and find a good solution for all without severely sacrificing performance on any of them. However, directly applying such optimization involves updating the parameters of the entire network, making it both computationally expensive and challenging. Thus, we introduce Controllable Prompt Tuning (CPT), which couples our approach with prompt-tuning techniques. On spurious correlation benchmarks, our procedures achieve state-of-the-art results across both transformer and non-transformer architectures, as well as unimodal and multimodal data, while requiring only $0.4%$ tunable parameters.

paragraphs: When training data contain different groups or domains, changes in their distribution can cause large performance drops. One response is to optimize performance on the worst-performing group. The paper highlights a tradeoff in that strategy: improving the worst group can come at the expense of performance on other groups.

The authors introduce an optimization scheme intended to find a good balance across groups without severely sacrificing any one of them. Applying this scheme to every network parameter would be computationally expensive and difficult. Controllable Prompt Tuning combines the scheme with prompt tuning, concentrating adaptation in a small set of tunable parameters.

On benchmarks involving spurious correlations, the procedures achieve reported state-of-the-art results while tuning only 0.4% of parameters. The evaluations cover transformer and non-transformer architectures, as well as unimodal and multimodal data. These findings support prompt tuning as an efficient vehicle for the proposed group-balancing objective, with demonstrated applicability across several model and data types.
summary.tldr: Controllable Prompt Tuning balances performance across groups while adapting only 0.4% of parameters in the reported robustness experiments.

title: Controllable Prompt Tuning For Balancing Group Distributional Robustness

abstract: Reconstructions of visual perception from brain activity have improved tremendously, but the practical utility of such methods has been limited. This is because such models are trained independently per subject where each subject requires dozens of hours of expensive fMRI training data to attain high-quality results. The present work showcases high-quality reconstructions using only 1 hour of fMRI training data. We pretrain our model across 7 subjects and then fine-tune on minimal data from a new subject. Our novel functional alignment procedure linearly maps all brain data to a shared-subject latent space, followed by a shared non-linear mapping to CLIP image space. We then map from CLIP space to pixel space by fine-tuning Stable Diffusion XL to accept CLIP latents as inputs instead of text. This approach improves out-of-subject generalization with limited training data and also attains state-of-the-art image retrieval and reconstruction metrics compared to single-subject approaches. MindEye2 demonstrates how accurate reconstructions of perception are possible from a single visit to the MRI facility. All code is available on Github: https://github.com/MedARC-AI/MindEyeV2

paragraphs: MindEye2 reconstructs visual perception from brain activity while reducing the amount of training data needed from a new person. Earlier approaches train separately for each subject and can require dozens of hours of fMRI data. This work pretrains across seven subjects, then fine-tunes using only one hour from a new subject.

The method first uses linear mappings to align brain data into a shared representation across subjects. A shared nonlinear mapping then converts this representation into CLIP image space. To produce pixels, the authors fine-tune Stable Diffusion XL to accept CLIP representations instead of text, connecting the brain-derived image representation to image generation.

The authors report high-quality reconstructions with that limited new-subject data, improved generalization across subjects, and state-of-the-art retrieval and reconstruction metrics compared with single-subject approaches. The one-hour result relies on the prior training across other people. Its practical significance is that this shared learning can make accurate perception reconstruction possible from data gathered during a single MRI visit.
summary.tldr: MindEye2 transfers learning across seven subjects to reconstruct visual perception using one hour of fMRI training data from a new subject.

title: MindEye2: Shared-Subject Models Enable fMRI-To-Image With 1 Hour of Data

abstract: Many real-world tasks require an agent to reason jointly over text and visual objects, (e.g., navigating in public spaces), which we refer to as context-sensitive text-rich visual reasoning. Specifically, these tasks require an understanding of the context in which the text interacts with visual elements within an image. However, there is a lack of existing datasets to benchmark the state-of-the-art multimodal models’ capability on context-sensitive text-rich visual reasoning. In this paper, we introduce ConTextual, a novel dataset featuring human-crafted instructions that require context-sensitive reasoning for text-rich images. We conduct experiments to assess the performance of 14 foundation models (GPT-4V, Gemini-Pro-Vision, LLaVA-Next) and establish a human performance baseline. Further, we perform human evaluations of the model responses and observe a significant performance gap of 30.8% between GPT-4V (the current best-performing Large Multimodal Model) and human performance. Our fine-grained analysis reveals that GPT-4V encounters difficulties interpreting time-related data and infographics. However, it demonstrates proficiency in comprehending abstract visual contexts such as memes and quotes. Finally, our qualitative analysis uncovers various factors contributing to poor performance including lack of precise visual perception and hallucinations. Our dataset, code, and leaderboard can be found on the project page https://con-textual.github.io/.

paragraphs: Understanding an image containing text often requires more than reading the words. A model must connect the text with surrounding visual objects and interpret that relationship in context. ConTextual provides a dataset of human-written instructions designed to test this combined reasoning ability, addressing a gap in existing multimodal evaluation.

The authors evaluate 14 foundation models and establish a human baseline. Human assessments of model responses reveal a reported performance gap of 30.8% between humans and GPT-4V, the strongest large multimodal model in their evaluation. This shows that the benchmark captures difficulties that remained substantial even for the best-performing tested model.

A closer analysis finds uneven capabilities. GPT-4V struggles with time-related information and infographics while showing proficiency with abstract contexts such as memes and quotes. Qualitative inspection identifies imprecise visual perception and hallucinations among the contributors to poor results. Together, these findings make the benchmark useful for examining which combinations of reading, seeing, and contextual interpretation remain difficult.
summary.tldr: ConTextual tests joint reasoning over image text and visual context, revealing a substantial gap between tested multimodal models and humans.

title: ConTextual: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Text-Rich Visual Reasoning in Large Multimodal Models

abstract: Moderate-sized large language models (LLMs) – those with 7B or 13B parameters – exhibit promising machine translation (MT) performance. However, they do not match the performance of state-of-the-art conventional encoder-decoder translation models or larger-scale LLMs such as GPT-4. In this study, we bridge this performance gap. We first assess the shortcomings of supervised fine-tuning for LLMs in the MT task, emphasizing the quality issues present in the reference data, despite being human-generated. Then, in contrast to supervised fine-tuning which mimics reference translations, we introduce Contrastive Preference Optimization (CPO), a novel approach that trains models to avoid generating adequate but not perfect translations. Applying CPO to ALMA models with only 22K parallel sentences and 0.1% parameters yields significant improvements. The resulting model, called ALMA-R, can match or exceed the performance of the WMT competition winners and GPT-4 on WMT’21, WMT’22 and WMT’23 test datasets.

The authors introduce Contrastive Preference Optimization, or CPO, to steer models away from translations that are acceptable yet fall short of the desired quality. The change shifts training toward translation preferences rather than relying only on reference imitation. The reported comparisons concern those translation evaluations, rather than general language-model capability.
summary.tldr: CPO improves ALMA translation models through preference-based training, producing competitive results with limited data and parameter updates.

title: Contrastive Preference Optimization: Pushing the Boundaries of LLM Performance in Machine Translation

abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) are commonly used for various downstream natural language processing tasks via fine-tuning. However, recent studies have demonstrated that PLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, which can mislabel poisoned samples to target outputs even after a vanilla fine-tuning process. The key challenge for defending against the backdoored PLMs is that end users who adopt the PLMs for their downstream tasks usually do not have any knowledge about the attacking strategies, such as triggers. To tackle this challenge, in this work, we propose a backdoor mitigation approach, PURE, via head pruning and normalization of attention weights. The idea is to prune the attention heads that are potentially affected by poisoned texts with only clean texts on hand and then further normalize the weights of remaining attention heads to mitigate the backdoor impacts. We conduct experiments to defend against various backdoor attacks on the classification task. The experimental results show the effectiveness of PURE in lowering the attack success rate without sacrificing the performance on clean texts.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model can retain a backdoor after ordinary fine-tuning, causing poisoned inputs to receive an attacker's chosen outputs. This creates a practical problem for downstream users: they may have clean task data but no knowledge of the attack strategy or its triggers. PURE is designed to mitigate backdoors under that information constraint.

The method combines two changes to the model's attention system. First, it uses only clean texts to identify and prune attention heads that are potentially affected by poisoned inputs. It then normalizes the attention weights of the remaining heads to further reduce backdoor effects. The two steps address both which heads remain and how their attention weights behave.

The authors evaluate PURE against several backdoor attacks on classification tasks. They report lower attack success rates without sacrificing performance on clean texts. This matters because a useful defense must reduce malicious behavior while preserving the model's intended task capability. The reported findings support that balance in the evaluated classification settings.
summary.tldr: PURE uses clean texts to prune suspicious attention heads and normalize remaining attention weights, reducing tested backdoor attacks while preserving clean-text performance.

title: Defense against Backdoor Attack on Pre-trained Language Models via Head Pruning and Attention Normalization

abstract: Online Knowledge Distillation (OKD) methods represent a streamlined, one-stage distillation training process that obviates the necessity of transferring knowledge from a pretrained teacher network to a more compact student network. In contrast to existing logits-based OKD methods, this paper presents an innovative approach to leverage intermediate spatial representations. Our analysis of the intermediate features from both teacher and student models reveals two pivotal insights: (1) the similar features between students and teachers are predominantly focused on the foreground objects. (2) teacher models emphasize foreground objects more than students. Building on these findings, we propose Asymmetric Decision-Making (ADM) to enhance feature consensus learning for student models while continuously promoting feature diversity in teacher models. Specifically, Consensus Learning for student models prioritizes spatial features with high consensus relative to teacher models. Conversely, Divergence Learning for teacher models highlights spatial features with lower similarity compared to student models, indicating superior performance by teacher models in these regions. Consequently, ADM facilitates the student models to catch up with the feature learning process of the teacher models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADM consistently surpasses existing OKD methods across various online knowledge distillation settings and also achieves superior results when transferred to offline knowledge distillation, semantic segmentation and diffusion distillation tasks.

paragraphs: Online knowledge distillation trains teacher and student models within one process, avoiding the need for a separately pretrained teacher. This paper examines intermediate spatial features as a source of knowledge transfer. Its analysis finds that features shared by teachers and students concentrate mainly on foreground objects, and that teachers emphasize those objects more strongly.

The proposed Asymmetric Decision-Making method gives the two models different learning priorities. Students emphasize spatial features that already show strong agreement with teachers. Teachers emphasize features with lower similarity to students, which the authors associate with stronger teacher performance in those regions. Agreement guides the student while divergence encourages the teacher to retain distinct strengths.

This arrangement is intended to help students catch up with teachers’ feature learning without making both models pursue identical representations. Experiments report consistent improvements over existing online distillation methods across multiple settings. The approach also transfers successfully to offline distillation, semantic segmentation, and diffusion distillation, supporting the usefulness of assigning complementary roles to consensus and diversity.
summary.tldr: ADM improves knowledge distillation by encouraging students to learn shared spatial features while teachers develop distinct feature strengths.

title: Asymmetric Decision-Making in Online Knowledge Distillation: Unifying Consensus and Divergence

abstract: Evaluating in-the-wild coding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is a challenging endeavor with no existing solution. We introduce Copilot Arena, a platform to collect user preferences through native integration into a developer’s working environment. Copilot Arena comprises a novel interface for comparing pairs of model outputs, a sampling strategy to reduce experienced latency, and a prompting scheme to enable code completion functionality. Copilot Arena has served over 4.5 million suggestions from 10 models and collected over 11k pairwise judgements. Our results highlight the importance of model evaluations in integrated settings. We find that model rankings from Copilot Arena differ from those of existing evaluations, which we attribute to the unique distribution of data and tasks contained in Copilot Arena. We also identify novel insights into human preferences on code such as an observed consistency in user preference across programming languages yet significant variation in preference due to task category. We open-source Copilot Arena and release data to enable human-centric evaluations and improve understanding of coding assistants.

paragraphs: Copilot Arena evaluates coding models inside developers’ working environments by collecting preferences between pairs of suggestions. This makes the evaluation reflect coding assistance as people encounter it during work. The platform includes an interface for comparing outputs, a sampling strategy that reduces experienced latency, and a prompting scheme for code completion.

This suggests that what developers are trying to accomplish is a meaningful dimension of coding-assistant evaluation. By releasing the platform and data, the authors provide a basis for studying these human preferences and evaluating assistants in integrated development settings.
summary.tldr: Copilot Arena gathers developer preferences during real coding work and reveals model rankings that differ from existing evaluations.

title: Copilot Arena: A Platform for Code LLM Evaluation in the Wild

abstract: Exploration is critical for solving real-world decision-making problems such as scientific discovery, where the objective is to generate truly novel designs rather than mimic existing data distributions. In this work, we address the challenge of leveraging the representational power of generative models for exploration without relying on explicit uncertainty quantification. We introduce a novel framework that casts exploration as entropy maximization over the approximate data manifold implicitly defined by a pre-trained diffusion model. Then, we present a novel principle for exploration based on density estimation, a problem well-known to be challenging in practice. To overcome this issue and render this method truly scalable, we leverage a fundamental connection between the entropy of the density induced by a diffusion model and its score function. Building on this, we develop an algorithm based on mirror descent that solves the exploration problem as sequential fine-tuning of a pre-trained diffusion model. We prove its convergence to the optimal exploratory diffusion model under realistic assumptions by leveraging recent understanding of mirror flows. Finally, we empirically evaluate our approach on both synthetic and high-dimensional text-to-image diffusion, demonstrating promising results.
