paragraphs: A neural network's output may need to satisfy hard linear constraints, rather than merely receive a penalty when it violates them. This paper proposes a differentiable layer that enforces such constraints through an implicit convex optimization problem. The layer seeks a constrained output that remains close to the unconstrained prediction according to a chosen measure of difference.

The authors connect this construction to familiar neural operations. With appropriate constraints and Kullback–Leibler divergence as the objective, the layer reduces to operations including Softmax, Sinkhorn, and tanh. This gives a common optimization perspective on otherwise separately designed layers. Replacing that divergence with Euclidean distance yields a closed-form solution, providing a highly efficient way to enforce the constraints in that variant.

The paper develops two layer variants, BLCLayer and GLCLayer, and corresponding neural solvers built on simple multilayer-perceptron or graph-neural-network-like backbones. Evaluations cover linear programming, partial graph matching, and portfolio allocation; the latter applications also involve discrete constraints. The contribution is a reusable mechanism for making linear feasibility part of the prediction computation, with the choice of distance determining the resulting layer.
summary.tldr: Differentiable convex-optimization layers enforce linear output constraints while connecting familiar neural operations to a common constrained-prediction framework.

title: Design Linear Constrained Neural Layers with Implicit Convex Optimization

abstract: LLMs see the world as a single stream of text, partitioned into roles like or . We trace prompt injection to role confusion: models perceive the source of text from how it sounds, not its labeled role. A command hidden in a webpage hijacks an agent simply because it sounds like text, despite its label. We design role probes to measure how LLMs internally perceive "who is speaking", and find that injected text occupies the same representational space as the trusted role it imitates. We demonstrate this with CoT Forgery, a zero-shot attack that injects fabricated reasoning into user prompts and tool outputs. Models mistake the forgery for their own thoughts, yielding 60% attack success against frontier models with near-zero baselines. Strikingly, the degree of role confusion predicts attack success before a single token is generated. This mechanism generalizes beyond CoT Forgery to standard agent prompt injections, revealing prompt injection as a measurable consequence of role perception. To the model, sounding like a role is indistinguishable from being one.

paragraphs: This paper investigates prompt injection as a failure to distinguish who is speaking. Although model inputs carry role labels, the authors find that models can infer authority from how text sounds. Untrusted content that imitates a trusted source can therefore be represented internally as though it came from that source, creating a route for instructions to cross trust boundaries.

The authors build role probes to measure this internal perception. They also introduce CoT Forgery, a zero-shot attack that places fabricated reasoning in user prompts or tool outputs. In their experiments, models mistake the injected reasoning for their own thoughts, and the attack reaches 60% success against frontier models where baseline success is near zero.

The measured degree of role confusion predicts attack success before the model generates its response. The authors also observe the mechanism in standard agent prompt injections, extending the analysis beyond fabricated reasoning. The contribution is a measurable account of how role imitation can influence behavior, linking internal representations of a text’s source to observed attack outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper links prompt-injection success to measurable role confusion, where models internally treat untrusted text as the trusted source it imitates.

title: Prompt Injection as Role Confusion

abstract: Collaborative perception (CP) significantly extends the sensing range of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs). However, its reliance on data fusion among multiple CAVs makes it inherently vulnerable to adversarial attacks from malicious participants. Existing defenses primarily rely on output-level consensus, assuming that malicious messages manifest as statistical outliers, while suffering from poor adaptability to environmental noise. This makes them vulnerable to stealthy adversarial attacks and prone to high false positive rates. To address this challenge, we shift the defense paradigm from superficial output-level consensus to deeper consistency within the internal feature space. Guided by this principle, we propose Cerberus, a novel defense framework against adversarial attacks in CP systems by leveraging multi-dimensional consistency in the feature space. By quantifying conflicts in topological structure, semantic direction, and energy distribution within feature maps, Cerberus effectively detects adversarial perturbations and provides dynamic protection against adversarial attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that Cerberus significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, effectively limiting the attack success rate to as low as 0.05% while restoring the AP to 0.88.

paragraphs: Connected autonomous vehicles can extend their sensing range by combining information from other vehicles. That collaboration also creates an opening for malicious participants to submit adversarial information. The paper argues that defenses based on agreement among final outputs can miss stealthy attacks and can mistake environmental noise for malicious behavior.

Cerberus instead checks consistency within the internal feature maps used for perception. It measures conflicts along three dimensions: topological structure, semantic direction, and energy distribution. These checks provide several views of whether shared features fit together, giving the defense information beyond whether the final predictions look like statistical outliers. The framework uses those signals to detect perturbations and provide dynamic protection.

The experiments report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art defenses, with attack success rates as low as 0.05% and restored average precision of 0.88. These are reported experimental outcomes rather than a guarantee for every attack. They support the paper’s central proposal that internal feature consistency can be a useful basis for protecting collaborative perception.
summary.tldr: Cerberus detects attacks on collaborative vehicle perception by checking structural, semantic, and energy consistency within shared feature maps.

title: The Latent Guardian: Defending Collaborative Perception via Feature-Level Consistency Verification

abstract: Latent diffusion models have enabled high-quality video synthesis, yet their inference remains costly and time-consuming. As diffusion transformers become increasingly efficient, the latency bottleneck inevitably shifts to VAE decoders. To reduce their latency while maintaining quality, we propose a universal acceleration framework for VAE decoders that preserves full alignment with the original latent distribution. Specifically, we propose (1) an independence-aware channel pruning method to effectively mitigate severe channel redundancy, and (2) a stage-wise dominant operator optimization strategy to address the high inference cost of the widely used causal 3D convolutions in VAE decoders. Based on these innovations, we construct a Flash-VAED family. Moreover, we design a three-phase dynamic distillation framework that efficiently transfers the capabilities of the original VAE decoder to Flash-VAED. Extensive experiments on Wan and LTX-Video VAE decoders demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines in both quality and speed, achieving approximately a 6$\times$ speedup while maintaining the reconstruction performance up to 96.9%. Notably, Flash-VAED accelerates the end-to-end generation pipeline by up to 36% with negligible quality drops on VBench-2.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aoko955/Flash-VAED.

paragraphs: Video diffusion systems must decode compact latent representations into visible frames. As their diffusion transformers become faster, this decoding step can account for more of the remaining latency. Flash-VAED targets the VAE decoder while preserving compatibility with the original latent distribution, allowing acceleration at this stage of the generation pipeline.

The framework combines two changes. Independence-aware channel pruning removes redundancy among channels, while stage-wise optimization targets the operators that dominate computation, including costly causal 3D convolutions. A three-phase dynamic distillation procedure transfers the original decoder's capabilities into the faster replacement. The design therefore couples architectural efficiency with training intended to retain reconstruction quality.

Experiments on Wan and LTX-Video decoders report approximately sixfold decoder speedup while retaining up to 96.9% of reconstruction performance. For the complete generation pipeline, the reported acceleration reaches 36%, with negligible quality drops on VBench-2.0. The distinction matters: accelerating one component does not multiply the speed of the whole system by the same factor, but it can still deliver a substantial overall improvement.
summary.tldr: Flash-VAED accelerates video VAE decoding by about sixfold and improves end-to-end generation speed by up to 36%.

abstract: In this paper we show that many kernel methods can be adapted to deal with indefinite kernels, that is, kernels which are not positive semidefinite. They do not satisfy Mercer's condition and they induce associated functional spaces called Reproducing Kernel Krein Spaces (RKKS), a generalization of Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS). Machine learning in RKKS shares many ``nice'' properties of learning in RKHS, such as orthogonality and projection. However, since the kernels are indefinite, we can no longer minimize the loss, instead we stabilize it. We show a general representer theorem for constrained stabilization and prove generalization bounds by computing the Rademacher averages of the kernel class. We list several examples of indefinite kernels and investigate regularization methods to solve spline interpolation. Some preliminary experiments with indefinite kernels for spline smoothing are reported for truncated spectral factorization, Landweber-Fridman iterations, and MR-II.

paragraphs: This paper extends kernel learning to indefinite kernels, which do not satisfy the positive semidefinite requirement of the usual framework. Their associated function spaces are reproducing kernel Krein spaces, generalizing reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The authors show that many kernel methods can be adapted to this setting while retaining useful geometric properties such as orthogonality and projection.

The change also affects the learning objective. In the proposed treatment, loss stabilization replaces loss minimization. The paper establishes a general representer theorem for constrained stabilization and derives generalization bounds using Rademacher averages of the kernel class. These results provide a theoretical basis for learning with kernels outside the standard positive semidefinite setting.

The authors give examples of indefinite kernels and investigate regularization for spline interpolation. They also report preliminary spline smoothing experiments using truncated spectral factorization, Landweber-Fridman iterations, and MR-II. The contribution combines a broader mathematical framework with initial computational investigations. The experimental claim is explicitly preliminary, while the representer theorem and generalization bounds supply the stated theoretical results.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts kernel learning to indefinite kernels through constrained loss stabilization, with representation theory, generalization bounds, and preliminary spline experiments.

title: Learning with non-positive kernels

abstract: In a data streaming setting, data points are observed one by one. The concepts to be learned from the data points may change infinitely often as the data is streaming. In this paper, we extend the idea of testing exchangeability online (Vovk et al., 2003) to a martingale framework to detect concept changes in time-varying data streams. Two martingale tests are developed to detect concept changes using: (i) martingale values, a direct consequence of the Doob’s Maximal Inequality, and (ii) the martingale difference, justified using the Hoeffding-Azuma Inequality. Under some assumptions, the second test theoretically has a lower probability than the first test of rejecting the null hypothesis, “no concept change in the data stream”, when it is in fact correct. Experiments show that both martingale tests are effective in detecting concept changes in time-varying data streams simulated using two synthetic data sets and three benchmark data sets.

Two martingale tests are developed to detect concept changes using: (i) martingale values, a direct consequence of the Doob’s Maximal Inequality, and (ii) the martingale difference, justified using the Hoeffding-Azuma Inequality. paragraphs: In a data stream, observations arrive sequentially, and the relationship a learner is trying to capture may change repeatedly. This paper develops a framework for detecting those changes as the stream unfolds. It extends an approach based on testing exchangeability online into two tests built around martingales, mathematical processes used to reason about sequential evidence.

The first test uses martingale values and follows from Doob's Maximal Inequality. The second uses martingale differences and is justified through the Hoeffding-Azuma Inequality. These provide two ways to turn accumulating evidence into a decision about whether the stream's underlying concept has changed.

Under certain assumptions, the authors show that the second test has a lower probability of falsely rejecting the hypothesis that no change has occurred. This is a conditional advantage concerning false alarms. Experiments with streams simulated from two synthetic and three benchmark datasets find both tests effective at detecting changes, providing empirical support alongside the theoretical comparison.
summary.tldr: Two martingale tests detect changes in data streams, with a conditional false-alarm advantage for the test based on martingale differences.

title: A martingale framework for concept change detection in time-varying data streams

abstract: The use of Bayesian networks for classification problems has received significant recent attention. Although computationally efficient, the standard maximum likelihood learning method tends to be suboptimal due to the mismatch between its optimization criteria (data likelihood) and the actual goal for classification (label prediction). Recent approaches to optimizing the classification performance during parameter or structure learning show promise, but lack the favorable computational properties of maximum likelihood learning. In this paper we present the Boosted Augmented Naive Bayes (BAN) classifier. We show that a combination of discriminative data-weighting with generative training of intermediate models can yield a computationally efficient method for discriminative parameter learning and structure selection.
originalAbstract: The use of Bayesian networks for classification problems has received significant recent attention. Although computationally efficient, the standard maximum likelihood learning method tends to be suboptimal due to the mismatch between its optimization criteria (data likelihood) and the actual goal for classification (label prediction). Recent approaches to optimizing the classification performance during parameter or structure learning show promise, but lack the favorable computational properties of maximum likelihood learning. In this paper we present the Boosted Augmented Naive Bayes (BAN) classifier. We show that a combination of discriminative data-weighting with generative training of intermediate models can yield a computationally efficient method for discriminative parameter learning and structure selection.

paragraphs: A Bayesian network can be trained to explain observed data well without being trained directly to predict class labels well. The paper identifies this mismatch as a weakness of standard maximum likelihood learning for classification. That learning approach is computationally efficient, but its objective can lead to suboptimal classification.

The proposed Boosted Augmented Naive Bayes classifier combines discriminative data weighting with generative training of intermediate models. The weighting directs learning toward the classification goal, while the intermediate models retain a generative training procedure. This separates the way the data guide learning from the way each intermediate model is fitted.

The authors show that this combination can provide an efficient method for both discriminative parameter learning and structure selection. Those two tasks concern the numerical settings of the classifier and the dependencies represented in its network. The contribution is a way to pursue label prediction more directly while retaining favorable computational properties associated with generative training, addressing the tradeoff identified at the outset.
summary.tldr: Boosted Augmented Naive Bayes combines discriminative data weighting with generative training for efficient classifier learning and structure selection.

title: Efficient discriminative learning of Bayesian network classifier via boosted augmented naive Bayes

abstract: This paper views clusterings as elements of a lattice. Distances between clusterings are analyzed in their relationship to the lattice. From this vantage point, we first give an axiomatic characterization of some criteria for comparing clusterings, including the variation of information and the unadjusted Rand index. Then we study other distances between partitions w.r.t these axioms and prove an impossibility result: there is no “sensible” criterion for comparing clusterings that is simultaneously (1) aligned with the lattice of partitions, (2) convexely additive, and (3) bounded.
originalAbstract: This paper views clusterings as elements of a lattice. Distances between clusterings are analyzed in their relationship to the lattice. From this vantage point, we first give an axiomatic characterization of some criteria for comparing clusterings, including the variation of information and the unadjusted Rand index. Then we study other distances between partitions w.r.t these axioms and prove an impossibility result: there is no “sensible” criterion for comparing clusterings that is simultaneously (1) aligned with the lattice of partitions, (2) convexely additive, and (3) bounded.

paragraphs: Different clustering methods can divide the same objects into different groups, creating a need for criteria that compare those divisions. This paper examines what such criteria mean mathematically. It treats clusterings as elements of a lattice of partitions and studies how distances between clusterings relate to that structure.

From this perspective, the authors give axiomatic characterizations of several comparison criteria, including variation of information and the unadjusted Rand index. An axiomatic characterization explains a criterion through the properties it satisfies. This provides a way to understand and compare measures beyond simply looking at their numerical outputs on particular examples.

The paper then tests other partition distances against these axioms and proves an impossibility result. Within its notion of a sensible comparison criterion, no measure can simultaneously align with the partition lattice, satisfy convex additivity, and remain bounded. The finding identifies a tradeoff among these three requirements: a comparison measure cannot satisfy the entire combination, so choosing among measures also involves choosing which properties to retain.
summary.tldr: An axiomatic analysis of clustering comparisons proves that lattice alignment, convex additivity, and boundedness cannot all hold together.

title: Comparing clusterings: an axiomatic view

abstract: We present a kernel-based algorithm for hierarchical text classiﬁcation where the documents are allowed to belong to more than one category at a time. The classiﬁcation model is a variant of the Maximum Margin Markov Network framework, where the classiﬁcation hierarchy is represented as a Markov tree equipped with an exponential family deﬁned on the edges. We present an eﬃcient optimization algorithm based on incremental conditional gradient ascent in single-example subspaces spanned by the marginal dual variables. Experiments show that the algorithm can feasibly optimize training sets of thousands of examples and classiﬁcation hierarchies consisting of hundreds of nodes. The algorithm’s predictive accuracy is competitive with other recently introduced hierarchical multi-category or multilabel classiﬁcation learning algorithms.

The classiﬁcation model is a variant of the Maximum Margin Markov Network framework, where the classiﬁcation hierarchy is represented as a Markov tree equipped with an exponential family deﬁned on the edges. We present an eﬃcient optimization algorithm based on incremental conditional gradient ascent in single-example subspaces spanned by the marginal dual variables. Experiments show that the algorithm can feasibly optimize training sets of thousands of examples and classiﬁcation hierarchies consisting of hundreds of nodes. The algorithm’s predictive accuracy is competitive with other recently introduced hierarchical multi-category or multilabel classiﬁcation learning algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses text classification when categories form a hierarchy and a document may belong to several categories simultaneously. These two properties make the output more structured than a single class label. The proposed kernel-based model represents the hierarchy explicitly while allowing multiple category assignments for the same document.

The model adapts the Maximum Margin Markov Network framework. It expresses the classification hierarchy as a Markov tree with an exponential-family specification on its edges. To train it efficiently, the authors use incremental conditional gradient ascent in subspaces associated with individual examples and their marginal dual variables, organizing optimization around smaller updates.

Experiments show that training is feasible for datasets containing thousands of examples and hierarchies containing hundreds of nodes. Predictive accuracy is competitive with other recently introduced methods for hierarchical multi-category or multilabel classification. The result supports the practicality of combining a structured representation of category relationships with an optimization procedure that can handle the tested training and hierarchy sizes.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based structured classifier handles multiple labels in category hierarchies with feasible training and competitive predictive accuracy.

abstract: We propose a new rule induction algorithm for solving classification problems via probability estimation. The main advantage of decision rules is their simplicity and good interpretability. While the early approaches to rule induction were based on sequential covering, we follow an approach in which a single decision rule is treated as a base classifier in an ensemble. The ensemble is built by greedily minimizing the negative loglikelihood which results in estimating the class conditional probability distribution. The introduced approach is compared with other decision rule induction algorithms such as SLIPPER, LRI and RuleFit.

paragraphs: The paper develops a rule-learning algorithm for classification through probability estimation. Decision rules are attractive because they are simple and interpretable. The authors build on that advantage by using individual rules as the component classifiers of an ensemble, giving multiple rules a role in the final predictive model.

The ensemble is constructed greedily by minimizing negative log-likelihood. This objective connects the selection of rules to estimating class probabilities: the learning procedure seeks rule combinations that better account for the observed class labels probabilistically. The approach therefore gives rule induction an explicit probability-estimation objective, rather than treating the final output only as a class assignment.

The paper compares the method with SLIPPER, LRI, and RuleFit. Its stated contribution is the construction of a rule ensemble through likelihood optimization, alongside those empirical comparisons. The abstract does not claim a particular comparative winner. The approach matters because it brings interpretable rule components into a common statistical objective, tying how the ensemble is built to the probability estimates it is intended to produce.
summary.tldr: The method builds interpretable rule ensembles by greedily optimizing likelihood to estimate class probabilities.

title: Maximum likelihood rule ensembles

abstract: In apprenticeship learning, the goal is to learn a policy in a Markov decision process that is at least as good as a policy demonstrated by an expert. The difficulty arises in that the MDP's true reward function is assumed to be unknown. We show how to frame apprenticeship learning as a linear programming problem, and show that using an off-the-shelf LP solver to solve this problem results in a substantial improvement in running time over existing methods --- up to two orders of magnitude faster in our experiments. Additionally, our approach produces stationary policies, while all existing methods for apprenticeship learning output policies that are "mixed", i.e. randomized combinations of stationary policies. The technique used is general enough to convert any mixed policy to a stationary policy.

paragraphs: Apprenticeship learning tries to learn a policy that performs at least as well as an expert's demonstrated policy. The setting is a Markov decision process whose true reward function is assumed unknown. That missing reward makes the task different from simply optimizing a known measure of success: expert behavior supplies the reference for learning.

The paper formulates apprenticeship learning as a linear program. This allows the problem to be solved with an off-the-shelf optimization solver. In the reported experiments, the approach substantially reduces running time relative to existing methods, with improvements reaching two orders of magnitude. That figure describes the experimental speedup, rather than a guaranteed speedup for every problem.

The formulation also produces stationary policies. The methods discussed as existing alternatives instead output mixed policies, meaning randomized combinations of stationary policies. The authors additionally present a technique general enough to convert any mixed policy into a stationary one. The work therefore changes both the computational route to apprenticeship learning and the form of the resulting policy.
summary.tldr: A linear-programming formulation produces stationary apprenticeship policies and runs up to two orders of magnitude faster in the reported experiments.

title: Apprenticeship learning using linear programming

abstract: We present new algorithms for inverse optimal control (or inverse reinforcement learning, IRL) within the framework of linearly-solvable MDPs (LMDPs). Unlike most prior IRL algorithms which recover only the control policy of the expert, we recover the policy, the value function and the cost function. This is possible because here the cost and value functions are uniquely defined given the policy. Despite these special properties, we can handle a wide variety of problems such as the grid worlds popular in RL and most of the nonlinear problems arising in robotics and control engineering. Direct comparisons to prior IRL algorithms show that our new algorithms provide more information and are orders of magnitude faster. Indeed our fastest algorithm is the first inverse algorithm which does not require solving the forward problem; instead it performs unconstrained optimization of a convex and easy-to-compute log-likelihood. Our work also sheds light on the recent Maximum Entropy (MaxEntIRL) algorithm, which was defined in terms of density estimation and the corresponding forward problem was left unspecified. We show that MaxEntIRL is inverting an LMDP, using the less efficient of the algorithms derived here. Unlike all prior IRL algorithms which assume pre-existing features, we study feature adaptation and show that such adaptation is essential in continuous state spaces.

paragraphs: Inverse optimal control seeks to learn from an expert's behavior. This paper develops algorithms within linearly-solvable Markov decision processes, recovering the expert's policy, value function, and cost function. This recovery relies on a special property of the framework: the policy uniquely determines the cost and value functions.

The fastest proposed algorithm avoids solving the forward control problem. Instead, it performs unconstrained optimization of a convex log-likelihood that is easy to compute. Direct comparisons report algorithms that provide more information and run orders of magnitude faster than earlier inverse reinforcement learning methods. The authors state that the framework covers grid worlds and most nonlinear problems arising in robotics and control engineering.

The paper also interprets Maximum Entropy inverse reinforcement learning as inverting a linearly-solvable MDP through the less efficient of the derived algorithms. Finally, it studies adapting features instead of assuming they are already supplied, and reports that this adaptation is essential in continuous state spaces. These contributions connect computational efficiency, recoverable information, and representation choice.
summary.tldr: Within linearly-solvable MDPs, inverse control algorithms efficiently recover an expert's policy, value, and cost functions.

title: Inverse Optimal Control with Linearly-Solvable MDPs

abstract: As machine learning algorithms enter applications in industrial settings, there is increased interest in controlling their cpu-time during testing. The cpu-time consists of the running time of the algorithm and the extraction time of the features. The latter can vary drastically when the feature set is diverse. In this paper, we propose an algorithm, the Greedy Miser, that incorporates the feature extraction cost during training to explicitly minimize the cpu-time during testing. The algorithm is a straightforward extension of stage-wise regression and is equally suitable for regression or multi-class classification. Compared to prior work, it is significantly more cost-effective and scales to larger data sets.
originalAbstract: As machine learning algorithms enter applications in industrial settings, there is increased interest in controlling their cpu-time during testing. The cpu-time consists of the running time of the algorithm and the extraction time of the features. The latter can vary drastically when the feature set is diverse. In this paper, we propose an algorithm, the Greedy Miser, that incorporates the feature extraction cost during training to explicitly minimize the cpu-time during testing. The algorithm is a straightforward extension of stage-wise regression and is equally suitable for regression or multi-class classification. Compared to prior work, it is significantly more cost-effective and scales to larger data sets.

paragraphs: The Greedy Miser addresses the cost of making predictions after a model has been trained. Test-time CPU use includes both running the prediction algorithm and extracting its features. The latter can vary substantially across a diverse feature set, so controlling prediction cost requires accounting for more than the model’s own computation.

The proposed algorithm incorporates feature-extraction costs during training, with the explicit aim of minimizing CPU time at test time. It is a straightforward extension of stage-wise regression and applies to both regression and multi-class classification. Its central design choice is to make the eventual cost of obtaining inputs part of how the predictor is learned.

The paper reports that Greedy Miser is significantly more cost-effective than prior work and scales to larger datasets. These findings connect a training-time decision to deployment-time efficiency: the method considers costs before the learned model is used for prediction. The contribution is a broadly applicable learning procedure for settings where feature computation is a meaningful part of the test-time budget.
summary.tldr: Greedy Miser accounts for feature-extraction costs during training to reduce test-time CPU use for regression and multi-class classification.
